key: trilhas seguras
title: TRILHAS SEGURAS
venue: Seminario Internacional de Investigación en Urbanismo
abstract:
The year 2022 was the most violent in Ecuador's history, with an 82% increase in violent deaths compared to 2021. In Quito, crimes rose by 46.3%, affecting the perception of security and quality of life. The lack of adequate infrastructure contributes to exclusion and inequality in access to public space. The mayor of Quito’s plan proposes the creation of gathering spaces to improve security and strengthen urban identity. It suggests that citizen security can be enhanced through the social construction of public space, promoting walkability, social cohesion, and interculturality. The Safe Pathways project aims to reclaim public space to encourage safe pedestrian mobility and improve social well-being. It is based on interventions such as lighting, traffic calming, and urban environment improvements, with a focus on socio-spatial equity, gender, security, sustainability, social capital, and transportation. Territorial analysis identified patterns for implementing these pathways, achieving a 30% reduction in crimes in the intervened areas and an increase in the perception of security. Additionally, infrastructure improvements have encouraged walkability and public space use, strengthening community life.
 O ano de 2022 foi o mais violento da história do Equador, com um aumento de 82% nas mortes violentas em comparação a 2021. Em Quito, os crimes aumentaram 46,3%, afetando a percepção de segurança e qualidade de vida. A falta de infraestrutura adequada contribui para a exclusão e desigualdade no acesso ao espaço público. O plano do prefeito de Quito propõe a criação de espaços de reunião para melhorar a segurança e fortalecer a identidade urbana. Ele sugere que a segurança do cidadão pode ser aprimorada por meio da construção social do espaço público, promovendo a caminhabilidade, a coesão social e a interculturalidade. O projeto Safe Pathways visa recuperar o espaço público para incentivar a mobilidade segura de pedestres e melhorar o bem-estar social. Ele se baseia em intervenções como iluminação, acalmia de tráfego e melhorias no ambiente urbano, com foco na equidade socioespacial, gênero, segurança, sustentabilidade, capital social e transporte. A análise territorial identificou padrões para a implementação dessas vias, alcançando uma redução de 30% nos crimes nas áreas intervencionadas e um aumento na percepção de segurança. Além disso, as melhorias na infraestrutura incentivaram a caminhada e o uso do espaço público, fortalecendo a vida comunitária.

key: transformations of violence and protection in the context of state erosion in syria sweida
title: Transformations of violence and protection in the context of state erosion in Syria: Sweida, July 2025 as a model
venue: International Journal of Historical and Social Studies
abstract: This study examines the events of Sweida in July 2025 as an explanatory case for understanding the transformations of violence in contexts of State erosion. It starts from a research problem represented by the inability of the literature to explain the transition from security violence to identity-based violence, where the explanation is often reduced to the collapse of institutional capacity without analyzing the intermediate mechanisms producing this transition. The research aims to explain how discursive delegitimization, in light of the decline of the state monopoly on violence, contributes to the reshaping of patterns of violence, protection and legitimacy. The analysis is based on a theoretical framework that combines the literature of state failure and spectroscopy theories, with procedural tracing adopting an approach to the analysis of causal mechanisms within the state. The key variables, erosion of institutional capacity, discursive delegitimization, intensity of violence, local protection, and legitimacy of violence, were operated on via observable indicators to ensure inference accuracy. The research is based on procedural tracing to analyze the causal mechanism within a single case. The study also systematically contributes to the employment of procedural tracing in the analysis of a contemporary conflict. The results show that the violence arose not only from local clashes, but was preceded by a rhetorical delegitimization process that redefined the Druze community within a threatening framework, contributing to the creation of a justifying environment for targeting. With the intervention of the state in a multi-actor environment, the monopoly of violence eroded and escalated, turning into identity-based violence characterized by targeting civilians and a high intensity of violations. This has led to a de facto transfer of protection functions to local actors, as the Druze community has reproduced autonomous security arrangements, in parallel with a shift in the legitimacy of violence towards a functional framework based on protection rather than a legal framework. The scientific novelty consists in showing that discourse does not act as a concomitant factor, but as a preliminary causal mechanism in the production of violence, in identifying the intensity of violence as an intermediate variable that accelerates the shift towards identity-based targeting, in addition to highlighting the role of local communities as actors reshaping protection in contexts of State erosion. The study contributes to providing an integrated causal model linking discourse, violence and legitimacy within an analytical sequence applicable to similar situations. The results indicate that late interventions to restore institutional control do not prevent the transfer of protection to the local level, and ignoring the rhetorical dimensions in the early stages contributes to accelerating the course of escalation,highlighting the importance of analyzing the discourse as part of the dynamics of violence and not as a secondary factor

key: social vulnerability and degrading labor analogous to slavery an analysis of the individua
title: SOCIAL VULNERABILITY AND DEGRADING LABOR ANALOGOUS TO SLAVERY: AN ANALYSIS OF THE INDIVIDUAL AND WORKER CONDITIONS
abstract: The exploitation of labor through conditions analogous to slavery represents one of the harshest violations of human rights and the fundamental principle of human dignity. Among these, the one manifested through the subjection of workers to degrading conditions stands out. This article aims to identify and analyze the social vulnerability conditions of rescued workers and the structural characteristics that define the degrading work environment in Brazil, seeking to provide theoretical and statistical subsidies for the improvement of repression and eradication actions of this practice. To achieve this goal, a basic methodology of a descriptive-explanatory nature was adopted, substantiated by bibliographic and documentary research with a mixed approach. The theoretical framework was based on the national legal doctrine and the constitutional order, while the empirical support was based on the analysis of data from the Social Vulnerability Atlas (Ipea), the 2022 Census (IBGE), the Smartlab platform (MPT), and the results of the recent Rescue Operation VI (MTE, 2026). The research results indicate that the form of degrading work is the most frequent in the country, corresponding to 94.90% of fiscal findings. It was revealed that the socio-economic profile of the rescued victims—markedly young, male, brown-skinned, with low schooling, and linked to rural agribusiness activities—is directly determined by historical and structural markers of social vulnerability outside the labor environment, concentrated in an undesirable manner in urban infrastructure and human capital deficits. Furthermore, it was evidenced that degrading environments are characterized by disrespect for the minimum civilized standard, with precarious accommodation, lack of sanitary facilities, and lack of access to potable water. It is concluded that the profile of life of the individual in their regions of origin acts as the determining factor for their recruitment by exploitation networks. It is imperative to improve cooperative public policies and provide information to break the process of acculturation and normalization of degradation, ensuring the consolidation of the fundamental objectives of the Republic.

key: beyond the polls the economic consequences of electoral violence in nasarawa state nigeria
title: BEYOND THE POLLS: THE ECONOMIC CONSEQUENCES OF ELECTORAL VIOLENCE IN NASARAWA STATE, NIGERIA
venue: Journal of Humanities and Social Science
abstract: This study examines the economic consequences of electoral violence in Nasarawa State, Nigeria, where recurring election-related conflict has often been discussed mainly in security and political terms rather than as a development problem. The research asks how electoral violence affects local economic activities and long-term development prospects. It adopts a convergent parallel mixed-methods design, combining a survey of 400 respondents in Karu, Lafia, and Akwanga LGAs with 15 key informant interviews and 6 focus group discussions, supported by secondary data and analysed using descriptive statistics, chi-square tests, ordinal logistic regression, and thematic content analysis. The findings show that 72.2% of respondents experienced electoral violence between 2015 and 2023, with political thugs identified as major perpetrators. Electoral violence was strongly associated with market closure and reduced economic recovery, while more than 60% of affected households reported financial losses above ₦50,000. Qualitative evidence further showed that violence disrupted trade, farming, supply chains, and investment confidence, while elite manipulation operated indirectly by intensifying conflict. The study concludes that electoral violence functions as a persistent economic shock that deepens vulnerability and reinforces a conflict trap. It recommends integrating economic resilience into electoral security planning, strengthening post-conflict recovery measures, and reducing the incentives for politically sponsored violence.

key: the criminalization of venezuelan immigration in the united states
title: The Criminalization of Venezuelan Immigration in the United States
abstract: The objective of this paper is to analyze the new forms of legal criminalization of immigration implemented by the government of Donald Trump at the beginning of his second term, focused on Venezuelan immigrants. Based on the newspaper review, as well as documents and com-muniqués from the U.S. government, the policies and implications of deporting Venezuelan immigrants to Guantánamo and El Salvador are analyzed. This paper finds an advance of au-thoritarianism as a model for managing migration that could lead to an era of flagrant violations of the human rights of Venezuelan immigrants and other nationalities.

title: The Impact of Fundamentalist Terrorism on School Enrolment: Evidence from North-Western Pakistan, 2004-2016

key: gang crackdowns
title: Gang Crackdowns
abstract: What are the consequences of restoring state authority in territories governed by criminal organizations? Combining household surveys and administrative records with detailed maps of former gang-controlled areas, we study how El Salvador’s 2022 State of Exception, which ended two decades of gang territorial control, reshaped Salvadoran society. We find that the removal of gang control integrated previously segmented labor markets, improving mobility, employment outcomes, household income, and financial inclusion. Areas with greater pre-2022 gang exposure also experienced larger increases in business formation and property investment. However, the legacy of criminal governance persists through residence-based discrimination: employers remain less willing to hire otherwise identical applicants from former gang-controlled neighborhoods. Finally, although overall support for the crackdowns remains high, individuals who witnessed police abuse report substantially greater distrust of the police and the national government, suggesting that abuses of state authority may undermine the political sustainability of tough-on-crime policies.

key: state of emergency
title: State of Emergency
abstract: Nayib Bukele’s presidency has transformed El Salvador into an electoral autocracy by systematically dismantling democratic institutions, subverting the constitution, and consolidating power under his New Ideas party. In response, grassroots collectives of victims’ families engage in quiet, poignant acts of defiance, preserving memory and demanding accountability within a highly restrictive civic space.

key: the need for revisiting the law of defamation in the cyber age an analysis of the conflict
title: The Need for Revisiting the Law of Defamation in the Cyber Age: An Analysis of the Conflicts, Challenges, and Opportunities in Sri Lankan Law
abstract: Abstract In the digital age, the unique characteristics of internet-based communications and online publications can cause unpredictable and irrevocable damage to a person’s reputation at minimal cost. Therefore, revisiting the law of defamation in Sri Lanka to examine its adequacy in addressing cyber defamation is important to maintain a balance between the right to freedom of expression and the right to reputation. The main objective of this article is to assess the adequacy and effectiveness of Sri Lankan law in addressing online defamation disputes. In doing so, this article explores the unique challenges associated with this area, as well as necessary legal reforms, drawing on developments in English and South African law.

key: security and socio spatial confi gurations in informal settlements of buenos aires argenti
title: Security and Socio-Spatial Confi gurations in Informal Settlements of Buenos Aires, Argentina
abstract:
This article explores how violence, security measures, and socio-spatial arrangements interact in three informal settlements in Buenos Aires, Argentina. Based on interviews and fieldwork (June 2024–April 2025), it shows how overlapping forms of violence fragment space, generate
 fear, and shape residents’ coping strategies. While community organizations provide important sites of support and cohesion, they also reflect a partial and uneven compensation for structural deficiencies. Overall, the findings suggest that violence, policing, and community action coproduce
 a contested landscape of both insecurity and care in the informal settlements of the Argentinian capital.

key: constitutions under pressure
title: Constitutions under Pressure
abstract: In an era marked by a global retreat from democracy, this book investigates ‘constitutional capture’, defined as the systematic and intentional weakening of constitutional checks and balances, to explain how constitutional change facilitates autocratization. Through innovative comparison of Poland, Hungary, Turkey, and Egypt, it details how incumbents subvert judicial independence to consolidate power. This subjugated judiciary then becomes a key facilitator, dismantling executive constraints and suppressing fundamental rights, from LGBTQ+ rights in Poland to collective ownership of national soil in Egypt, illuminating the mutually reinforcing relationship between constitutional manipulation and autocratization.

key: laundering and evasion in response to antislavery policies in brazil s cattle sector
title: Laundering and evasion in response to antislavery policies in Brazil's cattle sector.
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
abstract: Modern slavery remains pervasive across many economic sectors. Progress toward eradicating it has been partially hindered by a lack of tested, comprehensive policy responses. Using data on millions of cattle transactions in Brazil, we evaluated how ranchers changed their selling behavior after being added to the "Dirty List," a public registry that names and shames employers found to use modern slavery. Dirty Listed ranchers significantly reduced direct sales to slaughterhouses that signed sustainable supply chain commitments but evaded sanctions by laundering cattle through compliant intermediaries or selling to nonsignatory slaughterhouses. These responses weakened the financial cost of listing to ranchers, and likely allowed beef and leather linked to modern slave labor to enter international supply chains. Our findings highlight the limits of downstream enforcement and underscore the need to monitor upstream suppliers to ensure slavery-free supply chains.

key: electronic incitement and its repercussions on the family
title: Electronic incitement and its repercussions on the family
venue: AL-Qadisiya Journal For Law and Political Sciences
abstract: : This study examines the concept of electronic enticement (takhbib), defined as corrupting one spouse against the other through modern communication technologies. It analyzes its linguistic, juristic, and legal definitions, as well as its various forms affecting either spouse. The research affirms its prohibition in Islamic law, considering it a grave sin due to its destructive impact on family stability and social cohesion. It also evaluates the position of the Iraqi legislator in Personal Status Law No. 188 of 1959 and Penal Code No. 111 of 1969, comparing it with Jordanian legislation, and proposes explicit legal provisions criminalizing such acts to safeguard marital bonds.

key: force disguised as law enforcement in venezuela the 2026 capture of maduro hybrid justific
title: Force disguised as law enforcement in Venezuela: The 2026 capture of Maduro, hybrid justification and the erosion of article 2(4) of the UN charter
venue: Military Studies: Journal for Strategy, Technology and Defense Sciences
abstract:
On 3 January 2026, United States forces struck targets in and around Caracas, seized
Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores, and flew them to New York to
stand trial on narco-terrorism charges. Washington presented the raid not as a use of force against
Venezuela but as a law enforcement operation facilitated by the military. This article examines
two linked questions: whether that framing has any footing in the jus ad bellum, and whether the
reaction of other states was strong enough to protect the prohibition of force laid down in Article
2(4) of the UN Charter. Doctrinal analysis of the five justificatory strands advanced by the United
States (law enforcement, implicit self-defence, non-recognition of Maduro, the Noriega analogy
and the narco-terrorism designation) shows that none satisfies a recognised exception and that
their combination functions to avoid any single, testable legal claim. The original contribution of
the article is the Normative Response Index (NRI), a five-point coding scale (from -2, explicit
legal condemnation, to +2, explicit endorsement) applied to all 27 states that addressed the Se-
curity Council at its 10085th meeting on 5 January 2026. The mean NRI is -1.00 (SD = 1.18);
only 11 of 27 states (40.7%) characterised the operation as unlawful, 13 (48.1%) voiced concern
or equivocated, and 3 (11.1%) welcomed it. No Western European and Others Group speaker
described the operation as illegal. Sensitivity analysis keeps the mean between -0.89 and -1.11
under every alternative coding, which places the case in the category of contested rejection rather
than clear rejection. Compared with Panama in 1989, when the General Assembly condemned
the intervention by 75 votes to 20, the institutional response in 2026 stopped at debate. The
findings indicate that the discursive validity of Article 2(4) survives, but its institutional enforce-
ment layer has thinned, and that hybrid justification exploits precisely this gap.

key: rethinking banditry and terrorist in nigerias north west dynamic justice and security
title: Rethinking Banditry and Terrorist in Nigeria’s North West: Dynamic, Justice, and Security
venue: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF SOCIAL SCIENCES AND MANAGEMENT RESEARCH
abstract:
Banditry and terrorism have emerged as severe and persistent security challenges in
Nigeria’s North-West region, threatening lives, livelihoods, and national stability. This study
examines the dynamics of banditry and terrorism in the North-West, with particular attention
to their historical roots, patterns of occurrence, and the relevance of a dynamic justice and
security framework in addressing the menace. Anchored on Robert Merton’s Strain Theory
(1938), the study explains how socio-economic deprivation, poverty, unemployment,
marginalization, and weak governance structures create conditions that push vulnerable
youths toward banditry and terrorist-related activities. A descriptive research design was
adopted, relying on secondary data from online reports, scholarly literature, and security
incident records. The study reveals that banditry has evolved from localized farmer–herder
conflicts into organized criminal networks engaging in kidnapping, mass killings, cattle
rustling, highway attacks, and assaults on schools and places of worship across states such
as Zamfara, Katsina, Kaduna, Sokoto, Kano, Kebbi, and Jigawa. Findings further show that
the persistence of these crimes is linked to the inadequacy of Nigeria’s conventional justice
system, characterized by slow trials, weak enforcement, limited rural policing, and low public
trust. The study concludes that addressing banditry and terrorism in the North-West requires
more than combatant military responses. It recommends the adoption of a dynamic justice
system that integrates effective law enforcement, judicial reform, community collaboration,
negotiation mechanisms, socio-economic interventions, public sensitization, and the
deployment of modern security technologies. Such approaches are essential for restoring
public confidence, reducing insecurity, and promoting lasting peace and development in the
region.

key: preventing and addressing violence and harassment in the informal economy and through form
title: Preventing and addressing violence and harassment in the informal economy and through formalization
abstract: This brief examines why workers in the informal economy can face heightened risks of violence and harassment, including gender-based violence and harassment. It explores the structural drivers of vulnerability and outlines how international labour standards provide a framework for extending protection to all workers, regardless of their formal status.

key: layered catastrophe and temporal violence a study of disaster and vulnerability in vanni
title: Layered Catastrophe and Temporal Violence: A Study of Disaster and Vulnerability in Vanni
venue: Sanglap: Journal of Literary and Cultural Inquiry
abstract: Disasters have traditionally been understood as sudden, catastrophic events that rupture the normal flow of life; however, recent developments in disaster studies have challenged this event-based model by foregrounding the structural conditions that gradually produce vulnerability over time. Anthony Oliver-Smith defines “a disaster as a process/event involving the combination of a potentially destructive agent(s) from the natural and/or technological environment and a population in a socially and technologically produced condition of vulnerability” (303). This shift in perspective enables a more nuanced understanding of catastrophe as a process rather than an isolated event, one that unfolds across time and space and disproportionately affects already marginalized populations.

key: employing counterterrorism in international politics iraq as a case study
title: Employing Counterterrorism in International Politics: Iraq as a Case Study
venue: AL-Qadisiya Journal For Law and Political Sciences
abstract: : The phenomenon of terrorism, as a concept, its causes, motives, and methods of confronting it, is of paramount importance to all those concerned with local, regional, and international security, as well as with economic, educational, security, and social systems at all levels. The experience of confronting terrorism in Iraq and the Middle East has yielded new data, leading to numerous changes in the concept of terrorism, its creation, and its exploitation, and has generated new approaches to confronting and combating it. Terrorism is

key: the impact of the sudanese civil war on african stability
title: The Impact of the Sudanese Civil War on African Stability
venue: International journal of research and innovation in social science
abstract: The protracted civil war in Sudan has triggered intertwined political, security, and humanitarian crises that erode state integrity and pose significant risks to regional stability in Africa. This article examines the repercussions of the Sudanese civil war on African stability across three interlinked dimensions: regional security, socio-economic robustness, and the performance of regional and international mechanisms for conflict management. Employing a qualitative descriptive method that draws on literature reviews, policy papers, and reports issued by regional and international organizations, the study identifies a range of spillover effects, including refugee movements, cross-border arms trafficking, and the rise of transnational armed actors. The findings indicate that the conflict in Sudan undermines regional security architectures, overloads the capacities of neighboring states, disrupts trade networks and development initiatives, and challenges the credibility of institutions such as the African Union and IGAD in mediating and enforcing peace settlements. The article contends that, in the absence of coherent and coordinated regional strategies, the Sudanese civil war may entrench pockets of chronic instability that spread to other parts of the continent. Consequently, reinforcing preventive diplomacy, inclusive peace processes, and comprehensive post-conflict reconstruction is essential for preserving Africa’s long-term regional stability.

key: partition refugees in delhi a story of resilience against the odds
title: Partition Refugees in Delhi: A Story of Resilience Against the odds
abstract: This paper tries to look at the ways in which the life of some of the partition refugees unfolded over the years, stories which are an enduring testament to human grit and resilience. Beginning from real life stories of destitute women, it moves on to discuss novel ways which men devised to eke out a living in an unfamiliar land and in often hostile conditions. It also goes on to discuss how certain developments in the 1970s and 1980s, ultimately led to betterment of lives of these unfortunate victims of partition. It also briefly discusses how some of these refugees went on to become one of the most successful entrepreneurs in their chosen fields.

key: analise da jurisprudencia da adpf 635 a adpf das favelas
title: ANÁLISE DA JURISPRUDÊNCIA DA ADPF 635, A ADPF DAS FAVELAS
venue: Revista Ibero-Americana de Humanidades, Ciências e Educação
abstract: The Allegation of Non-Compliance with a Fundamental Precept number 635 was confirmed as a relevant instrument of the concentrated control of constitutionality applied to public security policies, especially with regard to the protection of fundamental rights and guarantees. However, the delay in the trial and the long validity of the precautionary measures ended up expanding, in an atypical way, the intervention of the Judiciary in matters related to Public Security, stressing the principle of separation of powers. Although it has contributed to reducing police lethality, the prolonged suspension of regular operations has ended up producing zones of state absence, favoring the territorial expansion of criminal organizations and compromising the constitutional duty to protect public security. The article demonstrates, from a legal-constitutional perspective, that judicial decisions of a structural nature can produce unwanted side effects when they affect complex public policies, revealing the need for greater institutional balance in the formulation of measures that impact the state presence in vulnerable territories.

key: searching for peace in israel
title: Searching for Peace in Israel
abstract: The turn to violence and the use of force cannot bring about a lasting peace between Israelis and Palestinians. Repeated cycles of war have failed to produce durable political outcomes, whereas strategies of conflict management have brought about mistrust and insecurity. Hence, a better and sustainable future requires a return to diplomatic efforts, including mutual recognition and a negotiated two-state framework that should evolve into a confederation blueprint, embedded within broader regional cooperation.

key: the historian is the keeper of memory in a time of crises and challenges
title: THE HISTORIAN IS THE KEEPER OF MEMORY IN A TIME OF CRISES AND CHALLENGES
venue: International Journal of Historical and Social Studies
abstract: Crises and challenges pose a significant threat to society. The collapse of security and stability resulting from wars and security crises leads to a loss of personal and institutional security, generating widespread violence and mass displacement. Furthermore, economic crises or disasters cause unemployment, poverty, the collapse of production and exchange networks, the depletion of national reserves, and a sharp economic downturn. In addition, serious crises and challenges lead to the fragility, weakness, and absence of essential services such as health and education, and contribute to the collapse of infrastructure. Poverty is perhaps one of the most serious challenges stemming from crises and challenges, as it dismantles society and contributes to increased tensions between social groups, the spread of tribalism or sectarianism, and social violence.

key: migrationsstrafrecht
title: Migrationsstrafrecht
abstract: This work is the first comprehensive study of the German criminal law on migration from a legal-scholarly perspective. It offers a critical analysis of the historical development, current structure, and social implications of the criminalization of migration brought about by the criminal provisions of the Residence Act, the Asylum Act, the Freedom of Movement Act, and the Nationality Act. The central question is to what extent the use of criminal law to enforce the rules of the administrative migration law can be justified , and which constitutional, EU, and international legal limits constrain such use. In addition, the author offers a comprehensive proposal for legislative reform, giving new impulses for the legal policy debate. This title is also available as Open Access.

key: the response to a finding of unfitness in international criminal law lessons from the kabu
title: The response to a finding of unfitness in international criminal law: Lessons from the Kabuga case.
venue: International Journal of Law and Psychiatry
abstract: The case of Félicien Kabuga before the International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals has cast light on the international criminal law framework governing situations in which an accused is found unfit to stand trial. The Trial Chamber's decision to institute an 'alternative finding procedure' in lieu of a criminal trial-later quashed by the Appeals Chamber as incompatible with the Mechanism's Statute-raised fundamental questions about how international courts should respond when an accused cannot meaningfully participate in their own trial, including whether a tribunal should relinquish or retain control over the case. The case also offered a timely opportunity, which the court ultimately did not take, to revisit applicable principles in light of evolving standards under the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities.

key: the corrosive nexus state capture discriminatory resource allocation and the erosion of mi
title: The Corrosive Nexus: State Capture, Discriminatory Resource Allocation, and the Erosion of Minority Rights
venue: Rule of Law and Anti-Corruption Center Journal
abstract: The corrosive nexus between institutionalized corruption, i.e., state capture and elite compacts, and the disproportionate decay of human rights in marginalized ethnic, religious, and indigenous minority groups is the focus of research in this article. We posit that the rule of law, instead of being a guarantor of equal protection, is often transformed into an instrument of unequal protection by sophisticated methods of institutional corruption to facilitate discriminatory distribution of resources, with a specific focus on infrastructure, land rights, and public finance. By looking at how procedural laws operate, the study shows that legal systems often end up protecting this kind of institutional theft, making repression look perfectly legal. To stop this, we need to completely shift our approach. Anti-corruption strategies must explicitly focus on human rights, taking direct aim at compromised legal frameworks and empowering civil society movements led by minorities. There are three primary objectives of the research: (1) tracing the legal and political tools used by state-captured elites to legalize de facto discrimination against minorities by corrupted law; (2) analyzing the impacts of procurement corruption and corrupt natural resource management on the social and economic rights (e.g., health, housing, education) of targeted minority groups; and (3) offering practical legal and policy solutions grounded in international human rights law to dismantle frameworks that keep minorities excluded. The research adopts an interdisciplinary legal-political economy (LPE) methodology, combining legal examination of anti-corruption laws and international human rights conventions with socio-economic data analysis, through the application of a strict triangulation method on three comparative case studies in infrastructure development, public health procurement, and judicial remediation failure. The evidence points to a clear trend. In areas with heavy state capture, elites do not just siphon off resources for personal wealth; they use this theft to tighten their grip on power by starving minority groups of justice and development. Rule of law institutions end up acting as a shield for this behavior, giving oppression a legal cover. Ultimately, corruption’s biggest threat isn’t just lost money, it is how it turns the legal system into a weapon for discrimination. Because of this, any real attempt to fight corruption must put human rights first, specifically working to tear down laws that institutionalize exclusion.

key: winning the double war urbicide informality and reconstruction in syrian cities after 2011
title: Winning the double war: Urbicide, informality, and reconstruction in Syrian cities after 2011
abstract: Syrian cities experienced extensive destruction during the 2011–2024 conflict, much of it inflicted by the Assad regime. Yet destruction did not end with the cessation of local hostilities; it persisted in formerly opposition-controlled enclaves through organized looting and mass municipal demolitions. This article asks why destruction was disproportionately concentrated in informal and formerly opposition-controlled areas, and especially at their intersection. It argues that these patterns were intentional, serving the regime’s double war: a military war to defeat the armed opposition, and an urban-economic war to incorporate undesirable urban forms into real-estate accumulation. Combining spatial autocorrelation analysis with Bayesian negative binomial and penalized logistic models across Damascus, Aleppo, and Homs, the study shows that destruction was spatially structured, concentrating where informality and opposition-control intersect, which jointly predict destruction beyond military necessity. This logic persisted across wartime, post-capture, and post-conflict periods. Urbicide thus operates as a dual-purpose modality for authoritarian urbanism: a wartime tactic and a mechanism of post-conflict socioeconomic reordering.

key: anti corruption confiscation in international treaties and anglo american and russian lega
title: Anti-Corruption Confiscation in International Treaties and Anglo-American and Russian Legal Systems
abstract: This article examines anti-corruption confiscation (Article 235(2)(8) of the Civil Code of the Russian Federation) from a comparative perspective. It considers the regulation and enforcement of this institution under international treaties and in common-law jurisdictions (the United States, the United Kingdom, Ireland, and Australia). The article presents two models of anti-corruption confiscation — in rem and in personam — and analyzes their regulation, advantages, and disadvantages. Particular attention is paid to doctrinal and case-law approaches to determining the legal nature of anti-corruption confiscation within the Russian legal system.

key: to hell or to connacht expropriation inequality and local legacies of settler colonialism
title: “To Hell or to Connacht”: Expropriation, Inequality, and Local Legacies of Settler Colonialism
abstract: Violent upheavals in landownership following conquest often change not only the concentration of land across individuals, but also the inequality of its distribution between groups. We argue that variation in landowners’ group identity has important implications for the provision of local public goods. We test this claim by studying the aftermath of the Cromwellian Settlement in seventeenth-century Ireland. Leveraging the lottery-based allocation of expropriated Catholic land to distinct groups of English Protestants, we find significant local variation in the extent of Protestant landownership. Drawing on rich original data, we find fewer local public goods in the long run in areas with more Protestant elites, with the largest reductions in goods that were either directly elite-funded or disproportionately benefited the Catholic majority. The results illustrate how conquest reshapes not just institutions but also long-run local inequalities, and highlight the distinct consequences of between-group inequality for the provision of public goods.

key: irans criminal policy toward customs crimes and offenses
title: Iran’s Criminal Policy Toward Customs Crimes and Offenses
venue: The Encyclopedia of Comparative Jurisprudence and Law
abstract: This article examines Iran’s criminal policy regarding customs crimes and offenses. The country’s criminal policies in this area have undergone significant transformations over the years, influenced by economic, social, and international developments. One of the main objectives of this study is to analyze the existing laws in this field, including the Law on Combating Smuggling of Goods and Foreign Exchange (2013) and the Customs Affairs Law (2011), as well as to identify their implementation challenges and obstacles. Using a library-based and descriptive–analytical method, this study analyzes the relevant laws and policies aimed at combating goods smuggling and customs violations, and ultimately assesses the performance of the institutions involved in this domain. The findings indicate that, despite the enactment of multiple laws and legal reforms intended to counter smuggling and customs offenses, significant challenges persist in enforcement and supervision. These challenges primarily arise from the lack of coordination among various institutions, the ambiguity in distinguishing between customs violations and crimes, and the administrative complexities associated with precise implementation of the law. Moreover, the imposition of severe penalties without adequate consideration of the specific characteristics of each offense or crime has, in some cases, resulted in adverse economic and social consequences. Finally, this article emphasizes the necessity of legislative and administrative reforms to enhance the efficiency of Iran’s criminal policy in addressing customs-related crimes.

key: los carteles son la ley organized crime criminal governance and illicit opportunities in m
title: “Los carteles son la ley”: Organized crime, criminal governance, and illicit opportunities in Mexico

key: exploitation for forced labour qualification issues in lithuanian criminal law
title: EXPLOITATION FOR FORCED LABOUR: QUALIFICATION ISSUES IN LITHUANIAN CRIMINAL LAW
abstract: Negative statistical data and the resulting trends indicate an exclusively worsening situation regarding the phenomenon of forced labor and its proliferation globally, as well as a considerably troubling situation in Lithuania. Moreover, the causality of forced labor, linked to contemporary realities - such as the migration of daily life into the digital sphere or even the war in Ukraine - further substantiates the trends of the consistent spread of this negative phenomenon. This demonstrates the relevance of the topic and underscores the need to continue research into the challenges surrounding the regulation and application of criminal liability for exploitation for forced labor in Lithuanian law. The research results of this article aim not only to provide new knowledge about exploitation for forced labor (services) as a criminal offense, but also to enable a better understanding of the newly emerging weaknesses in its legal elements, as well as the new challenges that arise when incriminating such acts in practice. Therefore, the purpose of the research is to analyze the problems of qualifying exploitation for forced labor (services) as a criminal offense in Lithuanian criminal law, thereby aiming to better understand the legal construction of this offense and identify the weaknesses in its constituent elements. Consequently, the tasks of the research are based on three main areas of this analysis: namely, the assessment of the objective and subjective elements of exploitation for forced labor (services), as well as the evaluation of additional qualifying features in Lithuanian criminal law. The article utilizes research methods such as comparative analysis, document analysis, systematic analysis, and generalization methods. The analysis in this article substantiated the difficulties arising in the assessment of certain objective and subjective elements of exploitation for forced labor (services) as a criminal offense, and provided specific solutions related to the proper evaluation of the modus operandi, the determination of guilt, and additional qualifying features, such as forcing someone to work under conditions of slavery or other inhuman conditions.

key: cost of unsustainable post conflict recovery in aceh
title: Cost of Unsustainable Post-Conflict Recovery in Aceh
abstract: Post-conflict Aceh presents one of the clearest development paradoxes in Southeast Asian history. Despite receiving one of the largest concentrations of post-conflict resources in the region, including more than seven billion US dollars in international reconstruction support and hundreds of trillions of rupiah through Special Autonomy funds since 2008, the province's poverty rate stood at 12.33 percent in March 2025, nearly four percentage points above the national average (BPS, 2025a). This article asks why this happened. Using qualitative document analysis, it examines the foundational legal instruments, institutional reports, and statistical data that governed Aceh's reconstruction from 2005 onward. The analysis integrates three frameworks: Roland Paris's Institutionalization Before Liberalization (IBL) as the primary theoretical lens, Roger Mac Ginty's Hybrid Peace as the secondary lens, and the UN-Habitat Sustainable Reconstruction Framework (SRF) as the operational analytical tool. The findings show that Aceh's reconstruction failed not because resources were absent but because they arrived before the institutional conditions required to manage them productively were built. Governance systems, policy architecture, community participation mechanisms, and service delivery models were all structurally insufficient at the moment fiscal liberalisation occurred. This enabled hybridisation dynamics in which international frameworks and autonomy funds were absorbed into local patron-client networks rather than directed toward development. The article concludes that sustainable post-conflict development requires the prior establishment of enabling conditions, and that transferring resources without those foundations produces not development but new forms of structural vulnerability.

key: digging a national security threat unpacking the link between illegal mining and ghanas vu
title: Digging a National Security Threat: Unpacking the Link Between Illegal Mining and Ghana’s Vulnerability to Terrorism
abstract: Ghana has waged a prolonged battle against illegal mining, which is wreaking havoc on the environment and causing severe socio-economic, health and security issues. This paper assesses the link between illegal small-scale mining and the potential for terrorism in Ghana, highlighting potential pathways that may contribute to terrorism. It draws on Resource Conflict Theory and adopts a qualitative research approach. The study samples 33 interviewees, including small-scale miners, academics and security experts. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews and documentary analysis. The data were analysed thematically. The findings reveal three principal pathways through which illegal mining increases Ghana’s vulnerability to terrorism: (a) the politico-mining complex; (b) the proliferation and circulation of small arms within illegal mining communities and (c) the involvement of foreign actors in illegal mining. The paper argues that Ghana’s counterterrorism strategy should move beyond its predominant focus on external threats from the Sahel to incorporate domestic governance failures associated with illegal mining. It concludes that strengthening governance, addressing political complicity, improving border management and reforming the regulation of artisanal mining are essential for reducing Ghana’s long-term vulnerability to terrorism and enhancing national security.

key: reimagining justice beyond borders bridging asean s reintegration gaps in transnational co
title: Reimagining justice beyond borders: Bridging ASEAN's reintegration gaps in transnational conditional release
abstract: Foreign national prisoners and people under supervision (FNPs) are an increasingly salient feature of Southeast Asian prison populations, yet the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) lacks an operational framework for transferring or recognizing post-release community supervision. In practice, many FNPs are deported at sentence completion with little structured aftercare, producing a reintegration cliff and avoidable public safety risk. Drawing on socio-legal comparative analysis and aggregated administrative data, this article proposes the BRIDGES model: a phased, rights-based blueprint centred on standardized social inquiry reporting (Litmas – Penelitian Kemasyarakatan), bilateral supervision protocols and secure digital information-sharing. Lessons from EU and Trans-Tasman arrangements are adapted for ASEAN's institutional and cultural context.

key: violence in islamic boarding schools an evaluation and the urgency of law amendment
title: Violence in Islamic Boarding Schools: An Evaluation and the Urgency of Law Amendment
abstract: The phenomenon of violence in pesantren is a social problem that has been going on for a long time. Thuggery in pesantren includes acts of violence, intimidation, extortion, and other forms of delinquency committed by a group of students against other students. This study aims to determine the causes of violence in boarding schools and efforts to prevent such violence from recurring. Using a qualitative approach and a comprehensive literature review, this research draws on primary legal materials in the form of relevant laws and regulations, secondary legal materials in the form of journal articles, and other materials such as news from the mass media and interviews. This research reveals that gangsterism in pesantren has long historical roots, related to the strong culture of seniority in pesantren. In addition, factors such as hierarchy and seniority, the closed attitude of pesantren, and a lack of supervision also contribute to the growth of violence. This research highlights the importance of amending the boarding school law by emphasizing rules on the prohibition of violence in the boarding school environment, and a whistleblowing system that requires supervision from all relevant parties. Reform of the education system in boarding schools also needs to be designed inclusively to instill an attitude of tolerance and respect for differences.

key: dry spells work and gendered violence in mexico
title: Dry spells, work, and gendered violence in Mexico
abstract: Every year, 245 million women are victims of intimate partner violence (IPV). Climate change is hypothesized to exacerbate this figure through its disruptive impact on household livelihoods, among other channels. In this paper, we use three IPV data sources to examine the effect of rainfall shocks in Mexico. We find robust evidence of increases in all measures of IPV in response to local precipitation deficits: as unanticipated exposure to days without rain in the previous month rises, IPV-related injuries recorded in the public health system, police reports, and IPV-related 911 calls all increase. The effects are stronger in regions highly dependent on agriculture, particularly when the shock occurs during the growing season. Linking our results to household labour-supply data, we show that rainfall shocks trigger a gendered labour reallocation: women working in agriculture withdraw hours with no offsetting diversification into other income sources, while men partially shift into off-farm work. Two channels follow: the erosion of women’s own economic contribution weakens their bargaining position, and their reduced time outside the home raises exposure to an abusive partner.

key: un and eu counter terrorism response mechanism
title: UN and EU Counter-Terrorism Response Mechanism
venue: BULLETIN of the L N GUMILYOV EURASIAN NATIONAL UNIVERSITY POLITICAL SCIENCE REGIONAL STUDIES ORIENTAL STUDIES TURKOLOGY Series
abstract: This article examines legal measures to combat international terrorism. The authors analyse the development and functioning of the mechanisms of the Al-Qaeda and Taliban Sanctions Committee and the UN Counter-Terrorism Committee in the context of UN Security Council Resolution No. 1267 (1999), by which the Council imposed sanctions in response to the Taliban’s refusal to hand over Osama bin Laden. In subsequent decisions, the UN Security Council modified the goals of the sanction to include Al-Qaida and its associations (according to the resolution 1390 (2002)) and highlight three main measures: an asset freeze (and related financial measures), an arms embargo, and a ban on movement. There is no doubt that funding is a prerequisite to any terrorist action, and freezing the flow of money to those engaged in terrorist activities is vitally important, therefore identify legal challenges in enforcement of freezing of assets and travel ban on terrorist suspects is also important. Accordingly, the article evaluates whether the UN and EU procedures for listing and delisting suspected terrorists comply with the principles of due process, legal certainty, and effective judicial protection. Particular attention is paid to the need to balance the effectiveness of counter-terrorism sanctions with the protection of fundamental human rights and individual freedoms.

key: at the heart of vulnerability when lack of oversight and political pressure redefine press
title: At the Heart of Vulnerability: When Lack Of Oversight and Political Pressure Redefine Press Freedom in Burundi
venue: Journal of humanities and social sciences studies
abstract: In a post-conflict setting in 2015 marked by a fragile economy and political tensions, the Burundian media have not been spared from this crisis. The aim of this article is to examine the conflictual relationship between economic dependence and editorial independence and its influence on the quality of information produced in the Burundian media. This research is based on a quantitative study of 77 local journalists using stepwise binomial logistic regression, which identified the factors determining the production of quality information. The results of the bivariate analysis show that four variables were significantly associated with the quality of information, including verification of sources, time and resources allocated to in-depth analysis, and, significantly, political and economic pressures. In terms of explanatory analysis, verification of sources, time and resources for in-depth analysis, and more specifically political pressure, were the determining factors in the quality of information. Logistic regression analysis reveals that the quality of information in Burundi is determined by source verification, the time allocated to analysis and, significantly, political and economic pressures, relegating socio-demographic factors to a secondary role.

key: thy brothers keeper attributions of blame and responsibility in the jewish and muslim dias
title: Thy Brother’s Keeper: Attributions of Blame and Responsibility in the Jewish and Muslim Diaspora
abstract: Abstract Political violence, ranging from terrorism to interstate conflict, have been a core concern of social scientists for decades. Yet, the study of these phenomena and their effects is often limited to the specific geographic area of their occurrence. We seek to understand how diaspora populations and linked groups to international actors are affected by their geopolitical actions. Namely, considered blameworthy for or responsible to speak out against the actions of states and/or transnational actors with whom they are often linked? We contend that the reporting of salient events associated with a particularly violent conflict, are likely to increase both blame and responsibility to speak out of groups associated with the perceived attacker. We test our hypotheses through three waves of survey experiments in the United States from 2022 to 2024. While support for our hypotheses is mixed, the clearest evidence for our expected effects appears only in the pre-conflict wave, prior to the October 7 attack and the subsequent war in Gaza. In the later wartime waves, these effects largely dissipate, suggesting that in a media environment already saturated with conflict reporting, exposure to a single additional conflict report may have limited marginal impact. More broadly, we find that blame and responsibility to speak function as distinct phenomenon targeting groups associated with international actors. Additionally, our work shows that those on the ideological right are much more likely to blame groups for the actions of associated international actors in conflict.

key: from counter insurgency to post lwe stabilisation state consolidation and the risk of resu
title: From Counter-Insurgency to Post-LWE Stabilisation: State Consolidation and the Risk of Resurgence in India
abstract: Ministry of Home Affairs data record a fall in LWE-related violent incidents from 1,936 in 2010 to 234 in 2025, and the number of districts officially classified as LWE-affected fell to zero in March-April 2026, although 38 districts remain under continuing support categories. This article asks how the contraction of Left-Wing Extremism (LWE) has changed India’s counter-insurgency challenge, particularly with regard to post-LWE stabilisation, state consolidation and the prevention of resurgence. Using qualitative document analysis and descriptive longitudinal evidence, it treats India as the macro-case and Chhattisgarh’s Bastar division as the principal illustration. The article distinguishes three dimensions of state presence: security reach, infrastructure and connectivity, and civilian institutional consolidation. It finds that the first two have expanded substantially, while civilian institutional consolidation is less clearly demonstrated: evidence on functioning civilian institutions in former core areas is limited and uneven, and some services are delivered through security camps. The article argues that the central challenge has shifted from suppressing insurgent capacity to converting security gains into durable civilian institutions, and treats resurgence as a conditional analytical risk rather than a prediction. Its contribution is a framework that separates stabilisation from state consolidation in analysing India’s post-LWE phase.

key: the impact of failed states on global security afghanistan iraq and syria
title: THE IMPACT OF FAILED STATES ON GLOBAL SECURITY: AFGHANISTAN, IRAQ AND SYRIA
venue: Pamukkale University Journal of Social Sciences Institute
abstract: Failed states are a complex phenomenon with significant implications for global security, governance, and development. They destabilize regions, empower non-state actors, and increase transnational threats. This study explores how failed states impact global security by analyzing the interplay between internal weaknesses and external interventions. Focusing on Afghanistan, Iraq, and Syria, it highlights how fragile institutions, sectarian divisions, and governance gaps—combined with foreign interference—worsen state failure and create global ripple effects. These states often become breeding grounds for terrorism, organized crime, and forced migration, further undermining regional stability and international governance. The study also examines the influence of global powers and regional actors in shaping these outcomes. Using comparative case studies and an interdisciplinary approach, it argues that addressing state failure is essential to maintaining global stability and calls for integrated strategies that consider both local dynamics and international responsibilities.

key: rank degrading treatment and the italyalbania agreement
title: Rank, Degrading Treatment, and the Italy‐Albania Agreement
abstract: In November 2023, Italy signed a five‐year agreement with Albania to transfer asylum seekers intercepted in international waters by Italian vessels to Italian‐run detention centres in Albania for asylum processing and deportation. The agreement has been controversial and raises several human rights issues. This article examines these human rights concerns and argues that the agreement is degrading by design. Analysing policy documents, legal cases, speeches, international human rights and refugee law, and philosophical and legal scholarship on the concept of degrading treatment, this article argues that the cumulative effect of subjecting people to unnecessary suffering, discrimination, and dehumanisation creates a structural risk of degrading human dignity that brings asylum seekers down in rank. This article makes an important contribution to the policy debates over the externalisation of asylum seekers in Europe by shedding light on the link between policy designs and the risk of degrading treatment.

key: the story of usaids demise
title: The Story of USAID’s Demise
abstract: The abrupt shutdown of USAID in 2025 exposed the contradictions at the heart of modern humanitarian aid. Long framed as an expression of American generosity, aid has always intertwined altruism with political, economic, and ideological interests. As competing narratives unravel, the future of global assistance remains uncertain, but the underlying human impulse to provide care and solidarity endures beyond any single institution.

key: the appeal of the bukele regime in latin america the scope and limits of citizen support
title: The Appeal of the Bukele Regime in Latin America: The Scope and Limits of Citizen Support

key: the securitization of global slow onset risks threats long covid a case study
title: The securitization of global slow-onset risks/threats: long COVID, a case study
abstract: This paper investigates why Long Covid, despite affecting millions globally and posing a serious threat to public health and economic stability, remains largely absent from contemporary security agendas. It argues that the condition’s chronic, diffuse nature presents a temporal mismatch with existing security frameworks designed for acute, visible crises. Drawing on the Copenhagen School’s securitization theory and Olaf Corry’s concept of “riskification,” the paper shows how structural, normative, and political obstacles—namely the difficulty of constructing chronic disability as collective harm within dominant security imaginaries—prevent Long Covid from being framed as an existential threat. Comparing the response to Long Covid with that of climate change and acute Covid-19, it reveals how scientific uncertainty, fragmented governance, and limited public awareness undermine mobilization. U.S. reluctance to lead, domestic political fragmentation, and a cultural emphasis on individual responsibility further diminish the prospects for securitizing moves. Internationally, institutions like the UN and WHO exhibit similar inertia due to ambiguous mandates and competing priorities. The paper concludes that Long Covid exposes critical gaps in traditional security thinking, particularly in addressing slow-onset, mass-disabling threats. As similar slow-onset disabling conditions may emerge in future biological crises, prevailing security conceptions could leave societies insufficiently prepared. The paper therefore uses securitization theory diagnostically to argue that political conceptions of security should better account for chronic harm and disability. Not applicable

key: de wwft van poort tot plicht
title: De Wwft: van poort tot plicht
abstract:
Anti-money laundering (AML) regulation has become a central instrument in contemporary crime control strategies. Accountants and civil-law notaries subject to the Wwft (the Dutch AML Act) – so-called ‘gatekeepers’ – are required to conduct customer due diligence (CDD) and report unusual transactions in order to prevent money laundering. Failure to comply with these obligations may result in criminal liability under the WED (the Dutch Economic Offences Act).
The study is motivated by growing criticism regarding the ability of gatekeepers to effectively comply with their AML-obligations. This potential inability raises questions concerning the legitimacy and limits of criminal liability, particularly in light of the principle of individual culpability, which requires that criminal liability be based on personal blameworthiness.
The central research question of this dissertation is:
How do the legal and practical possibilities and limitations experienced by accountants and civil-law notaries in complying with their core obligations under the Wwft relate to their criminal liability, in light of the principle of individual culpability?
The first part of the dissertation examines the legal framework governing preventive AML- obligations. Chapters 2 and 3 analyze the European and Dutch anti-money laundering framework, focusing on CDD and the reporting of unusual transactions. Chapter 4 addresses the criminalization of non-compliance. Chapter 5 explores the criminal law principle of individual culpability. The analysis centers on individual blameworthiness and one of the grounds for excluding culpability, known as absence of all guilt (afwezigheid van alle schuld, AVAS).
Against this theoretical background, the second part of the dissertation investigates how AML-obligations are experienced and implemented in practice. Chapter 6 sets out the methodological design of the empirical research, which consists of semi-structured interviews with Wwft-obliged accountants and civil-law notaries. The empirical findings are presented in Chapter 7. The interviews reveal that respondents experience significant challenges at three interconnected levels: (1) enforcement; (2) legislation; and (3) the Wwft-institution.
Chapter 8 integrates the doctrinal and empirical findings of the study. This chapter argues that the practical limitations should, depending on the circumstances of the specific case, play a more prominent role in the assessment of criminal liability. In particular, the principle of individual culpability requires careful consideration of the extent to which compliance was realistically achievable under the circumstances of the individual case. Therefore, it contends that AVAS should play a more significant role in cases involving alleged non-compliance with AML-obligations and that the requirement of intent should be applied substantively rather than merely formally.
The dissertation determines that the current AML-framework contains structural tensions between the risk-based approach and the open norms in the Wwft, and the practical capacities of gatekeepers. These tensions call for a more nuanced approach to criminal liability that emphasizes individual blameworthiness and actual realistic compliance possibilities, and the specific circumstances of the case.
The dissertation concludes in Chapter 9 with several recommendations. It advocates for strengthening both regulatory guidance and feedback mechanisms while preserving the professional discretion that is inherent in a risk-based regulatory framework. Furthermore, with regard to the obligation to report unusual transactions, the study proposes a framework to assist courts in assessing the awareness requirement (‘bekendheidsvereiste’) more consistently and in a more transparent manner.

key: media coverage fear of the police or social contagion assessing the mechanisms of french p
title: Media coverage, fear of the police, or social contagion? Assessing the mechanisms of French population lockdown during Covid-19 crisis in spring 2020

key: silenced by the state enforced disappearances in latin america
title: Silenced by the State: Enforced Disappearances in Latin America
abstract: Enforced disappearances persist as one of the most severe human rights violations in Latin America. This paper evaluates the effectiveness of distinct state responses to these crimes against humanity in Argentina, Colombia, and Mexico, more specifically, the Argentine Dirty War, Colombia's "falsos positivos" (false positives), and the Ayotzinapa case in Mexico. Although these countries have developed institutional mechanisms to battle this major challenge, their outcomes remain insufficient. Through a comparative case study of each nation’s truth commission reports and institutional systems, the study examines whether these mechanisms have led to accountability and effectiveness by examining the discovery of the truth, the prosecution of perpetrators, reparations, and guarantees against repetition. Many countries view Argentina as a leading figure and model, yet it continues to face significant obstacles in advancing the cause of victims. Colombia and Mexico have also demonstrated signs of expansion that combat enforced disappearances, but there are notable drawbacks and limitations. The findings suggest that, while legal and institutional reforms and frameworks are important, they are individually inadequate to ensure accountability and protection for victims.

key: perspectives the symbolic completion of sovereign power in post war azerbaijan
title: Perspectives: The Symbolic Completion of Sovereign Power in Post-War Azerbaijan

key: criminal law regulation of domestic violence problems and prospects
title: CRIMINAL LAW REGULATION OF DOMESTIC VIOLENCE: PROBLEMS AND PROSPECTS
venue: Bulletin of Institute of Legislation and Legal Information of the Republic of Kazakhstan
abstract: This article examines the extent to which the current criminal legislation of the Republic of Kazakhstan reflects the specific features of domestic violence, with a view to identifying legal gaps and proposing improvements. To achieve this aim, the study pursues the following objectives: 1) to analyze the legal definition of “close persons” under the criminal law of the Republic of Kazakhstan; 2) to assess its compliance with international legal standards, in particular the Istanbul Convention, as well as comparative foreign practice; 3) to substantiate the need for a differentiated approach to domestic violence, taking into account the nature of close relationships as a factor increasing the social harm of the offence; and 4) to develop proposals for legislative improvement. Limiting the range of subjects exclusively to formally registered family ties and close kinship does not reflect the real social nature of domestic violence, which is often committed within de facto marital and other intimate relationships. In this regard, the article substantiates the need to revise the content of the category of “close persons” in the criminal legislation of the Republic of Kazakhstan. It is proposed to expand this category by including persons who live or have lived together, as well as those who are or have been in de facto marital or other close relationships, regardless of their formal legal status. Such an approach allows for taking into account the actual social ties underlying domestic violence. In this context, it is proposed to strengthen criminal liability for acts committed in the sphere of domestic relations by introducing into criminal law a qualifying element — the commission of a criminal offense against a close person, which would allow for taking into account the increased social danger of such acts.

key: barriers to return rohingya perspectives on citizenship safety and international accountab
title: Barriers to Return: Rohingya Perspectives on Citizenship, Safety, ‎and International Accountability
venue: International Journal of Peace and Conflict Research (IJPCR)
abstract: The Rohingya displacement crisis is one of the most mass migration crisis in modern history. ‎Since 2017 military crackdown, more than a million Rohingya have fled to Bangladesh, ‎resulting in a significant social dislocation, security issues, and an overall humanitarian crisis. ‎Return is mostly unrealized although there have been bilateral and international efforts by both ‎countries to facilitate safe, voluntary, and dignified repatriation efforts. This study addresses a ‎critical research gap: a lack of refugee-centred research on the barriers to repatriation, ‎especially the views of Rohingya on citizenship, safety, and international responsibility. Based ‎on 50 semi-structured interviews and two focus groups (n=18) of Rohingya refugees in Coxs ‎Bazar, Bangladesh, the research uses thematic analysis to derive five important themes ‎including denial of citizenship and structural statelessness; militarized insecurity and fear of ‎recurrence; lack of credibility in international accountability; material reconstruction deficits; ‎and psychosocial rupture. The results show that refugees are not unconditionally but ‎conditionally against repatriation, which means that they have to restore their full citizenship, ‎demilitarize the Rakhine State, be subjected to credible international accountability, and be ‎rebuilt in livelihood statuses. Such discoveries highlight how much there is a strong urgency to ‎establish rights-based, structurally-grounded repatriation frameworks that put the agency of ‎refugees at the centre.‎

key: abuse of power in corruption crimes a criminological perspective
title: Abuse of Power in Corruption Crimes: A Criminological Perspective
abstract: Corruption is one of the serious problems that hinders development, social and economic stability, and public trust in state institutions. In Indonesian law, the crime of corruption is regulated in Law Number 31 of 1999 as amended by Law Number 20 of 2001 concerning the Eradication of Corruption, especially Article 2 which regulates the act of illegally enriching oneself or others that can harm the state's finances. Abuse of power is one of the factors that can encourage the occurrence of corruption crimes, especially when authority is used for personal or group interests. This study aims to analyze the abuse of power in corruption crimes based on a criminological perspective with a focus on the provisions of Article 2 of the Corruption Law. The research method used is normative legal research with a statutory approach and a conceptual approach. The data used are primary, secondary, and tertiary legal materials obtained through literature studies and qualitatively analyzed. The results of the study show that the abuse of power in corruption crimes is not only influenced by individual factors, but also by structural and social factors, such as weak supervision, low transparency, and gaps in the legal system and government administration. Criminological perspectives through anomic theory, rationalization theory, and social control theory can be used to understand the driving factors for the abuse of power in corruption crimes. Therefore, strengthening supervision, transparency, and social control systems is needed as part of efforts to prevent and eradicate corruption crimes in Indonesia.

key: fighting fire with fire why post secularity matters for safeguarding liberal democracy and
title: Fighting Fire with Fire: Why Post-Secularity Matters for Safeguarding Liberal Democracy and Inspiring Societal Transformation
abstract: Scholars interested in safeguarding liberal democracy and inspiring societal transformation are increasingly turning their attention to the role of the imagination and culture in both maintaining the status quo and triggering change. However, accounts of the imagination are often quite shallow. Drawing on theories of the post-secular, this article offers an accessible means of identifying the fundaments of an imaginary and of considering how it can be transformed. It does so in four steps. First, it explains how some of the most influential cultural theories of stasis and change emerge from the study of religion and that regaining their interpretive power requires applying categories from the study of religion to secular institutions and individuals. Second, it outlines a religious repertoires approach to characterizing the fundaments of an imaginary, focusing on magic, myth, and ritual. Third, it makes these enigmatic categories easy to understand and apply by offering the Splash-Ripple Frame for articulating how magic, myth, and ritual can connect to form a ‘chain of meaning’, and observing where these chains are and are not completed. Finally, by way of demonstrating its explanatory power, it applies this frame to understanding the liberal imaginary, rebutting common misconceptions about its fundaments, offering an alternative interpretation, and suggesting ways in which it might be transformed.

key: the atlantis problem statehood continuity and climate induced territorial loss
title: The Atlantis Problem: Statehood Continuity and Climate-Induced Territorial Loss
abstract:
The mythic nation of “Atlantis” has long captured humanity’s collective imagination – a civilisation reclaimed by the indifferent march of the sea.[1] As observed by Abhimanyu George Jain, several “low-lying, small island states” such as the Maldives, Tuvalu and Nauru face a similar threat, as a consequence of man-made climate change.[2] The adversities faced by such states highlight a considerable injustice, especially when you consider that such states have made relatively minor contributions to the climate crisis.[3] In the next 50-100 years, many such states could become entirely submerged.[4] Drawing from Jain’s influential work, this article will refer to the at-risk small island states as ‘Atlantis States’. 
This article examines the implications of such territorial loss in international law, with reference to the concept of statehood and maritime zones. It will also refer to existing treaty and customary law, including the Montevideo Convention. Furthermore, it argues that international law must, as a moral imperative, continue to recognise the existence of submerged states. 
 
 
[1]Abhimanyu George Jain, ‘The 21st Century Atlantis: The International Law of Statehood and Climate Change-Induced Loss of Territory’ (2014) 50(1) Stanford Journal of International Law 1, at 3. 
 
 
[2] ibid 
 
 
[3] Abhimanyu George Jain (n2). 
 
 
[4] Abhimanyu George Jain (n2).
