key: peace under the influence the role of illicit drug economies in peace processes and rebel
title: Peace Under the Influence? The Role of Illicit Drug Economies in Peace Processes and Rebel Splintering
abstract: How do the economic foundations of rebel groups shape civil war dynamics? While prior research has explored how different resource types affect conflict, less is known about how the illicit nature of certain resources—particularly drug economies—affects peace processes. We argue that the inherent illegality of drug-based financing imposes structural barriers to peace, distinguishing it from other forms of rebel revenue. Using cross-national dyadic data from 1990 to 2011, we find that drug-reliant rebel groups have 34 percent lower hazard of initiatiating peace talks and over six times more likely to fragment once peace processes begin. These findings suggest that drug-based financing generates a self-reinforcing cycle that sustains violence. In contrast to accounts emphasizing grievances produced by peace processes, we show that some groups may be structurally predisposed to reject peace altogether. Our findings call for theoretical and policy approaches tailored to the distinct challenges posed by illicit drug economies.

key: the shapla chattar atrocity 2013 in bangladesh a case of state perpetrated human rights vi
title: The Shapla Chattar atrocity (2013) in Bangladesh: A case of state-perpetrated human rights violations
abstract:
BackgroundThe 2013 Shapla Chattar event in Dhaka remains one of the most underreported state-perpetrated atrocities in South Asia; a peaceful protest was violently dispersed by state forces, resulting in mass casualties. For over a decade, media suppression, political repression, and the authoritarian climate silenced public discourse and academic inquiry. Following the regime’s collapse in August 2024, new evidence has emerged, warranting a fresh investigation from a human rights perspective. 
MethodsThis study was conducted based on secondary sources, including fact-finding reports from human rights organization including Odhikar and Human Rights Watch, government data, and media archives. It evaluates the Shapla incident within the framework of international human rights law and the criteria for crimes against humanity. 
ResultsAn estimated 93 to over 300 individuals were killed during the 5–6 May 2013 Shapla Chattar operation. Approximately 7,500 security personnel were deployed, and over 150,000 rounds of live ammunition were used. The demographic analysis of the 61 confirmed death cases shows that 80% of victims came from non-madrasa backgrounds. The use of excessive force, media blackout, and suppression of civil society point to a state-orchestrated assault. The Shapla atrocity satisfies all key criteria for crimes against humanity: it was widespread, systematic, targeted civilians, and was conducted with full knowledge of its consequences. 
Conclusion This study assessed the Shapla Chattar atrocity as a case of state-sanctioned violence, qualifying as a crime against humanity. It underscores the urgent need for judicial accountability and transparent investigation through the reformed International Crimes Tribunal.

key: between hope and despair r2p norm cascade and continuing challenges to atrocity prevention
title: Between Hope and Despair: R2P Norm Cascade and Continuing Challenges to Atrocity Prevention in Southeast Asia—Lessons from Myanmar and the Philippines
abstract: More than 20 years since the adoption of the Responsibility to Protect (R2P) in the UN General Assembly, the principle has not been fully embraced by states in Southeast Asia, a region that continues to face high risks for atrocities. Using the three pillars of the principle and the framework of norm cascade and implementation, this article finds three important lessons on the challenges and constraints in implementing R2P in the region using Myanmar and the Philippines as case studies. Specifically, it examines the continuing problem of democratic transitions in Myanmar (still dominated by the military) and in the Philippines (where political dynasties continue to rule), which accounts for resistance to the R2P norm particularly in holding state actors accountable for atrocity crimes. It also analyses the normative and structural limitations of ASEAN in responding to the Myanmar crisis after the February 2021 coup, and how geopolitics has undermined the role of both the United Nations and ASEAN in responding to atrocities in Myanmar. While many scholars have raised the question of whether ASEAN, in asserting its centrality, is still fit for purpose in managing regional peace and security, the more important question to raise is whether Myanmar is fit to continue as a member of the organisation as it unapologetically violates the group’s Charter principles. Meanwhile, despite the Philippines withdrawal from the Rome Treaty in 2019, the government in Manila opted to surrender former President Rodrigo Duterte to the International Criminal Court for atrocity crimes committed during his drug war campaign. This proves that the state’s resistance to R2P’s norm core is short-lived as the political dynamics in the country significantly changed following the political rift in the Marcos-Duterte alliance in 2022.

key: the voice of the landless or counter revolutionary activism of abahlali basemjondolo in ca
title: The Voice of the Landless or Counter-Revolutionary Activism of Abahlali baseMjondolo in Cato Manor: A Conflict Theory Perspective
venue: International Journal of African Renaissance Studies - Multi-, Inter- and Transdisciplinarity
abstract: Abstract Despite various land reform efforts by the democratic government in South Africa, landlessness—including a lack of adequate housing—persists, leading to illegal land occupations by grassroots movements. One such movement, Abahlali baseMjondolo (shack dwellers), has supported landless people in building informal settlements, including in Cato Manor. This article analyses the divergent stakeholder perceptions around Abahlali baseMjondolo land occupation in the context of landlessness and poor housing provision in Cato Manor. The study adopted a qualitative research method, sampling 33 participants, and used conflict theory as a theoretical lens to interpret the findings. Data were analysed using thematic analysis. The findings established that divergent views regarding Abahlali baseMjondolo exist in Cato Manor. The residents view Abahlali baseMjondolo as a vital force of empowerment, while municipal officials see the movement as a disruptive influence. Through conflict theory, the article argues that these opposing views emanate from positions of power (municipal officials) and marginalisation (residents). In advancing the debate on Abahlali baseMjondolo, it contends that the politics of naming settlement in Cato Manor construct advocates a counter-narrative to state authority by problematising the simplistic dualism of the state versus people experiencing poverty, using classical conflict theory.

key: criminal participation in human trafficking offenses co perpetration instigation and compl
title: Criminal Participation in Human Trafficking Offenses: Co-Perpetration, Instigation and Complicity
venue: Proceedings of The World Conference on Research in Social Sciences
abstract: This paper explores the complex phenomenon of criminal participation in human trafficking offenses, focusing on the legal and criminological distinctions among co-perpetration, instigation, and complicity. The purpose of the study is to analyze how these forms of participation are conceptualized and applied within national and European criminal law frameworks, with particular attention to Romanian legislation and its harmonization with EU directives and international instruments such as the Palermo Protocol. The research aims to clarify the boundaries between collective criminal intent, hierarchical coordination, and secondary involvement in trafficking networks. Using a comparative doctrinal method, the study examines court rulings, doctrinal commentaries, and case law of the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) and the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR). It highlights the challenges in differentiating co-perpetration from aiding or abetting, especially in organized crime contexts where the division of roles is fluid and overlapping. The findings indicate that inconsistencies in judicial interpretation may undermine proportional liability and the effective punishment of all participants. Therefore, the paper proposes a conceptual framework that integrates intent, contribution, and degree of autonomy as key analytical criteria. The study contributes to the development of a coherent European approach to criminal participation in human trafficking, reinforcing both legal certainty and victims’ protection through a harmonized understanding of shared culpability.

key: the hypocrisy of western states analyzing statements on accountability and justice in ukra
title: The Hypocrisy of Western States: Analyzing Statements on Accountability and Justice in Ukraine and Gaza
abstract:
Since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and the seemingly unrestrained Israeli actions in Gaza, Western states have been discussing the need for accountability. A number of these states (The Netherlands, Germany, France and the United Kingdom), are states parties to the International Criminal Court (ICC). The Netherlands is the ICC host state. The United States has been, while not an ICC member, occasionally supportive of some accountability-related initiatives. The question this article will answer is
 what
 do these select Western states
 say
 about the violence in Ukraine and Gaza, especially about expectations of justice and accountability. The article presents empirical research conducted over four years, in four languages, and encompassing over 1500 statements. The research findings reflect a deep lack of adherence to principles and an abundance of hypocrisy, which, while not new, unmask undeniable inconsistencies which could cause irreparable harm to any remaining credibility of the international justice system.

key: the unfulfilled promises of the solution to the problem of illicit drugs
title: The Unfulfilled Promises of the “Solution to the Problem of Illicit Drugs”
abstract:
The 2016 Final Peace Agreement with the FARC-EP articulated a new drug policy aimed at “definitively solving the problem of illicit drugs” in Colombia. At its core, this commitment recognized the illicit drug trade as a key source of funding for the FARC-EP and promised to rebuild the state’s relationship with coca-growing territories and populations. In this paper, we argue that this promise has remained largely unfulfilled. The policy agenda set out in the Agreement—which has broadly guided subsequent governments—has suffered from serious design and implementation flaws, the disruptive effects of post-FARC-EP armed realignments, and the structural limits imposed by a persistent global cocaine demand and a prohibitionist regime. As a result, the policy’s core components largely failed: to reduce the supply of cocaine, the productive inclusion of coca producers, and territorial integration through the provision of public goods in marginalized areas. The evolving geopolitical landscape and transformations in the global illicit drug economy underscore the need to rethink existing policy alternatives.
 El Acuerdo Final de Paz de 2016 con las FARC-EP propuso una nueva política de drogas con el objetivo de “resolver definitivamente el problema de las drogas ilícitas” en Colombia. Este compromiso partía del reconocimiento de que el comercio ilícito de drogas constituía una fuente clave de financiación de las FARC-EP y prometía reconstruir la relación del Estado con las regiones cocaleras y sus habitantes. En este artículo sostenemos que esa promesa no se materializó. La agenda de política definida en el Acuerdo, que ha orientado a los gobiernos posteriores, ha estado marcada por serios problemas de diseño y profundos vacíos de implementación. A ello se sumaron los efectos de la reorganización de los grupos armados tras la desmovilización de las FARC-EP, así como los límites estructurales impuestos por la persistente demanda global de cocaína y por el régimen internacional de prohibición. Como resultado, esta política no logró reducir la oferta de cocaína, promover la inclusión productiva de los campesinos cocaleros ni avanzar en la integración territorial mediante la provisión de bienes públicos en las regiones históricamente marginadas. El cambiante panorama geopolítico y las transformaciones de la economía global de las drogas ilícitas ponen de relieve la necesidad de repensar las alternativas de política disponibles.

key: agricultural pesticide exposures in ecuador and their spatial association with low birth w
title: Agricultural pesticide exposures in Ecuador and their spatial association with low birth weight: a combined cluster detection and Bayesian modelling approach.
abstract: Most evidence about the health consequences of pesticide exposures comes from occupational settings in high-income countries. However, larger populations can be exposed through agricultural drift, especially in low- and middle-income countries (LMIC). Despite the growing and widespread use of pesticides, there is scarcity of studies assessing the national level effect of environmental exposures to pesticides. Ecuador has one of the highest application rates as the country is highly dependent on its export-bound agricultural industry. We applied spatial analyses to explore the distribution of low birth weight (LBW) in Ecuador and its association with pesticide exposures for 2015 and 2016. We used a gridded global database of pesticide use estimates, PEST-CHEMGRIDSv1, and public records of ∼500,000 births. First, we applied spatial cluster analysis to assess the spatial distribution of LBW and identify areas of elevated risk. Then, we used a Bayesian spatial regression to evaluate the effect of application rates on LBW at the parish level (n = 1030). In addition, we used nested models to assess to what extent the covariates account for the spatial effect. Elevated risks of LBW were observed in the central Coast and Inter-Andean regions. Moreover, we found evidence that living in areas with high levels of pesticide use may be associated with increased odds of LBW (OR: 1.10, 95% CI: 1.01 - 1.20). The spatial variability of this association was partially accounted by environmental factors known to affect pesticide drift, such as wind speed, solar radiation, and temperature. Given the limited national-level studies on pesticide exposures globally, geospatial modelling offers valuable tools to estimate the burden of pesticide exposures and identify regions that may require further detailed assessments. This information is central to evaluate intensive export-led agriculture development projects and provide evidence for regulations around pesticide use in LMIC.

key: the hidden cost of bananas the effects of pesticides on newborns health
title: The Hidden Cost of Bananas: The Effects of Pesticides on Newborns’ Health
venue: Journal of the Association of Environmental and Resource Economists
abstract: This study examines the effects of aerial fumigation of banana plantations on newborns’ health during the period 2015–17 in Ecuador. Using the mothers’ addresses, the perimeter of the plantations, and the amount of pesticides applied in each plantation, we determine newborns’ exposure to pesticides. We then implement a difference-in-differences strategy that exploits seasonal variations in the use of pesticides to identify the causal effect of fumigations on newborns’ health outcomes. Our analysis shows that newborns with a high exposure to pesticides during gestation have a birth weight deficit of between 80 and 150 grams. Moreover, exposure to pesticides increases the likelihood of low birth weight and preterm delivery. We validate our results with a maternal fixed effect model that compares the health outcomes of siblings exposed and not exposed to intensive fumigations. We also carry out placebo and falsification tests considering newborns exposed to other crops not using aerial fumigations.

key: emerging contaminants in streams of doce river watershed minas gerais brazil
title: Emerging Contaminants in Streams of Doce River Watershed, Minas Gerais, Brazil
abstract: This study investigated the occurrence and risk assessment of ten pharmaceutical products and two herbicides in the water of rivers from the Doce river watershed (Brazil). Of the 12 chemicals studied, ten (acyclovir, amoxicillin, azithromycin, ciprofloxacin, enrofloxacin, fluoxetine, erythromycin, sulfadiazine, sulfamethoxazole, glyphosate and aminomethylphosphonic acid) had a 100% detection rate. In general, total concentrations of all target drugs ranged from 4.6 to 14.5 μg L−1, with fluoroquinolones and sulfonamides being the most representative classes of pharmaceutical products. Herbicides were found at concentrations at least ten times higher than those of the individual pharmaceutical products and represented the major class of contaminants in the samples. Most of the contaminants studied were above concentrations that pose an ecotoxicological risk to aquatic biota. Urban wastewater must be the main source of contaminants in waterbodies. Our results show that, in addition to the study of metal in water (currently being conducted after the Fundão dam breach), there is an urgent need to monitor emerging contaminant in waters from Doce river watershed rivers, as some chemicals pose environmental risks to aquatic life and humans due to the use of surface water for drinking and domestic purposes by the local population. Special attention should be given to glyphosate, aminomethylphosaphonic acid, and to ciprofloxacin and enrofloxacin (whose concentrations are above predicted levels that induce resistance selection).

key: the hidden cost of bananas pesticide effects on newborns health
title: The Hidden Cost of Bananas: Pesticide Effects on Newborns’ Health
abstract: We study the effects of aerial fumigation of banana plantations on newborns’ birth weight during the period 2015-2017 in Ecuador. We use mothers’ addresses and information on the perimeter of the plantations to create an individual measure of newborns’ exposure to pesticides. We use this measure to implement three independent identification strategies to address the endogeneity of exposure to aerial fumigations. First, we consider a difference-indifferences strategy that exploits seasonal variations in the use of pesticides across provinces. Second, we estimate a difference-in-differences model that considers geographical variations in the use of pesticides across comparable crops. Third, and finally, we estimate a maternal fixed effects model to examine the effect of pesticides on siblings who had a different residence during gestation and who were exposed to different levels of fumigations. Our first empirical model shows that newborns exposed to pesticides, when their first gestational trimester coincides with the periods of intensive fumigations of the plantations, have a birth weight reduction of between 38 and 89 grams. Moreover, exposure to pesticides increases the likelihood of low birth weight and low Apgar score at the first minute by around 0.35 and 0.33, respectively. The second model finds that newborns exposed to fumigated banana plantations have a birth weight deficit of between 29 and 76 grams, when compared to those exposed to other fumigated crops. Finally, the maternal fixed effect model shows that girl newborns exposed to pesticides have a birth weight deficit of 346 grams when compared to non-exposed siblings.

key: glyphosate and health in uruguay a 25 year review of research on agricultural worker expos
title: Glyphosate and health in Uruguay: A 25-year review of research on agricultural worker exposure.
abstract: In Uruguay, glyphosate is a widely used herbicide, applied across both small- and large-scale horticultural crops. Agricultural workers in direct contact with glyphosate during its application and handling constitute a vulnerable population exposed to this herbicide. The purpose of this report is to assess the health impacts of exposure to glyphosate on workers within the Uruguayan context. A PRISMA-guided bibliographic review was conducted using databases including PubMed, Scopus, and SciELO, Google Scholar, and academic and governmental repositories in Uruguay. Studies published between 2000 and 2025 were selected, focusing on research that directly or indirectly addressed the effects of glyphosate on agricultural workers in Uruguay. Of the eight studies identified, only two centered specifically on glyphosate, while the remaining included exposure to multiple pesticides. Primary routes of exposure to glyphosate were dermal and inhalational, particularly during mixing, loading, and application activities, with reported acute symptoms involving gastrointestinal, neurological, and muscular manifestations, and chronic effects including respiratory and skin conditions. Several studies underscored the importance of biomarkers in improving correlations between exposure levels and clinical outcomes. Additionally, one study highlighted a common misconception among workers, who, due to lack of odor of glyphosate, perceive it as less hazardous than other pesticides. This belief underscored the need to enhance education on the risks associated with glyphosate and other pesticides. This report provides key insights by reviewing studies on exposure to glyphosate among agricultural workers in Uruguay. Additionally, this work supports the international research agenda by emphasizing the importance of educational and regulatory measures to reduce occupational health risks associated with pesticide exposure in diverse agricultural contexts.

key: glyphosate residues in chinese tea a national survey contamination pathway and risk assess
title: Glyphosate residues in Chinese tea: a national survey, contamination pathway and risk assessment.
abstract:
BACKGROUND
The health risks and the pathways of glyphosate pollution are of great significance for glyphosate risk management in tea.


RESULTS
A total of 1013 Chinese tea samples were assayed, with 27.4% contaminated by glyphosate and 0.9% exceeding the Chinese maximum residue limit (1.0 mg/kg). Field experiments suggested that spray drift and translocation within the tea plant are the main sources of glyphosate residues in tea. Following soil application, the initial glyphosate residual concentrations in young shoots and mature leaves derived from drift were 1.19 and 41.1 mg/kg, respectively. In young shoots, glyphosate declined rapidly during Day (D)1, but rebounded to a relatively high level by D7. The loss of glyphosate, owing to translocation and/or degradation, proceeded slowly in mature leaves. Upon low-dose tea foliar application, glyphosate in young shoots and mature leaves had a relatively short residual period with half-lives of 0.5 and 1.9 days, respectively. Glyphosate residues decreased during both green and black tea processing, and the loss rate was between 36% and 61%. Both the detection rate and measured concentrations of aminomethylphosphonic acid (AMPA) were markedly lower than those of glyphosate in commercial and experimental tea samples. The hazard quotient calculated from glyphosate residues in tea was several orders of magnitude below the level of concern.


CONCLUSION
Detectable glyphosate residues have been found in Chinese tea, whereas estimated consumer exposure remains far below accepted reference values. Nevertheless, careful application and management of glyphosate use in tea plantations is important for controlling its residues. © 2026 Society of Chemical Industry.

key: influence of biohumates on agrochemical and biological properties of soils and crop yields
title: Influence of biohumates on agrochemical and biological properties of soils and crop yields (Review)
abstract: Modern agriculture is caught in a contradiction between the need to increase food production and the demands of environmental safety. The intensive use of mineral fertilizers and chemical plant protection products, while ensuring short-term yield increases, leads to soil degradation: a decline in humus content, soil compaction, suppression of beneficial microbiota, and pollution. In this context, the development and implementation of technologies that combine productivity with the restoration of soil fertility has become a pressing challenge. Biohumates and humic preparations are seen as effective biologically active substances capable of addressing this issue. This article substantiates the use of biohumates as an environmentally safe, resource-saving alternative that is no less effective than traditional agrochemical products. The study highlights the differences among biohumates, whose classification is based on the source of raw materials, production methods, formulation, chemical composition, additional components, and intended use. Drawing on an analysis of current domestic and international research, the article demonstrates the positive effects of biohumate application on the physicochemical and biological properties of soil, as well as on the quality and yield of agricultural crops. It is shown that applying biohumates improves soil structure and the water-air regime, mobilizes unavailable forms of nutrients, and increases the abundance, diversity, and activity of beneficial microbiota and soil enzymes. Examples are provided of the positive effects of using biohumates in various types of crop production, including horticulture, seed production, and vegetable growing. The article concludes that biohumates hold great promise for use in agriculture, as they help restore and enhance soil fertility, increase plant stress resistance, and ensure stable, ecologically clean yields.

key: environmental assessment of the use of the herbicide kelvin plus in the primorsky territor
title: Environmental assessment of the use of the herbicide Kelvin Plus in the Primorsky Territory
abstract: Under greenhouse conditions, a study was conducted on the sensitivity of agricultural crops to the herbicide Kelvin Plus and the persistence of its active ingredients in meadow-brown soil; additionally, the herbicide's phytotoxicity and its effect on grain yield were evaluated in a grain corn crop grown in a weed-free environment. The studies were conducted in 2022–2024 in the Primorsky Territory. The soil of the experimental plots is meadow-brown podzolized, with humus content in the arable horizon of 3–4%. Corn of the hybrid Canyons population was sown at a rate of 80 thousand seeds/ ha. The predecessor was soybean. The herbicide was applied in the phases of 5–6 and 7–8 leaves of corn at the recommended (0.4 kg/ha) and double (0.8 kg/ha) of the recommended consumption rates. The vegetation periods were characterized by alternating dry and rainy periods. In 2022, the daytime air temperature from the 3rd ten-day period of June until mid-August reached 29.3–33.7 °C. The herbicide, applied in the phase of 7–8 leaves of corn at both application rates from the moment of application until harvesting, had a significant phytotoxic effect on crop plants. This significantly affected the grain yield. Compared to the control (no herbicides), the corncobs in these variants were shorter, and the number of kernels, as well as the corncob and kernel weights, were lower. Test crops were selected to determine the duration of preservation of the active substances of the herbicide Kelvin Plus: tomatoes, mustard, beets, cabbage, barley and wheat. It has been established that the herbicide, at both application rates, degrades almost completely in meadow-brown soil after 10 months.

key: modeling the role of fertilizers and improved seeds on rice productivity in tanzania using
title: Modeling the role of fertilizers and improved seeds on rice productivity in Tanzania using a stochastic simulation approach
abstract: Climate change poses a significant threat to food production in Tanzania, particularly for smallholder farmers who rely on rain-fed agriculture. This study examines the role of improved seeds and fertilizers as climate adaptation strategies to boost rice productivity and food security. Using data from the 2019/20 National Sample Census of Agriculture (NSCA), the study analyzed 6,025 rice farms from Mainland Tanzania and Zanzibar. A Stochastic Simulation model was used to account for yield variability and uncertainty. Farms were classified by seed type (local or improved) and fertilizer use (organic, inorganic, or none). Findings show that using improved seeds with inorganic fertilizers significantly enhances productivity, with a 16% chance of achieving yields above 4.5 t/ha. This combination also reduced the risk of falling below food security thresholds. In contrast, farms using local seeds, even with fertilizers, had only a 10% chance of reaching that yield level. The impact was more notable in Mainland Tanzania (25%) than in Zanzibar (6%). While organic fertilizers improve soil health, they offer limited short-term yield gains. The study concludes that promoting access to improved seeds and inorganic fertilizers is crucial for enhancing rice productivity and achieving the SDG 2 goal of Zero Hunger in Tanzania.

key: occurrence and distribution of individual toxic chemical and pesticide residues in agricul
title: Occurrence and Distribution of Individual Toxic Chemical and Pesticide Residues in Agricultural Soils
abstract: The rapid growth of the global population has increased food demand, leading to the intensive application of chemical inputs in agriculture to enhance crop productivity. Although the use of agrochemicals has played a crucial role in reducing yield losses, their long-term and excessive application has raised serious concerns regarding environmental contamination and human health risks. Since the early twentieth century, a wide range of pesticides and chemical formulations have been introduced to control agricultural pests and diseases. However, subsequent studies have revealed that many of these substances, particularly those extensively used during the Soviet era, persist in agricultural soils despite currently being banned. The present study aimed to assess the presence and individual concentrations of toxic chemical and pesticide residues in agricultural soils, with a particular focus on long-term cultivated areas of the Samukh region, where intensive farming practices have been implemented for decades. Soil samples were collected from cultivated fields and analyzed through a monitoring-based approach to evaluate residue occurrence and potential accumulation patterns. The study further examined the possible implications of residual contamination for soil quality, environmental sustainability, and human health. The findings emphasize the importance of continuous monitoring of agricultural soils and highlight the need for environmentally sound management practices to minimize chemical contamination and support the development of sustainable and safe agricultural systems.

key: risks to human and environmental health associated with the intensive use of glyphosate an
title: Risks to Human and Environmental Health Associated with the Intensive Use of Glyphosate and Biological Alternatives for Its Treatment: A Mini-Review
abstract: Glyphosate is a non-selective, broad-spectrum herbicide commonly used to control various types of weeds in both urban and agricultural settings. Due to their high effectiveness, herbicide formulations containing glyphosate as the active ingredient are among the most widely used in agriculture worldwide. However, the extensive use of glyphosate has been associated with significant environmental contamination events and toxic effects on non-target organisms, including humans. To mitigate environmental contamination and the adverse impacts of glyphosate, it is essential to develop remediation alternatives and treatment methods. Bioremediation using microorganisms has been proposed as a viable solution to address glyphosate contamination. This review analyzes the environmental impacts and human health risks associated with glyphosate use, as well as biological alternatives based on the use of microorganisms, such as bacteria, for the treatment of glyphosate contamination.

key: modeling the impact of agrivoltaics on corn yield and water balance in the us
title: Modeling the Impact of Agrivoltaics on Corn Yield and Water Balance in the US
abstract: Corn farming occupies a substantial portion of agricultural land in the United States, yet the potential impacts of agrivoltaic systems on commodity crop yields remain poorly quantified at a national scale. Building upon our previous county-level modeling framework, we extended our approach to analyze the top 1000 corn-producing counties in the U.S. For each county, the model was calibrated by comparing 20 years of USDA-reported yield data with model predictions to reflect local growing conditions, management practices, and genetic improvements. Our analysis quantified the trade-offs between crop yield loss due to shading from sparse solar arrays and potential yield gains resulting from increased soil moisture retention under partial shading. The results indicate that corn yield decreases by approximately 0.55% per 1% shading, while drought stress, as measured by the Agricultural Reference Index for Drought (ARID), decreases by approximately 0.8% per 1% shading due to reduced evapotranspiration. The model also accurately captured the historical ~0.5% per year yield increase attributed to genetic improvements and advanced management practices. Furthermore, our findings suggest that modern corn varieties exhibit substantially higher drought resistance compared to traditional cultivars, such as McCurdy 84aa, used in previous crop models.

key: persistence of seed applied pesticides in soybeans environmental influences and implicatio
title: Persistence of seed-applied pesticides in soybeans: environmental influences and implications for crop protection.
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Early soybean (Glycine max (L.) Merr.) planting is increasingly adopted in Indiana and the upper Midwestern USA to maximize yield potential, yet seedlings may be more vulnerable to early-season pests and environmental stressors. Seed-applied systemic insecticides and fungicides are widely used to mitigate these risks, but their in-plant concentrations under cold and wet spring soil conditions remain undefined. We quantified thiamethoxam, mefenoxam, fludioxonil, and sedaxane across planting dates, growth stages, and locations.


RESULTS
During a 2-year field study at three Indiana locations, soybeans were planted from early April to late May. Tissues were sampled at five growth stages: VE, VC, V1, V2, and V3/V4. Thiamethoxam was detectable in plant tissues up to later vegetative stages (V4) in both early- and late-season plantings, whereas fungicides persisted only to the first trifoliate (V1) stage. Thiamethoxam concentrations were highest at emergence (~30 000-60 000 ng/g), primarily in cotyledons, and declined sharply by V4 (~50 ng/g). Associations between tissue concentrations and planting date or abiotic conditions varied by compound, year, tissue, and growth stage. No uniform planting date effect was observed.


CONCLUSION
Seed-applied pesticides were concentrated in early seedling tissues and declined after emergence. No consistent relationships were observed between planting dates or abiotic conditions examined and pesticide residues in soybean tissues, making predictions about alignment between in-plant concentrations and early-season pest risk difficult. These early-season field observations complement a literature base indicating that seed-applied pesticides provide a brief, inconsistent window of protection that does not extend beyond the earliest growth stages. © 2026 The Author(s). Pest Management Science published by John Wiley & Sons Ltd on behalf of Society of Chemical Industry.

key: yield versus quality unravelling the nitrogen source trade off in baby corn production
title: Yield versus quality: Unravelling the nitrogen source trade-off in baby corn production
abstract: An experiment was conducted during summer 2026 at the Eastern Block of Tamil Nadu Agricultural University, Coimbatore, Tamil Nadu, India, to study the effects of different organic nitrogen sources combined with inorganic fertiliser on the growth, yield and quality of baby corn. The experiment was laid out in a factorial randomised block design (FRBD) with two factors: organic sources (S1- poultry manure, S2- vermicompost, S3- pig manure, S4- goat manure) and organic-inorganic ratio of recommended dose of nitrogen (RDN) (R1–50 : 50, R2 – 25 : 75). Three additional treatments (C1 - 100 % RDN through organic manure, C2 - 100 % RDN through inorganic fertiliser and C3- absolute control) were included outside the factorial structure and compared with treatment combinations using Dunnett’s test. Results revealed that the use of vermicompost significantly increased soil plant analysis development (SPAD) value (46.4), root length (52.5 cm), dry matter (95.0 g plant-1), baby corn yield (12642 kg ha-1) and green fodder yield (28326 kg ha-1) compared with the other sources. The percentage of baby corn yield and green fodder yield over absolute control were 148.6 % and 121.3 %, respectively. Between the two ratios, 25 % RDN through organic source recorded greater plant height, dry matter and baby corn yield, while 50 % RDN recorded higher ascorbic acid (32.9 mg 100 g-1) and total soluble solids (6.6 °Brix). These results indicate that vermicompost combined with inorganic fertiliser, particularly with 25 % of RDN supplied through vermicompost, can enhance the growth and yield of baby corn, whereas the 50 : 50 ratio may favour selected quality attributes, suggesting that integrated nutrient management practices can be adapted to specific production objectives in baby corn.

key: direct seeded rice
title: Direct seeded rice
venue: Climate Neutral and Resilient Farming Systems
abstract: Chapter 6 provides a summary of research findings from the case studies in India that showed significant benefits of another climate-smart rice system, namely the direct seeded rice (DSR), which shows positive outcomes compared to puddled transplanted rice in terms of (i) higher water productivity, (ii) reduction in labour and production costs, and (iii) lower methane emissions. However, there are some challenges for adopting DSR which include poor weed control, need for specific water and nutrient management, availability of suitable varieties for DSR, increased damage by soil pathogens and nutrient disorders, especially N and micronutrients. Possible solutions to overcome these challenges that will make it easier for adoption by farmers will be analysed in this chapter. Field data/evidence from India and other previous studies under both dry and wet conditions were presented to support the solutions. The options for scaling up DSR combined by need-based farmer trainings, accessibility to good quality seeds, availability and use of drum seeders and selective herbicides were discussed.

key: practice of toxic pesticide and insecticide application in farming case from nepal
title: Practice of Toxic Pesticide and Insecticide Application in Farming Case from Nepal
venue: A Peer Reviewed Journal on Social Sciences
abstract: Purpose of the study is the practice of toxic pesticide and insecticide application in farming case from the Nepal. The researcher used descriptive, cross-sectional, and mixed methods. The first hand data were collected through a structured tool through directly used interview method. Researchers search Google for related topics and literature reviews. The research concludes that farmers do not use pesticides judiciously in the production of vegetable and fruit crops. They not apply Integrated Pest Management (IPM) system. In 2025 Nepal's overall pesticide imports is bio pesticides 0.015%.  In the South Asia region use of agricultural chemicals like fertilizers and pesticides has adverse impacts founded in the water and air pollutions, soil contamination, greenhouse gas emissions, loss of aquatic and terrestrial species, change of species compositions, and degraded ecosystems of the surrounding environment. In Nepal, pesticide use is rising rate is 10 to 20% normally, with an average of 396 grams per ha; however, in the areas of vegetables grown commercially, this rate is significantly higher, at 1600 g/ha. Pesticide imports increased fivefold from 132 tons in 2007- 08 to 635 tons in 2017-18. Malpractice of toxic effects on human health for skin, eyes, headache, diarrhoea, gastric, asthmas, heart, neuron, indigestion, cancer, kidney damage, joint pain, pressure, reduced life expectancy, weak immunity systems, fertility problems and death in the end. Nepal has announced Karnali Province declared an organic Province. It is one of the nation's province in seven provinces. The waiting period of insecticide total 54% of farmers harvested vegetable crops within 72 hours for marketing after toxicity used. Total 90-95% farmers’ west management used rubbish for disposal of bottle and pack after used insecticide and pesticide. It is dangerous for environment, flora and fauna as well as animal and human health.

key: the role of irrigation over rainfed farming systems in improving rice productivity in tanz
title: The Role of Irrigation over Rainfed Farming Systems in Improving Rice Productivity in Tanzania: Policy Insights From the National Sample Census of Agriculture
abstract: Rice is central to Tanzania's food security and economic development; however, persistent yield gaps, exacerbated by climate variability, threaten to undermine production targets. This study examines the role of irrigation in boosting rice productivity compared to traditional rainfed systems using nationally representative data from the 2019/2020 National Sample Census of Agriculture. A stochastic simulation approach assessed yields by water source across major agroecological zones (AEZs) under two productivity thresholds: (i) the national benchmark (≤ 1.5 and ≥ 3.0 t/ha) and (ii) the global high‐yield benchmark (≤ 2.0 and ≥ 4.5 t/ha). The results show that irrigation significantly improves yields and reduces downside risk. Nationally, irrigated farms were far more likely to exceed both benchmarks; for the ≥ 4.5 t/ha threshold, they had an over fivefold advantage compared to rainfed systems. Gains were evident across most AEZs, except the Western AEZ, which faces climatic and water constraints. These findings underscore irrigation's role in narrowing yield gaps, strengthening resilience and driving inclusive agricultural transformation. The evidence supports prioritizing irrigation expansion alongside inclusive water governance and complementary innovations such as improved seeds and extension services, contributing to SDGs 1, 2, 8 and 13. Targeted investment in underserved AEZs should be central to Tanzania's agricultural policy agenda.

key: agricultural practices as natural climate solutions in the canadian prairies
title: Agricultural practices as natural climate solutions in the Canadian Prairies.
abstract: Management practices focused on environmental outcomes in agriculture can increase soil organic carbon (SOC) and reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, complementing farm production practices that provide food and a wide variety of other social-ecological services. However, evidence of the efficacy of such practices for mitigation of climate change is inconsistent and no one recent study brings it all together for the Canadian Prairies, a globally important agricultural region and ecosystem. We reviewed 140 field-based studies (published 2000-2024) examining nine practices: shelterbelts, perennial cover, organic soil amendments, reduced tillage, cover crops, diversified crop rotations, rotational grazing, nitrogen (N) management, and wetland rewetting. Using meta-analysis techniques, we extracted mean and standard deviation of variables related to SOC and GHG from tables, figures, and text. Almost all practices showed beneficial effects on SOC or GHG emissions but with high variability, indicating where further research can fill knowledge gaps, such as rotational grazing and wetland rewetting. Significant SOC effects were apparent (5-10%, 4-17 Mg C/ha) for practices focused on perennial cover and reduced tillage. Nitrous oxide emission reductions (19-88%, 85-941 kg CO2e/ha) were significant for shelterbelts, perennial cover, organic soil amendments, N management, and diversified crop rotations. Our findings can support evidence-based prioritization of farm-level practices and strategies for climate change mitigation in semi-arid agricultural regions.

key: management of soil organic matter in sugarcane cultivation in brazil
title: Management of soil organic matter in sugarcane cultivation in Brazil
authors: Vladiel de Freitas Almeida Soares das Dores
abstract: Brazil is one of the world's leading producers of sugarcane, with its cultivation playing a central role in the supply of bioethanol for domestic use and export markets. As demand for renewable fuel continues to grow, there is an increasing need to enhance sugarcane productivity while ensuring environmental sustainability. Soil organic matter (SOM) is a critical determinant of soil health and productivity, and its dynamics are strongly influenced by agricultural management practices. Depending on the management approach adopted, sugarcane cultivation systems can either act as a net source or sink of carbon to the atmosphere. This review examines the key agricultural management practices that influence SOM dynamics and carbon sequestration in Brazilian sugarcane production systems. Evidence from the literature indicates that three management strategies are particularly effective in preserving SOM: (i) the adoption of “green cane” harvesting—which retains crop residues on the soil surface rather than burning them; (ii) the implementation of minimum tillage or no-till practices during crop replanting operations; and (iii) the maintenance of permanent soil cover throughout the cropping cycle. Together, these practices contribute to reducing soil carbon losses, improving soil structure, and supporting the long-term sustainability of sugarcane cultivation in Brazil.

key: ecological risk assessment of pesticide residues in diverse farming landscapes of central
title: Ecological risk assessment of pesticide residues in diverse farming landscapes of central Zambia
abstract: Agricultural intensification in Zambia has led to widespread reliance on pesticides to safeguard crop yields, yet concerns about their ecological consequences remain insufficiently addressed. This study helps to fill this gap by evaluating the extent and ecological risks associated with pesticide contamination in soils from Chibombo and Mkushi Districts in Central Zambia. We used a two-stage nested research design. First, locations (districts) contained different farming systems (commercial, emergent, and smallholder). Within each farming system, we measured and compared the levels of various pesticide residues, followed by ecological risk assessments (single pollution index and comprehensive pollution index). Pesticide residues were extracted using a modified QuEChERS method and analyzed by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) and gas chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (GC-MS/MS). The analysis of pesticide residues indicated that there were significant variations between farming systems in several pesticide residues (acetamiprid, chlorpyriphos, cypermethrin and profenofos). However, there were no significant differences in pesticide residue accumulation between districts. Smallholder farms were generally associated with high insecticide residues (especially chlorpyrifos with a range of 1,494–5,961 μg/kg), emergent farms showed elevated levels of both insecticides and herbicides (notably cypermethrin and fomesafen), while commercial farms were dominated by herbicide residues (acifluorfen, fomesafen, glyphosate and its primary metabolite; aminomethylphosphonic acid). Ecological risk indices indicated significant threats to soil microbial communities, underscoring the potential for long-term disruption of ecosystem services. The data highlights chlorpyrifos and cypermethrin as key pollutants of concern. The study concludes that current pesticide management practices in Central Province pose measurable ecological risks, necessitating urgent policy interventions and adoption of sustainable pest management strategies.

key: sustainable intensification how grafting boosts coffee production in vietnam
title: Sustainable intensification: how grafting boosts coffee production in Vietnam
abstract: Improved crop varieties have been crucial in enhancing productivity, food security and resilience against biotic and abiotic stressors. While this has been investigated in annual staple crops, empirical evidence on the effectiveness of vegetative propagation methods such as grafting remains scarce. This paper presents the first empirical evidence on the yield performance of grafting in coffee, one of the most traded commodities globally, which supports the livelihood of millions of smallholder farmers. We estimate a log-linearized Cobb-Douglas production function using plot-level data from 1,321 coffee plots in four provinces in the Central Highlands of Vietnam. To address potential selection bias in adoption, we apply an instrumental variable approach. The results show that coffee grafting increases yield by 61%, and findings are robust to alternative model specifications, production function assumptions, and estimation strategies. Given the impacts of climate change on coffee production and predictions showing substantial decrease in yield and coffee-suitable land, practical and easily scalable agricultural technologies such as grafting could play crucial roles in ensuring coffee supply and sustaining smallholder farmers’ livelihood. Our findings provide important policy implications, highlighting the need for agricultural extension services, training programs, and institutional support to promote the adoption of grafting as a pathway to climate-resilient livelihoods and long-term agricultural sustainability.

key: impact of conservation agriculture and biochar interventions on labour demand and producti
title: Impact of conservation agriculture and biochar interventions on labour demand and productivity in Uganda: evidence from a field experiment
abstract: Conservation agriculture (CA) and the use of biochar as a soil amendment can promote productive, resilient, and sustainable smallholder farming. However, adopting these practices requires a shift from conventional methods, potentially changing labour use and returns, the extent of which remains poorly understood. Using data from a randomized controlled trial (RCT) of 400 farmers designed to be representative of smallholder farmers in two districts of Uganda, this study assesses how an informational intervention (delivered through instruction and participatory field demonstrations) on CA methods with and without biochar affect labour use and productivity. Control group farmers were compared to those receiving (i) CA and (ii) CA+BIOCHAR interventions. First difference and inverse probability–weighted regression-adjustment model results indicate that the CA+BIOCHAR intervention increased labour use, with no significant labour productivity gains, compared to the control group. Labour input rose by about 36%, driven by a 54% increase in family labour, while hired labour input declined. Extra work was hence met by family labour rather than paid work. Labour savings occurred only in land preparation, and overall returns to labour were roughly 45% lower than conventional practice. The shifts in labour use and productivity are largely attributable to the information intervention, which increased cultivated area, area under minimum tillage, crop diversity, and biochar application. Taken together, these findings show that, over the study period following the intervention, the promoted CA and biochar package was associated with higher labour demand and no clear labour productivity gains. Bundling training with complementary interventions that tackle the labour burden inherent in smallholder agriculture may be necessary to achieve both labour-saving and labour productivity gains from CA and biochar adoption.

key: agroforestry hedges either increase or decrease soil organic carbon stocks depending on th
title: Agroforestry hedges either increase or decrease soil organic carbon stocks depending on the use of plastic mulch in Southern Quebec (Canada).
abstract: Agroforestry hedges (AFH), including windbreaks and riparian buffers, can mitigate climate change and improve agroecosystem resilience. Many studies report positive effects of AFH on soil organic carbon (SOC) stocks, yet outcomes remain variable. The factors controlling SOC dynamics under AFH, particularly management practices, therefore must be better understood. We quantified C stocks in soils (0-20 and 20-50 cm), tree biomass, litter and woody debris across 36 AFH located in Southern Quebec (Canada), and compared them with adjacent croplands. These AFH varied in age (5-46 years), tree composition, soil texture and mulch type (none or limited vs. continuous plastic strip). SOC stability was assessed through physical size fractionation into mineral-associated organic matter (MAOM) and particulate organic matter (POM). Contrary to expectations, SOC stocks in the whole profile (0-50 cm) were slightly lower (-6.4 ± 3.9%; mean ± SE) under AFH compared to adjacent fields, due to losses (-13 ± 4%) in the subsoil. These losses were not observed in more developed AFH, suggesting a gradual recovery over time. In the topsoil, SOC increased (+24 ± 5%) in the absence of continuous plastic strips, but decreased (-12 ± 5%) when strips were present. The labile POM fraction accounted for most SOC accrual under AFH (+67 ± 14% relative to controls without plastic strip in the topsoil), while MAOM declined across all layers. Despite these soil responses, total C stocks increased by 21 ± 7 Mg C ha-1 in AFH, mainly due to tree biomass. Biomass C sequestration peaked at 3.7 Mg C ha-1 yr-1 23 years after plantation. Our results highlight that management practices during AFH establishment can strongly influence SOC dynamics and that plastic mulch may offset potential SOC gains, even though overall C sequestration remains positive due to tree biomass accumulation.

key: experimental assessment of the impacts of fire and agriculture on the carbon dynamics of a
title: Experimental assessment of the impacts of fire and agriculture on the carbon dynamics of a páramo grassland in northern Ecuador
abstract:
Prescribed fires, associated to extensive cattle raising, and the expansion of crop agriculture are two of the main threats to the integrity and functionality of páramo ecosystems in the Northern Andes. In addition to affecting plant and animal communities, these practices could significantly affect soil carbon storage and hydrological regulation. In this study, we present results from a field experimental assessment of the impacts of fires and potato cultivation on carbon dynamics in a grassland ecosystem in the páramo of Northern Ecuador. Using the static chamber method and a portable gas analyzer, we characterized carbon dynamics in 27 experimental 6.25 m
 2

Unlike Control plots, Burning and Potato plots predominantly lost carbon during the first half of the experiment, and then shifted to negative values of net carbon exchange (NEE) around day 150. Specifically, NEE in the potato plots decreased from an average of 0.9 g CO

Low rates of NEE in Control plots suggest that daytime carbon uptake capacity may be reduced under the evaluated conditions, although annual carbon balance cannot be inferred from the present dataset. These results underscore the need to further evaluate the practice of anthropogenic fires in páramos and limit the expansion of agriculture, as critical strategies for the long-term maintenance of páramo ecosystem services.

key: evaluation of herbicide alternatives to glyphosate for weed control in fallow fields
title: Evaluation of Herbicide Alternatives to Glyphosate for Weed Control in Fallow Fields
abstract: Efficient weed control in fallow fields prior to maize planting faces critical challenges due to herbicide resistance and the need to reduce reliance on glyphosate. This study evaluated non-selective and selective herbicide strategies in an on-farm strip-plot validation trial (6 ha) with nested subsampling (n = 6 quadrats per treatment plot). Nine treatments were evaluated, including synthetic herbicides (glyphosate, 2,4-D, paraquat, glufosinate-ammonium, and saflufenacil + clethodim) and commercial bioherbicide (BH02). Weed control efficacy was evaluated using the European Weed Research Society (EWRS) visual rating scale at 14 and 28 days after application (DAA). For perennial grasses (Sorghum halepense and Cynodon dactylon), glyphosate applied at higher rates (4 + 1 L ha-1 of glyphosate + 2,4-D) achieved 91.0% and 48.3% sustained control at 28 DAA, respectively, whereas contact herbicides permitted severe vegetative regrowth (< 45% control). For annual grasses (Urochloa panicoides and Leptochloa panicea), glyphosate combinations and BH02 provided high control (> 88.8% at 28 DAA), while glufosinate-ammonium alone or with 2,4-D yielded 79.5-92.7% control. For Ipomoea cordatotriloba, glufosinate-ammonium alone (90.5%) and glufosinate + 2,4-D (87.5%) suppressed regrowth at 28 DAA. Product-only economic analysis (2024 commercial rates in MXN ha-1) showed that BH02 ($3,525.00 ha-1) was 2.8-fold more expensive than standard glufosinate-ammonium ($1,622.50 ha-1) and 3.1-fold more expensive than standard glyphosate ($1,125.00 ha-1), limiting its current commercial adoption. Overall, single postemergence applications do not fully eradicate perennial grasses, but glufosinate-ammonium mixtures represent technically effective alternatives for annual grass and I. cordatotriloba suppression during fallow periods.

key: trends in fertiliser use and efficiency in the great barrier reef catchment area
title: Trends in fertiliser use and efficiency in the Great Barrier Reef catchment area.
abstract: Time series data of annual fertiliser application in river basins provide a foundational record of crop management practices and environmental change. Here we produce an annual time series of synthetic nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P) fertiliser application for the river basins of the Great Barrier Reef (GBR) catchment area of north-eastern Australia spanning from 1910 to 2024. We draw on statistical data of basin-scale land use for various crop types coupled with known application rates to develop the time series, accounting for the uncertainties in both crop area and application rates. The compilation shows that N and P application has declined across four of the six natural resource management regions over the past one to two decades, however, there is considerable variability at the basin-scale, particularly in the timing of peak fertiliser application. This variability reflects changes in land use including shifts in crop types and/or cropped areas, as well as reductions in fertiliser application rates. We also show that mill mud/ash application to sugarcane crops provides extra plant-available N and P that should be incorporated into farm-scale nutrient budgets. Finally, we evaluate the long-term trends in N use efficiency in sugarcane, the dominant crop in the GBR catchment area, and reveal that the industry has improved markedly over the past one to two decades while maintaining consistent yields. These data contribute an important line of evidence for evaluating long-term trends in water quality and provide insights into the changing environmental footprint of croplands within the GBR catchment area.

key: evaluation of natural farming system in capsicum for sustainable plant health management
title: Evaluation of natural farming system in capsicum for sustainable plant health management
abstract: The indiscriminate use of chemical pesticides and fertilizers has seriously threatened the ecosystem and led to the eradication of beneficial microflora and fauna, besides having adverse effects on human health. Natural farming (NF) offers an environmentally friendly and sustainable approach to address these issues. In order to compare the impact of a NF system with conventional farming (CF) system for capsicum cultivation in the mid-hills of Himachal Pradesh, India, the current study was conducted during 2023 and 2024. The experiment was initiated in February for both years and the cropping period continued until September 2023 and 2024, respectively. The factorial experiment was laid out in a Randomized Block Design having ten replications per treatment. At the time of land preparation, ghanjeevamrit was applied @1.5 t/ha. After seed treatment with beejamrit, capsicum seedlings were transplanted in the field. French bean was grown as an intercrop, while finger millet was planted as a border crop. For nutrient management, jeevamrit was applied as a 10% drenching solution at 15-day intervals. Need-based sprays of rog nashi dawayain and keetnashi astra were applied for the management of diseases and insect pests. In CF plots, standard recommended agronomic practices were followed. Soil analysis revealed significant improvements in the physico-chemical and microbiological properties of the soil under the NF system. In addition, a significant reduction in soil-borne diseases and aphid population was observed compared to the CF system. The NF system recorded a higher average crop equivalent yield (365.8 q/ha) and greater net returns (₹11,71,660/ha) compared to the CF system, which produced 347.6 q/ha yield and net returns of ₹7,43,570/ha. These results indicate that the NF system can be effectively adopted for capsicum cultivation to improve soil health, promote sustainable plant health management, enhance biodiversity, reduce the cost of cultivation, and increase economic returns. However, further research is needed to develop effective management strategies for foliar diseases such as powdery mildew under the NF system.

key: effect of different herbicide application timings on the 1000 seed weight of soybean
title: EFFECT OF DIFFERENT HERBICIDE APPLICATION TIMINGS ON THE 1000-SEED WEIGHT OF SOYBEAN
abstract: The article presents the results of field studies conducted in 2023-2025 in the foothill zone of the Kabardino-Balkarian Republic, investigating the effect of herbicide application timings on the 1000-seed weight of soybean variety SK Riana. The experiment evaluated pre-emergence and post-emergence applications of the herbicides Tracer, EC; Python, EC; and Zontran, SC. It was established that in all herbicide-treated variants, the 1000-seed weight exceeded that of the untreated control. The highest values of this parameter were obtained with pre-emergence pesticide application. The results demonstrated that early application of herbicides promotes the formation of larger soybean seeds. The findings indicate the advantage of pre-emergence herbicide treatment as an effective component of soybean cultivation technology.

key: strategies of conservation and adaptation measures for sustainable agriculture against cli
title: Strategies of conservation and adaptation measures for sustainable agriculture against climate change
abstract: Climate variability and change on the agricultural sector are projected to steadily manifest directly from changes in land and water regimes. Climate change is expected to result in long-term water and other resource shortages, worsening soil conditions, drought and desertification, disease and pest outbreaks on crops and livestock, sea-level rise, and so on. Vulnerable areas are expected to experience losses in agricultural productivity, primarily due to reductions in crop yields. Global estimates predict (without consideration of CO2 fertilization effects or adaptation) a 20–30 percent reduction in grain production. Latest research results revealed that gains in soil organic carbon have been overestimated and are partly or completely offset by increased N2O emissions. Seed banks that maintain a variety of seed types provide an opportunity for farmers to diversify, allowing them to both counter the threat of climate change and develop a profitable specialization. Some strategies for stabilizing the yield of agriculture crops need to be developed on war footing and major among them could be both mitigation strategies as well as adaptation strategies. The former includes shift towards renewable energy, sustainable agriculture and even sustainable transport system which involves least fuel consumption. However, the adaptation strategies may include planed infrastructure development, restoration of ecosystem and above all climate resilient agriculture including reduced waste consumption.

key: agricultural transformation and regional disparities in bihar an analytical assessment bas
title: Agricultural Transformation and Regional Disparities in Bihar: An Analytical Assessment Based on Agricultural Statistics (2001–2025)
abstract:
Agriculture in Bihar has changed considerably over the past two decades, but these changes have not been the same in all parts of the state. This study looks into agricultural transformation and regional differences in Bihar during the period 2001–2025.Paper examines the relationship between irrigation, fertilizer use, and cropping intensity on the one hand, and foodgrain production and land productivity on the other. The analysis relies on CAGR to track how key variables have changed over time, OLS regression to see which factors most affect yield, and one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s post hoc test to check whether the four agro climatic zones of Bihar differ significantly from one another.
The empirical results underscore a discernible shift within Bihar's primary agricultural sector. Key indicators of agricultural performance show marked improvement over the period. Average yields of foodgrains in the state have risen from 1,480 kg/ha during 2001–05 to 2,820 kg/ha during 2021–25 (CAGR 2.73%). This increase has been associated with faster growth in fertilizer use (CAGR 3.58%) and a steady expansion of net irrigation coverage (CAGR 1.29%). The regression model explains most of the variation in productivity (R² = 0.942, p < 0.001) and identifies chemical fertilizer application (β = 6.12, p < 0.001) and the net irrigation ratio (β = 12.84, p = 0.001) as the main factors behind the rise in yields. Nonetheless, the ANOVA examination (F = 8.42, ρ = 0.0002) refutes the hypothesis of regional uniformity, exposing notable productivity divergences among the various sub-regions. The leading productivity performance in South-West Bihar (Zone III-B) is attributed to superior canal infrastructure and heightened adoption of inputs, in contrast to the limitations faced by North-Eastern (Zone II) and South-Eastern (Zone III-A) districts due to waterlogging and seasonal moisture challenges. The study advocates for tailored infrastructure development strategies, formalization of tenant credit mechanisms, and expansion of market linkages to foster more inclusive agricultural growth.

key: from the spray tank to the bee nest translocation and persistence of fungicide residues in
title: From the spray tank to the bee nest: translocation and persistence of fungicide residues in Osmia cornuta food provisions.
abstract: Pesticide exposure is a central component of pollinator risk assessment. Yet, how field application rates translate into actual bee exposure remains poorly understood. We traced translocation of the fungicide tebuconazole from the spray tank to flowers, pollen and nectar, up to the body of adults and larval food provisions of the solitary bee Osmia cornuta foraging on oilseed rape and apple. Tebuconazole levels measured on the day of application and the day after were notably higher than previously published records. We found that, relative to the spray tank concentration (100%), residues decreased consistently across bee-relevant matrices in the following order: flowers (16-20%) > pollen (2-14%) > provisions (1.5-3.6%) > nectar (0.12-0.13%) ≥ bees (0.02-0.17%). Comparisons of our results with RUD (Residue per Unit Dose) distributions revealed crop- and matrix-specific deviations in residue levels. We also investigated fungicide degradation rates on flowers and in larval provisions within the bee nest of four fungicides with contrasting modes of action (tebuconazole, boscalid, pyraclostrobin and captan). Residues dissipated rapidly on flowers but remained largely stable for up to 12 days in stored pollen-nectar provisions. These results show that food provisions act as fungicide reservoirs, with larvae experiencing full exposure levels well after provisions are built. Consequently, exposure levels calculated from on-flower pollen-nectar measurements may grossly underestimate actual larval exposure. We combined food consumption estimates from the literature with our residue measurements to estimate fungicide intake in O. cornuta adults and larvae.

key: land suitability and sustainable management options for cotton production in bafime and la
title: LAND SUITABILITY AND SUSTAINABLE MANAGEMENT OPTIONS FOR COTTON PRODUCTION IN BAFIME AND LARAZOUROU, KORHOGO DEPARTMENT, COTE D IVOIRE
abstract: Cotton yields in the Northern Basin of Cote d Ivoire have declined under the combined effects of pests, diseases, soil degradation, water stress and poor crop management, a situation made worse by the scarcity of detailed site-level pedological data. This study characterized soil fertility constraints and evaluated land suitability for cotton in two representative villages of Korhogo Department, Bafime and Larazourou. Six composite topsoil samples (four from Bafime, two from Larazourou) and two complete soil profiles (0-100 cm, one per village) were collected in 2021 and analysed using standard laboratory methods. Climatic suitability was assessed from 1980-2020 ERA5 reanalysis data, and both components were evaluated with the FAO/Sys et al. (1993) crop-requirement framework. The soils were slightly acidic to near-neutral (mean pH 6.52) with moderate base saturation (55.6%), but their overall fertility was low.
