key: evaluation of inline emitter clogging in drip irrigation system with groundwater and chemi
title: Evaluation of inline emitter clogging in drip irrigation system with groundwater and chemical compounds in greenhouse
venue: Journal of Kerbala for Agricultural Sciences
abstract: This study was conducted to evaluate the impact of various irrigation treatments on the performance and efficiency of a drip irrigation system used in tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) cultivation. The research focused on the effects of emitter clogging, emission uniformity (EU), and Christiansen's coefficient of uniformity (CU) on system reliability and crop productivity. Six different treatments were assessed, and the results demonstrated highly significant differences among them. Treatments T3 and T5 consistently showed superior performance, maintaining high EU and CU values with manageable clogging levels, resulting in significantly higher yields and water use efficiency. In contrast, treatments T1, T2, and T4 exhibited moderate clogging and intermediate performance, while T6 performed poorly all parameters, despite having the lowest clogging index, suggesting deeper design or pressure-related issues. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and cluster analysis further validated these findings, with treatments grouping according to their clogging behavior and irrigation performance. PCA revealed that over 94% of the dataset's variability was explained by emitter clogging, highlighting its dominant role in irrigation efficiency. Strong negative correlations were observed between clogging and yield, especially at the final stage, confirming the progressive nature of performance decline under poorly maintained systems. The study concludes that emitter clogging is the primary cause of reduced water distribution uniformity and yield, but that optimal design and regular maintenance can significantly mitigate its effects. These findings provide practical insight into the neproactively managing clogging to sustain high irrigation efficiency and crop productivity in protected agriculture systems.

key: the effect of some treatments with mitigated frost damage on mango trees under desert soil
title: The effect of some treatments with mitigated frost damage on mango trees under desert soil conditions
abstract: The present study was carried out during the 2024 and 2025 seasons on 10-year-old ‘Naomi’ mango cultivar trees grown in an orchard located on Abo Ghaleb Road, Egypt. In this study, we examine the effects of foliar sprays of salicylic acid at (5, 10, and 20 gl-1), potassium silicate at (15, 30, 45 ml l-1), glycine betaine at (7.5, 15 and 30 g l-1) and mono-potassium phosphate at (0.01, 0.02 and 0.04 g l-1) foliar spraying in mid-November, December and January. Leaf area, chlorophyll content (SPAD reading), macro- and micronutrient levels in leaves, yield, and fruit characteristics were used to assess the influence. The results indicated that all spray treatments yielded the best results in terms of leaf area, proline, and leaf chlorophyll content, while improving the yield and quality characteristics of ‘Naomi’ mango fruits compared to the control in both seasons. Glycine betaine (GB) at 15 g l-1, followed by potassium silicate (KS) at 15 ml l-1 outperformed all other spray treatments and recorded the highest values across all studied characteristics. Finally, treatments have increased the trees’ tolerance to frost stress; it is advisable to apply them as an agronomic practice in mango trees grown under frost stress.

key: herbicide use in ivory coast application practices and ecotoxicological exposure in peri u
title: Herbicide Use in Ivory Coast : Application Practices and Ecotoxicological Exposure in Peri-Urban Horticulture
abstract: Horticultural production in peri-urban areas supports livelihoods and supplies fresh produce, but herbicide handling near surface waters may create occupational and environmental exposure. This study characterised herbicide-use practices among horticulturists in four villages of the Azaguié basin, southern Ivory Coast. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews and direct field observations. The surveyed farmers were predominantly young men; 61.7% were aged 18–40 years, 47.5% had no formal schooling, and 68.6% reported no training in herbicide use. All surveyed farmers reported using herbicides. Glyphosate was used by 100%, while 2,4-D and nicosulfuron were reported by 63.0% and 28.7%, respectively. No farmer reported calibrating spraying equipment before application, and 67.1% determined application amounts empirically rather than solely following manufacturer recommendations. Personal protective equipment use was very limited, with 97.0% reporting no use. Empty containers were abandoned in the agricultural environment by 45.7% of farmers, and 75.7% washed sprayers in nearby watercourses. Principal component analysis identified three farmer profiles differentiated mainly by training, technical practices, and proximity of plots to watercourses. The findings indicate that limited training, empirical application practices, inadequate waste management, and close contact between production areas and surface waters are important features of herbicide use in the study area. Practical training and measures adapted to riparian production settings may help reduce exposure.

key: influence of environment and management practices on soybean seed composition in north car
title: Influence of environment and management practices on soybean seed composition in North Carolina
abstract:
Soybeans [
 Glycine max
 (L.) Merrill] are a valuable source of protein and oil used for industrial, agricultural, and culinary purposes. It is important to understand how shifts in management practices influence not only soybean yield but also soybean quality parameters, like protein and oil content. Between 2019 and 2023, field trials were installed at 19 different environments across North Carolina for a total of 2775 plots used in this analysis. Trials were set up to access the impact of management factors, such as soybean planting date and maturity group (MG), on soybean yield, soybean protein and oil content, and soybean damage and purple seed stain. Soybean protein and oil content were inversely related across NC regions, MGs, and planting dates. The relationship between soybean yield and protein was minimal. Soybean protein content was typically higher for later maturing varieties (>MG4), while the inverse was observed for oil content, which was lower with later maturing varieties. Across all environments, as average reproductive temperatures increased, yield, protein, and oil generally increased as well. There was a minimal relationship between soybean yield and soybean seed damage and purple seed stain. Growers can use this information to make more informed management decisions regarding the impact of planting date and MG selection on soybean seed composition and quality.

key: agriculturally relevant pesticide exposure scenario induces early life lipid metabolism di
title: Agriculturally relevant pesticide exposure scenario induces early-life lipid metabolism disruption and physiological stress in Caiman latirostris.
abstract: Pesticide use in extensive agriculture generates complex exposures for wildlife, however, early-life effects in reptiles remain underexplored. In this study, we evaluated whether embryonic exposure at manufacturer-recommended concentration for field use: glyphosate (GLY at 1 and 2%), 2,4-D (at 0.06 and 0.12%), chlorantraniliprole (CAP at 0.015 and 0.03%), imidacloprid (IMI at 0.1 at 0.2%) and three mixtures at the lowest concentrations (M1: GLY+2,4-D; M2: CAP + IMI; M3: M1+M2) disrupt lipid metabolism, lipoperoxidation and corticosterone levels in Caiman latirostris hatchlings. Hatching success declined under 2,4-D 0.06%, CAP 0.03%, and IMI 0.2%. Residual yolk showed alterations in polyunsaturated fatty acids, together with yolk-cholesterol and α-tocopherol depletion, particularly under CAP 0.03% and in the complex mixtures M1, M2, and M3. Changes in plasma lipid profiles, hepatic aminotransferase activities as well as alteration of NADPH-producing gene expression in blood were observed in M2 and M3. Higher lipoperoxidation levels were observed at the highest concentration across single compounds and in M1 and M3; whereas corticosterone increased in 2,4-D 0.12%. These findings demonstrate that early life stages of caimans are highly sensitive to these xenobiotics, affecting lipid metabolism and associated physiological processes. Moreover, mixtures induced stronger and more complex responses than single compounds, leading to metabolic disruption during early development. Our findings highlight the importance of evaluating realistic agrochemical mixtures to better assess their ecological risk.

key: intercropping relatively salt tolerant and salt sensitive crops to improve agricultural ef
title: Intercropping Relatively Salt-Tolerant and Salt-Sensitive Crops to Improve Agricultural Efficiency in Saline Environments
abstract:
As climate change rapidly increases sea levels, soil salinity in coastal agricultural regions rises, and
food security in affected areas may decline. This study investigated whether intercropping relatively
salt-tolerant crops with salt-sensitive crops optimizes plant growth efficiency and survival under varied
saline conditions. In a controlled environment, relatively salt-tolerant crops (kale and sugar beet) and
salt-sensitive crops (cilantro and lettuce) were germinated at seawater concentrations of 0%, 25%, 50%,
and 75%. Live seedling percentage (the percentage of planted seeds with a live, visible seedling at
each count, combining germination and short-term survival), plant height (measured through ImageJ),
and root-zone electrical conductivity (EC) were observed over 17 days. Surviving seedlings were
transferred into two large trays: Tray A (cilantro centered within surrounding kale and beets) and Tray
B (central rows of beets adjacent to rows of cilantro) under a 50% seawater concentration. By 50 days
after transplant, results indicated that elevated salinity initially reduced live seedling percentage and
early growth, especially in salt-sensitive crops like cilantro and lettuce. However, the EC levels sharply
declined between days 49 and 67 across all treatments, corresponding with continued plant survival. In
Tray A, the cilantro displayed notable growth even under high saline concentrations. These observations
are consistent with the hypothesis that specific intercropping patterns with salt-tolerant crops may
reduce root-zone electrical conductivity—a proxy for the concentration of dissolved salts in the growth
medium surrounding plant roots—and create more favorable growing conditions for salt-sensitive crops.
However, because no non-planted or monoculture control was included, these data cannot isolate plantmediated
salt uptake from other possible contributors to the observed EC decline (e.g., irrigation dilution,
leaching, or general plant water uptake). Because plant tissue ion content was not measured, these data
do not demonstrate salt removal by any species; plant-based salt removal warrants further investigation
as a sustainable, low-cost strategy for saline agriculture. Future controlled experiments to confirm these
findings are warranted to help advise crop selection and spatial design for floating farm systems in floodaffected
coastal regions.

key: impact of glyphosate management techniques on residue levels and chemical composition of c
title: Impact of glyphosate management techniques on residue levels and chemical composition of Coffea arabica and Coffea canephora beans.
abstract: Glyphosate is the most extensively applied herbicide and can be absorbed by non-target plants potentially altering their chemical profile. Coffee, the second most consumed beverage worldwide, relies on glyphosate use to sustain productivity. However, limited evidence exists regarding absorption of soil-applied glyphosate, its possible translocation into coffee beans, and chemical changes. This study investigated the impact of different glyphosate application techniques on chemical composition and residue accumulation in Coffea arabica and Coffea canephora beans. Plants were subjected to seven treatments varying in spray nozzle types (flat-fan and cone) and application schedules (October and December; October and February; and October, December and February). Glyphosate residues were quantified by LC-MS/MS, while gravimetric analyses assessed moisture, ash, and soluble extract yield; chlorogenic acids and caffeine were determined by UHPLC-PDA. Results demonstrated that glyphosate is absorbed and translocated to beans, with residue levels ranging from 0.0 to 0.5 mg/kg. Nonetheless, applications performed in October and December resulted in lower residues levels compared to schedules performed until February, with no significant alterations related to the negative control. Contrary to expectations, chlorogenic acids levels were not affected by glyphosate application. Similarly, despite isolated differences, none of the evaluated parameters were significantly influenced by glyphosate use. These findings were supported by PCA and PERMANOVA, which revealed that sample discrimination was influenced exclusively by species and crop year. Further studies investigating additional coffee bean compounds, particularly from a food safety perspective, are needed to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the effects of glyphosate on coffee beans.

key: the dynamic impact of land use changes on soil organic carbon
title: The dynamic impact of land-use changes on soil organic carbon
abstract: This study examines the response of soil organic carbon (SOC) to land-use changes (LUCs) across Europe. Using field data from the LUCAS survey and satellite-based Corine Land Cover data, we find that SOC losses due to conversions to cropland are immediate (63% occurs within the first 1.5 years) whereas SOC accumulation following conversions from cropland to grassland or forest is more gradual (10–20 years) but still with a notable peak in the first 1.5 years. Our dynamic approach reveals a potentially much higher carbon sequestration from LUC (an indicative 572 MtC between 1990 and 2021) than reported by current national inventories (76 MtC), although both approaches come with substantial limitations. These findings suggest that conservative IPCC Tier 1 estimates may understate the mitigation potential of land-use policies. We provide ready-to-use, country-specific emission factors to improve the precision of national greenhouse gas inventories and to support compliance with public regulation, though further validation is needed for forest-related LUCs due to small sample sizes and the possible incorporation of forest litter into topsoil measurements.

key: the effect of groundwater table depth on soil fertility restoration in rice systems
title: THE EFFECT OF GROUNDWATER TABLE DEPTH ON SOIL FERTILITY RESTORATION IN RICE SYSTEMS
venue: 3i: intellect, idea, innovation - интеллект, идея, инновация
abstract: Prolonged flooding of paddy fields exceeding 60–80 days triggers water-bogging, gleying of the soil profile, and a reduction in total soil porosity by at least 25–30%. The article addresses the challenges associated with the reclamation state of rice irrigation systems in the Kyzylorda region. The study aims to scientifically substantiate the optimal parameters for groundwater table depth and mineralization to prevent irrigation-induced salinization and effectively restore soil fertility. Field and laboratory experiments were carried out in 2022–2023 at the Karaultobe experimental site covering an area of 16 hectares. The research methodology involved stationary water level monitoring, systematic hydrochemical sampling, and phenological observations of plant development. It was established that during the initial flooding phase, pore water salinity in the arable layer sharply increases to 3.2–6.5 g/L. This induces seedling suppression, reduces stand density to 80–120 plants per square meter, and results in an average yield drop of 1.6 t/ha. Lowering the groundwater level to 1.8–2.0 m within 20–25 days during the irrigation interval restores proper soil aeration and increases rice yield to 4.0–5.0 t/ha. These findings justify the need to regulate the initial irrigation modules and transition toward subsurface horizontal drainage construction.

key: the influence of herbicides on weed infestation and winter wheat yield in the northwestern
title: The influence of herbicides on weed infestation and winter wheat yield in the Northwestern zone of the Rostov region
abstract:
Purpose: to evaluate the influence of herbicide treatments on weed infestation and winter wheat yield depending on the predecessor (bare fallow and winter wheat) in the Northwestern zone of the Rostov region. 
Materials and methods. The study was carried out from 2021 to 2024 in the Northwestern zone of the Rostov region. The experiment was two-factorial: factor A was the predecessor (bare fallow, winter wheat), factor B was the herbicide treatment. The experimental design included variants with the application of herbicides Granat, VDG (0.025 kg/ha), Pixel, MD (0.3 l/ha), Primadonna Super, KKR (0.75 l/ha), Fenizan, VR (0.2 l/ha), Zinger, SP (0.01 kg/ha), a tank mixture of Granat, VDG + Primadonna Super, KKR (0.015 kg/ha + 0.4 l/ha). In winter wheat crops (Cinderella variety), weed infestation and yield were recorded. The influence of the predecessor on the species composition of the weed component was determined: the proportion of perennial weeds, such as field bindweed (Convolvulus arvensis), Canadian thistle (Cirsium arvense) increases after the winter wheat predecessor. 
Results. The application of preparations at the three-leaf phase of the crop ensured a significant reduction in the number of weeds. The herbicides Primadonna Super, KKR, Fenizan, VR, and a tank mixture (Granat + Primadonna Super) demonstrated the greatest effectiveness in controlling a wide range of weeds, including hard-to-eradicate species (Canadian thistle, field bindweed). The reduction in the number of Canadian thistle was 98.1–100 % and field bindweed was 86.2–97.6 %. The effectiveness of the herbicides varied depending on the precursor, which is associated with changes in the weed species composition and the phytosanitary condition of the field. 
Conclusions. All herbicide variants provided a significant increase in yield compared to the control. Maximum economic efficiency was achieved with the herbicide Zinger, SP, which provided the greatest yield increase with both predecessors: 1.14 t/ha (30.3 %) after bare fallow and 0.98 t/ha (34.6 %) after winter wheat.

key: factors influencing the productivity of typical chernozem in organic farming
title: Factors influencing the productivity of typical chernozem in organic farming
abstract: This study examined the interrelationship between the bulk density of typical chernozem of the Eastern Forest-Steppe, the soil nutrient regime and crop productivity under variable hydrothermal conditions in organic farming. The research was carried out in a long-term field experiment near Kharkiv, Ukraine, in a four-field crop rotation comprising a winter wheat predecessor, winter wheat, sugar beet and spring barley. The predecessors of winter wheat were peas, vetchling, maize for silage, a vetch– oat mixture, soybean and fallow, and organic fertilisation relied on non- commodity crop residues. Over fourteen years soil bulk density ranged from 1.02 to 1.26 t m⁻³ in the 0–15 cm layer and from 1.04 to 1.30 t m⁻³ in the 15– 30 cm layer. Higher temperatures combined with reduced precipitation increased soil density. The incorporation of sugar beet tops significantly decreased bulk density of the 0–15 cm layer in the following year, and increasing the amount of tops from 7 to 14 t ha⁻¹ raised subsequent grain yield from 2 to almost 7 t ha⁻¹. Higher precipitation from February to July reduced the content of available nitrogen. Maximum root yield of sugar beet was obtained when the sum of mean ten-day air temperatures from April to July reached 140–145 °C. Crop productivity in organic systems is therefore determined by the joint action of hydrothermal conditions, soil agrophysical properties, the nutrient regime and the fertilising effect of plant residues.

key: subnational variation in sustainable nitrogen management across indian croplands and its l
title: Subnational variation in sustainable nitrogen management across Indian croplands and its linkage with state-level governance
abstract: Sustainable food production requires the reconciliation of agricultural productivity with environmental protection, a challenge especially acute in rapidly intensifying systems. India exemplifies this tension through heavy reliance on synthetic fertilizers and strong regional variation in nitrogen use efficiency. Yet subnational trajectories of nitrogen sustainability and their drivers remain poorly understood. Using five decades of district-scale data, we show that India’s Sustainable Nitrogen Management Index (SNMI), which integrates nitrogen yield and nitrogen use efficiency, improved nationally, declining from 1.02 to 0.84, mainly through productivity gain. However, spatial variation nearly doubled over the same period. The Indo-Gangetic Plains showed relatively stable SNMI trajectories, whereas the central-western plateau experienced a more than three-fold increase in variability. Even neighboring states with similar agroclimatic conditions diverged sharply. Within Western Plateau region, Madhya Pradesh achieved almost threefold higher nitrogen yield while maintaining lower nitrogen surplus than Maharashtra, reflecting differences in crop diversification, irrigation, procurement and input-use patterns. These findings show that governance and management contexts can strongly shape nitrogen sustainability, highlighting the need for region-specific sustainable intensification strategies. Nitrogen sustainability in India has improved mainly through higher productivity, but regional disparities have nearly doubled as governance and management drive divergent trajectories, based on five decades of district-level nitrogen yield and use-efficiency data.

key: farmland and cropping pattern dynamics in myanmar implications for food security and susta
title: Farmland and Cropping Pattern Dynamics in Myanmar: Implications for Food Security and Sustainable Agriculture
abstract: Myanmar, an agriculture-based economy, is one of the most important agricultural countries in mainland Southeast Asia. Although previous studies have documented changes in agricultural land-use and cropping patterns, trends in farmland area, cropping patterns, and food sufficiency across Myanmar’s 14 states/regions remain limited. This study addresses these gaps by using land-cover data from the global 30 m dynamic dataset and statistical data from 2000 to 2025, and household surveys from selected areas. GIS-based spatial analysis, trend analysis, and multivariate analysis of variance were applied to analyze both the direction and magnitude of farmland and cropping pattern changes over time. The results showed that Myanmar’s farmland area increased significantly (τ = +0.52, p < 0.01), expanding by 23.6% over the study period. Double cropping remained an important system, increasing by 55.9%. In the central dry zone, sufficient water availability showed the strongest effect on crop production and farmland area (F = 11.191, p < 0.001, η2p = 0.037), followed by soil fertility loss (F = 10.263, p < 0.001, η2p = 0.034). The analysis estimated that domestic consumption requirements were approximately 7.97 million tons of rice, 3.12 million tons of wheat, and 0.42 million tons of maize. These findings can support sustainable farmland use planning and inform food security policy decisions in Myanmar.

key: integrating natural farming for enhanced seed yield soil health and profitability in onion
title: Integrating natural farming for enhanced seed yield, soil health and profitability in onion seed production
abstract:
Aim: The study conducted from 2022–2024 aimed to study the impact of natural farming on the growth, yield, seed quality and economics on onion seed production and, to identify natural treatments that could serve as sustainable alternatives to conventional farming.

Methodology: Thirteen treatments involving different cropping systems and natural sprays such as buttermilk and Sounthaster were evaluated, including a conventional control. Plant height, leaf count, umbel diameter, seeds per umbel, 1000-seed weight and disease incidence, severity were among the field metrics that were noted. Seed quality traits, soil parameters were assessed using standard procedures and economic returns were expressed in terms of Benefit: Cost ratio.

Results: Maximum plant growth, days to flowering, highest seed yield, minimum days to seed harvest, and lowest disease incidence was recorded in T10- Onion sole crop with 4 sprays of Butter milk. T4 - Onion+Fenugreek with 4 sprays of Butter milk performed statistically at par with T10 and T13. Both T10 and T4 also recorded superior seed quality and higher Benefit: Cost ratio.

Interpretation: The results showed that the natural farming, particularly buttermilk-based treatments, improves soil health, plant growth, and seed vigour, resulting in increased yield and quality. Hence, for the production of high-quality onion seeds, treatments T10 and T4 are therefore appropriate and profitable choices.

Key words: Buttermilk, Jeevamrit, Natural farming, Onion seed

key: benefits in crop yield and soil properties of straw return across chinas agricultural regi
title: Benefits in Crop Yield and Soil Properties of Straw Return Across China’s Agricultural Regions
abstract: Published syntheses showed that straw return generally benefits crop production and soil quality. However, direct evidence is still needed to determine whether these benefits are consistent and how they vary among regions and cropping systems. The analysis included 379 treatment-comparator records from 24 monitoring sites in a national field experimental network covering six major agricultural regions of China. Specifically, 2800 outcome-specific effect sizes, each expressed as the ratio of the straw return treatment to its paired straw removal comparator, were compiled for crop yield and nine soil indicators. Compared with straw removal, straw return was associated with 3.6% higher crop yield (95% CI, 0.9% to 6.5%); pooled estimates were also higher for soil organic matter (11.5%), total nitrogen (5.7%), available phosphorus (9.0%), available potassium (14.7%), volumetric soil water content (6.1%), water-stable aggregates (17.8%), and plough-layer thickness (16.4%). Heterogeneity among agricultural regions was detected for crop yield, available phosphorus, available potassium, water-stable aggregates, and plough-layer thickness; because agricultural region is strongly confounded with cropping system in this network, these differences are region-associated rather than attributable to geography itself, and several regional strata were represented by only two or three monitoring sites. Among cropping systems, heterogeneity was detected for available potassium, water-stable aggregates, and plough-layer thickness, but not for crop yield. The shorter-duration category had a larger available phosphorus response, whereas the longer-duration category had larger aggregate and plough-layer responses but did not show an additional mean yield benefit. The observed profiles suggest that P-K balance and soil structure monitoring merit priority in rice paddies in southern China. Similarly, residue placement in Northeast China, soil test-based K management in North China, and coordinated water and nutrient management in Northwest and Southwest China are indicated as monitoring priorities rather than as validated prescriptions. Overall, straw return was associated with higher crop yield and with higher values of multiple soil properties, although the response profiles differed among regions. These patterns indicate a need for locally validated, region-specific strategies if the national benefits of straw return for both crop yield and soil quality are to be realized.

key: autumn application of the new combined herbicide bomba flo od to protect winter wheat crop
title: Autumn application of the new combined herbicide Bomba Flo, OD to protect winter wheat crops in the Krasnodar Territory
venue: Achievements of Science and Technology in Agro-Industrial Complex
abstract: The studies were conducted to investigate the biological and economic efficiency of using the modern three-component herbicide Bomba Flo, OD (150 g/l tribenuron-methyl + 120 g/l thifensulfuron-methyl + 60 g/l florasulam) in winter wheat crops. The work was carried out in 2023-2025 in the Krasnodar Territory in accordance with the guidelines for registration tests of herbicides in agriculture. The field experiment design included the following options: herbicide Bomba Flo, OD at rates of 0.05 and 0.10 l/ha in pure form and together with 0.1% of the volume of the working fluid surfactant Adju, F; the standard was the herbicide Bomba, WDG at rates of 0.02 and 0.03 kg/ha together with the surfactant Adju, F (0.1% of the working fluid volume), the control was without the use of herbicides. The crops were treated in autumn, in the phase of 2-3 leaves of winter wheat and early stages of weed growth, manually using a PULVEREX sprayer, the working fluid consumption rate was 200 l/ha. The initial weed infestation on average over 2 years of research was 107 specimens/m2. The use of the herbicide Bomba Flo, OD on winter wheat provided high biological efficiency (79.7-100%) against annual dicotyledonous weeds: catchweed bedstraw, common speedwell, corn poppy and starry grasswort without a phytotoxic effect on the crop. The biological efficacy of Bomba Flo, OD at rates of 0.1 l/ha alone and 0.05 l/ha combined with the surfactant Adju, F was higher than that of the standard Bomba, WDG at a rate of 0.02 kg/ha mixed with the surfactant Adju, F. The herbicidal activity of the combined application of 0.1 l/ha of the test product and 0.03 kg/ha of the standard with adjuvant was virtually identical. When evaluating the economic efficacy of the products, a statistically significant yield preservation rate of 7.4-8.9% was observed.

key: the effect of biological fertilisation on the intensity of nitrogen carbon cycling in crop
title: The effect of biological fertilisation on the intensity of nitrogen-carbon cycling in crop rotations in the forest-steppe
abstract: The aim of the study was to determine the parameters of a novel integrated stoichiometric model of the interrelated nitrogen and carbon cycles under conditions involving the implementation of different types of crop rotations, alternative types of organic fertilisation and varying methods of mechanical soil cultivation in the agrocenoses of the forest-steppe of Ukraine. The research methodology was based on a combination of long-term field observations and an integrated stoichiometric framework for evaluating nitrogen, as well as carbon balances under different fertilisation systems and soil tillage practices. It was established that the type of organic fertiliser directly correlates with the level of CO₂ emis - sions resulting from mineralisation processes: when manure is applied, the range of emissions is usually 25–85 tonnes, whereas the use of by-products increases this level to 80–160 tonnes. In the first scenario, a more intensive nitrogen removal relative to its input was observed, whereas in the second, a progressive increase in total stocks was recorded. An increase in CO₂ emissions in such cases is accompanied by an improvement in the soil carbon balance and an in - crease in the overall yield of the system. An assessment of the impact of black soil tillage methods showed that with non-inversion tillage technology - regardless of the type of crop rotation or fertiliser – a positive trend in soil carbon balance is observed, whereas with ploughing, the nature of the increase in organic matter deficit has a non-linear (para - bolic) form. Ploughing is characterised by a wider range of CO₂ emissions, indicating more active mineralisation. The results of the study confirmed the high efficiency of using shredded crop by-products in combination with appropriate nitrogen compensation via mineral fertilisers. The practical significance of the results lies in substantiating the effec - tiveness of using crop by-products and non-inversion tillage to stabilise nitrogen-carbon cycling, restore the fertility of chernozems and increase the productivity of agrocenoses in the forest-steppe of Ukraine.

key: aquacropdndc modeling of rice yield and greenhouse gas emissions under alternate wettingdr
title: AquaCrop–DNDC Modeling of Rice Yield and Greenhouse Gas Emissions Under Alternate Wetting–Drying and Climate Change in Coastal Peru
abstract: Paddy rice on the arid Peruvian coast is water- and emission-intensive; alternate wetting and drying (AWD) lowers both, yet their joint response under climate change is rarely quantified. AquaCrop-OSPy and DNDC were coupled one-way under a single bias-corrected forcing, each calibrated on its own 2023 observable, for Oryza sativa cv. INIA 515 Capoteña, and projected to 2100 under three CMIP6 scenarios. Canopy cover was reproduced within 0.3 to 1.7 percentage points in-sample and 1.8 to 5.2 out-of-sample, although the grain yield was underestimated by 24 and 39%. AWD20 saved 27.5% of the irrigation water for 7.9% less grain (+27% water productivity) and cut the global warming potential by 76% as measured in 2023 and by 86–89% as simulated, representing a model ceiling. Carbon fertilization sustained the yield to 2100 in every scenario; the late-century downturn under SSP5-8.5 proved specific to the CO2 formulation of the crop model, and flowering sterility was never reached. Adaptive irrigation changed nothing, but pairing AWD20 with a rescheduled planting window increased the yield by 14% and preserved 86% of the mitigation. Emission projections remain conditional on the crop carbon input, which the one-way coupling transfers only as a seasonal total.

key: evaluating the effects of foliar sulfur application timings on nutrient acquisition and so
title: Evaluating the effects of foliar sulfur application timings on nutrient acquisition and soybean performance
abstract:
A reduction of atmospheric sulfur (S) deposition and increased S removal by high‐yielding crops in recent years have caused more frequent occurrences of S deficiency in crop‐producing regions of the United States. It is necessary to explore solutions for mitigating S deficiency to optimize soybean [
 Glycine max
 (L.) Merr.] yield and seed quality. A field study was conducted from 2019 through 2021 at two locations in eastern South Dakota to determine the effect of foliar S application on soybean performance and nitrogen (N) and S accumulation at different growth stages. The study included 11 S application treatments of ammonium sulfate: five single foliar applications at rate of 5.6 kg S ha
 −1
 , applied at V4, R2, R3, R4, and V4 + micronutrient; three treatments with multiple foliar applications at V4 + R2, V4 + R3, and R2 + R3 growth stages with each application at rate of 5.6 kg S ha
 −1
 . Two preplant applications at rates of 5.6 and 11.2 kg S ha
 −1
 and control were also included. Overall, multiple foliar applications increased S concentration in most recent mature leaves at R4 growth stage, S accumulation in leaves and stems at R6, S accumulation in stover at R8 growth stage. S applications decreased grain N:S ratio compared to control. However, S applications had no effect on S accumulation in pods and seeds, grain yield, grain protein, and oil content. The results suggest that foliar S application is not expected to be a widely recommended practice for soybean S management in eastern South Dakota.

key: maximizing maize yields while minimizing soil erosion in mollisol regions of china and the
title: Maximizing maize yields while minimizing soil erosion in Mollisol regions of China and the United States
abstract: As vital global granaries in Mollisol regions, the Upper Mississippi River Basin (UMRB) in the U.S. and Songhua River Basin (SHRB) in China face growing demands to improve maize yields while avoiding soil erosion. We evaluated effects of individual and integrated technologies on maize yield, yield stability, and soil erosion from 2001 to 2018 with a fully calibrated Soil and Water Assessment Tool (SWAT) model. Results showed that mean yields in the SHRB lagged 4.0 t ha−1 behind the UMRB, although both regions exhibited large yield variations (CV > 10%). High-density planting provided limited yield gains, but reduced erosion by ~30%. Irrigation markedly increased yield by 11% for UMRB and 33% for SHRB, and improved yield stability (CV < 5%), but increased erosion by >10%. Integrated irrigation and high-density planting boosted yields, mitigated erosion, and increased net returns. Yet a 1.5 t ha−1 difference remained between China and the U.S., underlining the need for germplasm improvement to close the productivity divide.

key: effects of one time application of controlled release compound fertilizer on peanut yield
title: Effects of one-time application of controlled-release compound fertilizer on peanut yield and nitrogen loss in sloping farmland
abstract:
Nitrogen (N) loss via surface runoff is a critical issue in sloping farmland, contributing to non-point source pollution and limiting crop productivity. In peanut (Arachis hypogaea L.) production, improving nitrogen use efficiency (NUE) while minimizing environmental risks is essential for achieving sustainable agricultural development. Controlled-release compound fertilizers (CRF) may provide a promising approach to synchronizing N release with crop demand and reducing nutrient losses in runoff. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of one-time basal application of CRF on N runoff losses, NUE, and peanut yield in sloped peanut fields.

 Compared with 100%CF treatment in 2022 and 2023, 100%CRF treatment significantly reduced NO

key: a humus balance model for promoting rapeseed in regenerative agriculture and a low carbon
title: A humus balance model for promoting rapeseed in regenerative agriculture and a low-carbon economy in the Russian Federation
abstract:
The aim of the study is to evaluate the applicability of rapeseed as a crop for promoting regenerative agriculture and to determine the crop's potential for stimulating the development of a low-carbon economy in the Russian Federation (RF). A state-of-the-art domestic model for managing the humus budget (HB) for soils in agroecosystems was used. HB calculations for spring and winter rapeseed were based on rapeseed yield data publicly available from state statistics. Two options for generating humus-forming biomass were considered: 1) reduced – the sum of root and stubble plant residues; 2) expanded – the sum of root, stubble plant residues and by-products. The НB in the reduced version of the humus-forming biomass of winter rapeseed was positive, and the soil accumulated approximately 2.2 c/ha. In this version of growing spring rapeseed, the НB was negative, and the soils annually lose approximately 1.4 c/ha of humus. With the expanded in of humus-forming biomass into the soil, the НB for winter and spring rapeseed was positive. The soils demonstrated extended fertility restoration, which corresponds to the goals of regenerative agriculture. Winter rapeseed can be used for regenerative farming without restrictions. Spring rapeseed can only be used in the case of increased biomass input for humus formation. Cultivation of winter rapeseed results in humus fixation in the soil, which, when converted into carbon units, amounts to +0.48 t CO
 2
 -eq/ha. Cultivation of spring rapeseed results in humus loss of –0.30 t CO
 2
 -eq/ha. Because the area under spring rapeseed is fourfold greater than that under winter rapeseed, the total amount of carbon units in the RF is –0.433 million t-CO
 2
 -eq. With increased input of humus-forming biomass, winter and spring rapeseed production can result in soil absorption of approximately 5.714 million tons of CO
 2
 -eq, which represents approximately 5% of the annual carbon emissions of the Russian agricultural sector in year 2022. The use of winter rapeseed for the development of a low-carbon economy in the RF is permitted without restrictions. The use of spring rapeseed for these purposes is only possible with increased input of humus-forming biomass.

key: method of producing and application of slow release fertilizers for use in agriculture
title: Method of Producing and Application of Slow-Release Fertilizers for Use in Agriculture
abstract:
Introduction. Modern fertilizers effectively replenish nutrient deficiencies in the soil, reduce environmental impact, and ensure food security for the planet's growing population. Theaim of this study is to develop amethod for producing slow-release fertilizers and to evaluate their effectiveness in the field. 
Materials and Methods. Laboratory experiments were carried out to develop anovel slow-release fertilizer encapsulated in apolymer matrix made of cellulose ether. Key performance metrics of the resultant cellulose-containing fertilizers were evaluated, focusing particularly on the content of diverse nitrogen forms at intervals of 7, 14, 21, and 28 days post-soil application. Furthermore, microbial cellulolytic activity was assessed 21 days following fertilizer application. 
Results. In the course of this research, amethodology for synthesizing anovel type of slow-release cellulose-containing fertilizer intended for agricultural applications was developed. Field trials confirmed the effectiveness of the resulting materials. Moreover, optimal component ratios were established to maximize the performance of the newly formulated fertilizers – by the final day of the experiment, the cellulose-containing fertilizer N8P36 demonstrated maximum nitrate (NO3–) retention – 7.6 mg/kg, indicating amore uniform and balanced conversion of nitrogen compounds when applying theaverageamount of nitrogen in the cellulose-containing fertilizer compared to the control. Microbiota analysis indicates that the synthesized fertilizers at dosages of N8P36 and N4P18 achieve maximum bacterial colonization relative to the control. 
Conclusion. The proposed technology holds promise for contemporary crop cultivation methods. The developed materials will be able to ensure sustained nutrient delivery into the soil, minimizing nitrogen and phosphorus loss, optimizing plantabsorption, and ultimately enhancing agricultural efficiency. Given the experimental outcomes, it becomes evident that the developed technology shows substantial potential for generating eco-friendly and cost-effective fertilizers characterized by controlled nutrient release profiles. Future investigations will concentrate on refining the matrix formulation and augmenting fertilizer stability across varied soil compositions and climates.

key: assessing the impact of nitrogen and weed management on weeds and productivity of dry dire
title: Assessing the impact of nitrogen and weed management on weeds and productivity of dry direct-seeded rice in eastern India
abstract: The objective of this study was to identify effective nitrogen and weed management options to manage weeds and improve productivity of dry direct-seeded rice. This study was conducted during kharif 2020 at Central Rainfed Upland Rice Research Station (CRURRS), Hazaribagh, Jharkhand. A split plot design replicated thrice was used. The tested treatments include: three nitrogen (N) doses in main plots, viz. No N, with recommended dose (RDF) of phosphorus (P) and potash (K) only [No N (RDF of P and K)]; RDF: 80 N:17 P:33 K kg/ha with N applied in 3 splits i.e. 50% basal +25% at tillering +25% at panicle initiation stage [RDF (N:P:K=80:17:33 kg/ha)]; 50% N using farm yard manure (FYM) + 50% N as need based top dressing up to panicle initiation stage, using leaf colour chart (LCC) [50% FYM + RTNM (LCC)]. Four weed management treatments assigned to sub-plots include: un-weeded control (UWC), weed-free control (WFC), pre-emergence application (PE) of pendimethalin 1.5 kg/ha followed by (fb) brown manuring with Sesbania aculeata (by knocking down Sesbania at 25 days after seeding (DAS) with bispyribac-Na 25 g/ha), pendimethalin 1.5 kg/ha PE fb bispyribac -Na 25 g/ha at 25 DAS. The grassy weeds were most dominant. Amongst weed management treatments, brown manuring with Sesbania aculeata significantly reduced weed density by 79.6 % and 88.8% and weed dry biomass by 90.6%, and 96.6 % at 40 and 70 DAS, respectively and increased rice grain yield by 31.06 % over un-weeded control. In case of N management practices, the combined use of FYM and LCC based N management produced highest grain yield with reater reduction in weed density, weed dry biomass, WI and increasing WCE (64.1 % and 76.4% at 40 and 70 DAS, respectively) and WCI (70.5% and 72.9% at 40 and 70 DAS, respectively) with highest overall B:C ratio (2.65), proving to be the most profitable combination in the study.

key: regenerative agriculture we need better evidence to inform policy
title: Regenerative agriculture: we need better evidence to inform policy
abstract: Regenerative agriculture (RA) is increasingly promoted as a means of reducing the environmental impacts of food production while maintaining agricultural productivity. However, evidence for its effects on crop yields and greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions remains highly variable, creating uncertainty about its overall climate benefits. We argue that evaluating RA requires a system-wide perspective that considers productivity, land-use change, and production displacement alongside field-scale emissions. To illustrate this, we developed a stylised land-use simulation representing a UK arable landscape and explored a range of plausible yield and production-emission outcomes reported for RA and its constituent practices. Production shortfalls were met through conventional domestic and international production under alternative intensification and extensification pathways, while yield gains released land for habitat restoration. The analysis shows that system-level climate outcomes are highly sensitive to assumptions about yield response. Yield reductions increased land demand and, where additional production required agricultural expansion, emissions from land-use change frequently outweighed reductions in production emissions. Conversely, maintaining or increasing yields reduced land requirements and created opportunities for habitat restoration and carbon sequestration. Although illustrative rather than predictive, our analysis demonstrates that the climate impact of RA cannot be inferred from field-scale emissions alone. Assessments and policy should explicitly consider uncertainty in productivity, land-use change, and displacement effects when evaluating the climate mitigation potential of regenerative agriculture.

key: machine learning for the developing world
title: Machine Learning for the Developing World
venue: ACM Transactions on Management Information Systems
abstract: Researchers from across the social and computer sciences are increasingly using machine learning to study and address global development challenges. This article examines the burgeoning field of machine learning for the developing world (ML4D). First, we present a review of prominent literature. Next, we suggest best practices drawn from the literature for ensuring that ML4D projects are relevant to the advancement of development objectives. Finally, we discuss how developing world challenges can motivate the design of novel machine learning methodologies. This article provides insights into systematic differences between ML4D and more traditional machine learning applications. It also discusses how technical complications of ML4D can be treated as novel research questions, how ML4D can motivate new research directions, and where machine learning can be most useful.

key: terrorism geopolitics and oil security using remote sensing to estimate oil production of
title: Terrorism, geopolitics, and oil security: Using remote sensing to estimate oil production of the Islamic State
abstract: As the world’s most traded commodity, oil production is typically well monitored and analyzed. It also has established links to geopolitics, international relations, and security. Despite this attention, the illicit production, refining, and trade of oil and derivative products occur all over the world and provide significant revenues outside of the oversight and regulation of governments. A prominent manifestation of this phenomenon is how terrorist and insurgent organizations—including the Islamic State group, also known as ISIL/ISIS or Daesh—use oil as a revenue source. Understanding the spatial and temporal variation in production can help determine the scale of operations, technical capacity, and revenue streams. This information, in turn, can inform both security and reconstruction strategies. To this end, we use satellite multi-spectral imaging and ground-truth pre-war output data to effectively construct a real-time census of oil production in areas controlled by the ISIL terrorist group. More broadly, remotely measuring the activity of extractive industries in conflict-affected areas without reliable administrative data can support a broad range of public policy and decisions and military operations.

key: how much oil is the islamic state group producing evidence from remote sensing
title: How much oil is the Islamic state group producing ? evidence from remote sensing
abstract: Accurately measuring oil production in low-governance contexts is an important task. Many terrorist organizations and insurgencies -- including the Islamic State group, also known as ISIL/ISIS or Daesh -- tap oil as a revenue source. Understanding spatial and temporal variation in production in their territory can help address such threats by providing near real-time monitoring of their revenue streams, helping to assess long-term economic potential, and informing reconstruction strategies. More broadly, remotely measuring extractive industry activity in conflict-affected areas and other regions without reliable administrative data can support a broad range of public policy decisions and academic research. This paper uses satellite multi-spectral imaging and ground-truth pre-war output data to effectively construct a real-time day-to-day census of oil production in areas controlled by the terrorist group. The estimates of production levels were approximately 56,000 barrels per day (bpd) from July-December 2014, drop to an average of 35,000 bpd throughout 2015, before dropping further to approximately 16,000 bpd in 2016.

key: hardware accelerated detection of unauthorized mining activities using yolov11 and fpga
title: Hardware-Accelerated Detection of Unauthorized Mining Activities Using YOLOv11 and FPGA
venue: International Journal of Advanced Computer Science and Applications
abstract: —Illegal mining activities present significant environmental, economic, and safety challenges, particularly in remote and under-monitored regions. Traditional surveillance methods are often inefficient, labor-intensive, and unable to provide real-time insights. To address this issue, this study proposes a computer vision-based solution leveraging the state-of-the-art YOLOv11 Nano and Small models, fine-tuned for the detection of illegal mining activities. A specific dataset comprising aerial and ground-level images of mining sites was curated and annotated to train the models for identifying unauthorized excavation, equipment usage, and human presence in restricted zones. The proposed system integrates the hardware-software design of YOLOv11 on the PynqZ1 FPGA, offering a high-performance, low-latency, and energy-efficient solution suitable for real-time monitoring in resource-constrained environments. This hardware-accelerated approach combines FPGA’s parallel processing capabilities with the lightweight deep learning models, enabling efficient deployment for automated illegal mining detection. By providing a scalable, real-time monitoring tool, this work contributes to the development of automated enforcement tools for the mining industry, ensuring better control and surveillance of mining activities. To validate the efficiency of deep learning deployment on edge devices, YOLOv11n was implemented on an FPGA, utilizing 70% of available LUTs, 50% of FFs, and 80% of DSPs, with 8.3 Mbits of on-chip memory. The design achieved 100.33 GOP/s throughput, 18 FPS at 55 ms latency, consuming 4.8 W, and delivering an energy efficiency of 20.90 GOP/s/W.

key: prevention of agricultural market risks by agricultural production entities in hubei provi
title: Prevention of Agricultural Market Risks by Agricultural Production Entities in Hubei Province
abstract: Different agricultural production and operation entities face the same market risks. Since there is a huge gap in market risk prevention ability between agricultural market operation entities, the gap of risk prevention effect is huge. Using statistical analysis and comparative analysis methods, this paper analyzed characteristics and influencing factors of agricultural market risks and pointed out characteristics of agricultural market and special characteristics of agricultural production and operation entities in Hubei Province. Based on SWOT analysis on market risk prevention ability of agricultural production and operation entities in Hubei Province, it came up with three recommendations, including upgrading agricultural production and operation entities, enlarging the production and operation scale, and strengthening the ability of balancing the market demand and supply and bargaining power and pricing power.

key: analysis of indemnification of income risk at sector level the case of slovenia
title: Analysis of indemnification of income risk at sector level: the case of Slovenia
abstract: Using Monte Carlo simulations, the impact of different levels of risks on indemnification through an income stabilisation tool is investigated at the sector level. The presented approach, using the IACS database, allows analyses of differences across farms with respect to farm type and farm size, applying average-based approaches. Such preliminary information is useful for policy makers responsible for the design and introduction of measures to tackle income risk issues and to identify potential beneficiary groups among farmers. The analysis shows that on average 25 per cent of farms would be indemnified annually, the majority in fruit production, the dairy sector and hop production. Mixed farm types, with a share 34 per cent, receive only 15 per cent of total sum of indemnity. However, if EUR 12,000 of average income is set as the threshold for participation in such a tool, only 6 per cent of farms participate and only 13.3 per cent of them would be indemnified. Indemnity at farm level would range between EUR 82 and 40,870. Taking into account all farms in the sector, the average indemnity is EUR 918 per farm and almost EUR 13,500 for the second case.

key: agricultural monopolistic competitor and the pigovian tax
title: Agricultural monopolistic competitor and the Pigovian tax
abstract: A monopolistically competitive agricultural market structure has some features of competition and some features of monopoly. Monopolistic competition has the following attributes: (a) many sellers; (b) product differentiation; and (c) free entry. In the long-run equilibrium, price equals average total cost, and the agricultural firm earns zero economic profit. The aim of this paper is to construct a relatively simple chaotic long-run monopolistic competitor’s agricultural output growth model that is capable of generating stable equilibria, cycles or chaos. A key hypothesis of this work is based on the idea that the coefficient plays a crucial role in explaining local stability of the monopolistic competitor’s agricultural output, where d is the coefficient of the marginal cost function of the agricultural monopolistic competitor; b is the coefficient of the inverse demand function; [] is the coefficient of average cost growth; m is the Pigovian tax rate; and e is the coefficient of the price elasticity of demand.

key: internal control over financial reporting and mortgage fraud
title: Internal Control over Financial Reporting and Mortgage Fraud
abstract:
Mortgage fraud was a leading force behind the 2008 financial crisis. We measure the fraudulent income overstatement at the bank-ZIP Code-year level as the difference in the local growth between reported income in mortgage applications and the income based on IRS data. We find that overstated income is positively associated with banks’ internal control weaknesses over financial reporting and negatively associated with subsequent remediation of such weaknesses. The associations are concentrated among banks that integrate their accounting and operation processes, as proxied by the adoption of an Enterprise Resource Planning system. Finally, using the removal of internal control provisions in the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation Improvement Act in 2005 as a shock to internal control quality, we find that affected banks experience increased income overstatement on mortgage applications.

key: the effectiveness of budgeting policies to optimize the implementation of poverty alleviat
title: The Effectiveness of Budgeting Policies to Optimize the Implementation of Poverty Alleviation and the Eradication of Extreme Poverty by Local Governments
venue: Journal of Governance, Taxation and Auditing
abstract: Poverty is a multidimensional issue linked not only to low income but also to limited public access to education, healthcare, productive employment, social protection, basic infrastructure, and economic opportunities. In the context of fiscal decentralization, local governments hold a strategic position, as the majority of public service and development interventions that directly impact the community are implemented through the Regional Budget (APBD). This study aims to analyze the effectiveness of local government budgeting policies in optimizing efforts to alleviate poverty and eradicate extreme poverty, as well as to identify the factors determining the effectiveness of budget allocation. The study employs a qualitative-descriptive approach, utilizing literature reviews and policy analysis of regulations, planning and budgeting documents, statistical data, and empirical research findings regarding local government spending and poverty. The analysis reveals that the effectiveness of budgeting policies is not determined solely by the size of the budget allocation but also by targeting accuracy, collaboration among local government agencies, the alignment between development planning and regional budgeting documents, the quality of beneficiary data, a results-oriented approach, and the monitoring and evaluation of policy implementation. Fragmented budgeting policies risk producing numerous programs with limited impact. Conversely, budgeting based on data, location, target groups, and results can enhance the effectiveness of local government interventions. Therefore, optimizing the regional budget for poverty alleviation and the eradication of extreme poverty requires a strategy that combines reducing expenditure burdens, increasing income, and addressing pockets of poverty through an integrated approach.

key: consumption and saving patterns in switzerland new evidence based on administrative tax da
title: Consumption and saving patterns in Switzerland: new evidence based on administrative tax data
venue: Swiss Journal of Economics and Statistics
abstract: We use administrative data on income and wealth of taxpayers in the canton of Bern to impute consumption based on the budget constraint. We validate the imputed consumption and use the panel data on consumption, income and wealth to provide stylized facts on consumption and saving patterns in Switzerland for the period 2002-2022. We document a large drop of the saving rate in the first ten years after retirement and show that 75% of permanent income shocks and 40% of transitory income shocks transmit to total consumption expenditures.

key: analysis of special instruments for reducing income inequality and poverty used in eu coun
title: ANALYSIS OF SPECIAL INSTRUMENTS FOR REDUCING INCOME INEQUALITY AND POVERTY USED IN EU COUNTRIES
abstract: This article analyzes special policy instruments employed by European Union countries to reduce income inequality and poverty. The conducted research focuses on targeted and universal mechanisms such as social transfers, tax-benefit systems, minimum income schemes, in-work benefits, social vouchers, and active labour market policies, examining their role in improving income distribution and social inclusion. Using a comparative analytical approach, the paper evaluates the effectiveness of these instruments across EU member states, with attention to their design, their coverage, targeting efficiency, and their fiscal sustainability. Key inequality and poverty indicators, including the Gini coefficient, at-risk-of-poverty rate, and material and social deprivation indices, are used to assess the outcomes. The analysis highlights the best practices and common challenges, such as balancing universality with targeting, ensuring adequate benefit levels, and maintaining work incentives. The findings suggest that integrated policy mixes, combining income support with the employment and social services, are most effective in reducing poverty and inequality. The paper concludes by outlining policy lessons relevant for countries seeking to align social protection systems with EU standards and strengthen social cohesion. Additionally, the study emphasizes the importance of policy coordination and institutional capacity in ensuring the effective implementation and long-term sustainability of these instruments.

key: impact of the collection mode on salaried labour income data evidence from colombia before
title:
Impact of the Collection Mode on Salaried Labour Income Data: Evidence From Colombia Before and During the
 COVID
 ‐19 Pandemic
venue: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics
abstract: The strict confinement implemented by the National Government of Colombia in 2020 to contain the expansion of the COVID‐19 pandemic created challenges in data collection operations conducted through household surveys. As a result, surveys that traditionally relied on face‐to‐face collection methods transitioned to a remote mode using telephone surveys. We exploit a quasi‐experimental design based on the geographical‐temporal exogenous variation in the collection mode of the leading household survey for the Colombian labour market and the linkage of this survey to the nationwide social security administrative record to measure the impact of the change in the collection mode on the reported salaried labour income. We find that the change in collection mode reduces the measured salaried labour income by approximately 4.4 percentage points and increases its variance and dispersion, with differences between population groups. These findings have implications for the development of mixed data collection methods and the analysis of income‐based statistics.

key: an empirical analysis of agricultural credit s impact on wheat productivity and farm incom
title: An empirical analysis of agricultural credit's impact on wheat productivity and farm income in India
abstract:
This study aims to assess the impact of agricultural credit on productivity and farm income on wheat in India. Based on national sample survey data for the year 2018–19, the endogenous switching regression (ESR) model was employed to estimate the true effect of the credit access. Our findings reveal that while credit access helps to boost productivity, it does not proportionally increase income due to external factors like market conditions and price fluctuations. The study highlights a negative selection bias, where lower-yield farmers access credit but may not fully benefit.
 
 
 
 To estimate impact of access to farm credit on farmers productivity and income, various empirical models have been used in the literature, including OLS regression, Propensity Score Matching (PSM) and ESR. Each method has its strengths and limitations, with ESR being well-suited for this type of analysis. This model estimates separate equations for treated and untreated groups, incorporating a selection equation that captures decision to participate in the treatment. ESR is particularly effective in situations where unobserved factors influence both treatment and outcome, as it includes a stochastic error term to control the latent variables.
 
 
 
 Access to credit has potential to increase productivity as well as farm income of wheat. The estimated treatment effect on the treated (ATT) reveals a remarkable increase in the productivity of farmers who had access to credit. This highlights the crucial role that credit availability plays in enhancing the productivity of wheat farmers. However, while examining the impact of credit access on farm income, the estimation of ATT was found to be non-significant.
 
 
 
 The findings reveal that credit access enhances wheat productivity, as it enables farmers to invest in modern inputs like improved seeds, fertilizers and machinery. However, this increase in productivity does not translate into a proportional rise in farm income. Additionally, household characteristics like age, education, gender and social status differentially influence credit access. To address these challenges, policy measures should include targeted financial products for disadvantaged groups, gender-inclusive lending practices, training programs on financial literacy and strengthening agricultural cooperatives are crucial for ensuring that productivity gains from credit access leads to sustained income for wheat farmers.
 
 
 
 It is crucial to examine the real impact of institutional credit on wheat farming. Wheat, being one of the most important staple crops in India, not only sustains millions of farmers but also plays a vital role in the country's food security. Therefore, understanding how credit access influences wheat productivity and the income of wheat-growing farmers is of paramount importance. This study aims to address this critical gap by identifying the major determinants of credit access for wheat production and assessing its effects on the productivity and income of wheat farmers at the farm household level in India.

key: farm input subsidies and energy poverty evidence from malawi
title: Farm Input Subsidies and Energy Poverty: Evidence From Malawi
abstract: Farm input subsidies in sub‐Saharan Africa are widely recognised for their role in reducing income poverty by improving household incomes. However, their spillover effects to non income‐based poverty receives comparatively less attention, despite the potential. Using data from the 2020 Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey, this paper investigates the effects of Malawi's farm input subsidy programme on energy poverty. To address potential endogeneity in the selection process for subsidy participation, political clientelism is used as an instrumental variable. The analysis reveals that programme participation reduces energy poverty by 20.4 percentage points. This result is robust across various definitions of energy poverty and is further supported by the Lewbel technique, an alternative quasi‐experimental method. The study identifies increased household wealth among beneficiaries as a key mechanism driving the reduction in energy poverty. These findings suggest that expanding access to input subsidies could be a valuable policy tool for simultaneously addressing both income and non‐income poverty in Malawi and similar contexts.

key: restricoes a robos em pregoes eletronicos impactos nos leiloes de cafe do comprasnet
title: Restrições a robôs em pregões eletrônicos: impactos nos leilões de café do Comprasnet
abstract: O estudo analisa os impactos econômicos de duas regras que restringiram o uso de programas de computador para submissão automática de lances em pregões eletrônicos do Comprasnet. A “Regra dos 20s” impôs o intervalo mínimo de 20 segundos entre lances subsequentes de um mesmo fornecedor. A “Regra dos 3s” impôs o intervalo mínimo de 3 segundos para cobrir a melhor oferta. A Regra dos 3s teria causado um aumento de preços de aproximadamente 15%, correspondendo a um aumento de R$7,5 milhões nos gastos do Governo Federal com aquisição de café entre janeiro de 2014 e dezembro de 2015.

key: cutting special interests by the roots evidence from the brazilian amazon
title: Cutting special interests by the roots: Evidence from the Brazilian Amazon
abstract: Government policies may impact economic outcomes directly but also indirectly through effects on political equilibria. This paper examines the effects of the PPCDAm – a centralized environmental policy that synced real-time satellite deforestation data with enforcement on the ground – on the behavior and electoral outcomes of a powerful special-interest group operating in the Brazilian Amazon: farmers. Exploiting close elections, we document that municipalities governed by farmer mayors had higher deforestation rates and CO2e emissions, earmarked more resources to agriculture, and experienced more land-related conﬂict before, but not after, the PPCDAm was implemented. Any electoral advantage these mayors had before the policy also disappears with the introduction of the PPCDAm. Our ﬁndings are consistent with a political agency model where candidates use their occupation to signal commitment to deforestation.

key: acessibilidade na amazonia legal delimitacao da area de influencia e riscos ambientais
title: Acessibilidade na Amazônia Legal: Delimitação da Área de Influência e Riscos Ambientais
abstract: Diante desse cenário, investimentos em infraestrutura logística são considerados fundamentais para melhorar a conexão da Amazônia Legal com mercados domésticos e internacionais, impulsionando o desenvolvimento econômico da região. Entretanto, a experiência das últimas décadas sugere que investimentos em logística na Amazônia Legal enfrentam desafios de implementação e geram consideráveis danos socioambientais. Esses custos modificam a análise de custo-benefício de projetos de logística na região. Por exemplo, somente o custo do carbono liberado pelo desmatamento decorrente da implementação de projetos de infraestrutura logística na Amazônia, frequentemente supera o próprio custo fiscal de implementação dos projetos.

key: efficient forestation in the brazilian amazon evidence from a dynamic model
title: Efficient Forestation in the Brazilian Amazon: Evidence from a Dynamic Model
abstract: This paper estimates the Brazilian Amazon’s efficient forestation level. We propose a dynamic discrete choice model of land use and estimate it using a remote sensing panel with land use and stock of carbon of 5.7 billion pixels, at 30 meters resolution, between 2008 and 2017. We estimate that a business as usual scenario will generate an inefficient loss of 1,075,000 km2 of forest cover in the long run, an area almost two times the size of France, implying the release of 44 billion tons of CO2. We quantify the potential of carbon and cattle production taxes to mitigate inefficient deforestation. We find that relatively small carbon taxes can mitigate a substantial part of the inefficient forest loss and emissions, while only very large taxes on cattle production would achieve a similar effect.

key: stimulant or depressant resource related income shocks and conflict
title: Stimulant or Depressant? Resource-Related Income Shocks and Conflict
abstract: We provide evidence on the mechanisms linking resource-related income shocks to conflict, focusing on illegal crops. We hypothesize that the degree of group competition over resources and the extent of law enforcement explain whether opportunity cost or contest effects dominate. Combining temporal variation in international drug prices with spatial variation in the suitability to produce opium, we show that higher prices increase household living standards and reduce conflict in Afghanistan. Analyzing shifts in conflict tactics and using geo-referenced data on drug production networks and territorial control highlight the importance of opportunity costs, and reveal heterogeneous effects consistent with our theory.

key: godfather politicians and organized violence the good the bad and the bloody
title: Godfather Politicians and Organized Violence: The Good, the Bad, and the Bloody
abstract: Social order is compromised when mafias fight violently to resolve disputes. Ironically, a corrupt local politician – instead of an honest one – may serve as an impartial arbitrator (“Godfather”) to safeguard local peace. This paper builds a model of politician-mafia interaction to show, both theoretically and empirically, that a rent-seeking local politician, with the power of the state, may provide credible commitment to enforce peaceful mafia negotiations. However, when such godfather politicians are eradicated, the local power vacuum leads to surges of local violence. The anti-corruption campaign in China since 2012 – an institutional shock to eradicate corrupt politicians – provides a unique natural experiment to corroborate our theory. A difference-indifferences test suggests that violence surged by 30% in regions with local officials eradicated due to collusion with mafias, compared to the regions without. We also conduct a series of robustness checks and placebo tests to confirm the link between the violence surge and the removal of corrupt local officials.  Chen: Fudan University, E-mail: cs@fudan.edu.cn; Fan: Cheung Kong Graduate School of Business, E-mail: xyfan@ckgsb.edu.cn. Wang: Fudan University, Email: 16300680009@fudan.edu.cn .

key: avocados mexico s green gold the u s opioid crisis and its impact on mexico s drug cartel
title: Avocados: Mexico's Green Gold. The U.S. Opioid Crisis and its Impact on Mexico's Drug Cartel Violence
abstract: The global increase in the demand for avocados has attracted the attention of rent-seeking criminal organizations in Mexico. As a result, farmers and packing houses have become the targets of drug trafficking organizations (DTOs). This paper aims to answer whether declining drug revenues have motivated cartels to target licit businesses, such as avocado farms, rather than continue specializing in the production and distribution of illicit drugs. To do this, I exploit exogenous variation in the demand for pure heroin in the U.S. between 2011 and 2019. In particular, I use the introduction of Fentanyl in the U.S. as a proxy for the reduction in the demand for pure heroin in Mexico to answer whether this led to an increase in homicides and cartel presence in avocadoand poppy-growing municipalities. Using municipal level data, I show that the decrease in the demand for heroin increased homicide rates (including those of agricultural workers) in avocado-growing municipalities. I find no evidence of higher cartel presence in these municipalities, suggesting that, while DTOs do not seem to be moving into these municipalities, they have become more violent toward civilians. Furthermore, I find that the fall in the demand for heroin led to a decrease in cartel presence and homicide rates in poppy-growing municipalities. Overall, this paper provides evidence of inter-sector spillovers resulting from drug demand changes. title: Fueling Organized Crime: The Mexican War on Drugs and Oil Thefts
abstract: We show that the War on Drugs launched by the Mexican President Felipe Calderón in 2007 pushed drug cartels into large-scale oil thefts. Municipalities that the presidential candidate’s party barely won at the local elections in 2007-2009 exhibit a larger increase in illegal oil taps over the following years, compared to municipalities in which the presidential candidate’s party barely lost the elections. Challenger cartels in the drug market leapfrog incumbent drug cartels when entering the new illegal activity, analogous to what is typically observed in legal markets. Since challengers and incumbents specialize in diﬀerent criminal sectors, the expansion of challengers does not increase violence in municipalities traversed by oil pipelines. At the same time, the municipalities traversed by a pipeline witness a decrease in schooling rates. PAN candidates who succeeded in the ﬁrst mayoral elections held after the start of the War on Drugs (2007-2009) favored the coordination of the crackdown on narcotics at the local level. Therefore, she estimates the eﬀect of government crackdowns on drug-related violence and drug-traﬃcking routes by comparing municipalities in which PAN candidates won or lost by a narrow margin. Using the same Regression Discontinuity (RD) design within the sub-sample of municipalities traversed by oil pipelines, we show that municipalities in which the PAN candidate won a local election by a narrow margin in 2007-2009 had more taps over the following period, 2007-2014, compared to municipalities in which the PAN candidate lost by a narrow margin. key: wildlife trade policy and the decline of wildlife
title: Wildlife Trade Policy and the Decline of Wildlife
abstract: The Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES) is the international agreement that regulates international trade in wildlife to prevent its decline. Little is known about the effectiveness of its trade restrictions and bans. Combining the largest available panel database on wildlife population sizes of vertebrates with the history of species’ inclusion into CITES, we find that populations increase by 20% after their species’ inclusion into CITES. This effect is driven by populations in countries with thorough enforcement. Outright trade bans increase wildlife, but restrictions that incentivize sustainable use have more immediate positive effects.

key: the brazilian amazons double reversal of fortune
title: The Brazilian Amazon’s Double Reversal of Fortune
abstract: We use high-resolution satellite data to determine how Amazonian deforestation changes discretely at the Brazilian international border. We document two dramatic reversals. In 2000, Brazilian pixels were 37 percent more likely to be deforested, and between 2001 and 2005 annual Brazilian deforestation was more than three times the rate observed across the border. In 2006, just after Brazil introduced policies to reduce deforestation, these differences disappear. However, from 2014, amid a period of economic crisis and deteriorating commitment to environmental regulation, Brazilian deforestation rates jump back up to near pre-reform levels. These results demonstrate the power of the state to affect whether wilderness ecosystems are conserved or exploited.
