key: the accumulation of crime and the crime of accumulation narcopolitics the entrenchment of
title: “The Accumulation of Crime and the Crime of Accumulation”: Narcopolitics, the Entrenchment of Violence, and States of Internal War in Latin America
venue: Revista Mexicana de Ciencias Políticas y Sociales
abstract: The article examines the ⁠relationship between drug ⁠control and global capitalism since the colonial ​era, ⁠using ‍a historical-structural approach ‍and ⁠panel ‌data (2013–2022). ​It analyzes the cycles ‌of narcocapital accumulation, characterized by ‍inequality, ⁠the criminalization ‍of ‍the narcoproletariat, and ‍the ​impunity of the ‌narcobourgeoisie. Key factors driving violence in ‍Latin America are identified as narco-financial networks, the militarization of internal security, ‌and the perpetuation of inequality. Despite limitations due ‍to incomplete data in some ⁠countries, the ​study provides a robust analysis of ‍the impact of narcocapital on ​state ⁠formations ⁠and democracy. ​It reviews critical ⁠alternatives ‌to the war on drugs, such as Colombia’s ‍“Total ‌Peace” strategy, cannabis legalization in ⁠Uruguay, ‍and ‌the ‍community revaluation of coca ​in Bolivia. The study concludes that reducing ‍violence requires dismantling narco-financial networks, transforming socioeconomic ​structures, ‍and prioritizing equality as the ⁠foundation for strengthening democracy ​and fostering a more just social coexistence.

key: imperial boomerangs and the militarization of human rights from port au prince to rio de j
title: Imperial boomerangs and the militarization of human rights: From Port-au-Prince to Rio de Janeiro
abstract:
This article examines the connections between Brazil's participation in the United Nations Stabilization Mission in Haiti (MINUSTAH), and the consolidation of militarized approaches to human rights in domestic security in Brazil. Drawing on the concept of the “boomerang effect,” it argues that the Brazilian involvement in Haiti played a central role in updating practices of counterinsurgency and militarized social control that would later be employed domestically. The article draws on the methodology proposed by Go J (2024)
 Policing Empires: Militarization, Race, and the Imperial Boomerang in Britain and the US
 . Oxford University Press]. for analyzing the transnational travels of policing practices, which focus on sites, practices, importers, and relations. It is based on a review of official documents produced by the Brazilian government and an analysis of discourse by Brazilian authorities. The article analyses the MINUSTAH experience, as well as three internal security policies in Brazil. It argues that a militarized approach to human rights was consolidated from these experiences, through which violent police and army incursions came to be framed as actions intended to guarantee the rights of populations living in impoverished urban territories, even as they generated massive violations of those very rights. In doing so, it helped legitimize, under a democratic banner, the use of state violence as a means of controlling marginalized populations.

key: gomes lund and herzog a pattern of brazilian resistance to conventionality control
title: GOMES LUND AND HERZOG: A PATTERN OF BRAZILIAN RESISTANCE TO CONVENTIONALITY CONTROL
authors: Amanda Gabrielle Do Nascimento Santos Ribeiro
abstract: This article examines the pattern of resistance displayed by the Brazilian legal order to the conventionality control exercised by the Inter-American Court of Human Rights (IACtHR), based on the cases Gomes Lund et al. (“Araguaia Guerrilla”) v. Brazil (2010) and Herzog et al. v. Brazil (2018). In both judgments, the IACtHR declared the Brazilian Amnesty Law (Law No. 6,683/1979) incompatible with the American Convention on Human Rights, requiring the criminal accountability of state agents responsible for grave violations committed during the civil-military regime — a ruling that contradicts the position adopted by the Brazilian Federal Supreme Court (STF) in Arguição de Descumprimento de Preceito Fundamental No. 153. The study investigates to what extent the theory of double control, formulated by André de Carvalho Ramos, offers an adequate response to this jurisdictional conflict, and assesses whether Brazil’s compliance with international rulings is full or selective. The research is bibliographic and documentary, with a deductive approach, grounded in Inter-American Court case law and specialized doctrine. The findings show that Brazil consistently complies with the pecuniary dimension of international rulings but resists the dimension that would require reopening criminal accountability or revising positions already settled by the STF. The article concludes that the double control theory is observed as a full normative standard but applied only partially in Brazilian institutional practice, characterizing a consolidated regime of financial reparation still lacking an effective regime of non-repetition of violations.

key: legitimacy rebellion and the sanctification of violence rethinking international law theol
title: Legitimacy, rebellion, and the sanctification of violence: Rethinking international law, theology, and human rights in Africa's armed conflicts
venue: Transformation: An International Journal of Holistic Mission Studies
abstract: War and violence in Africa's postcolonial conflicts are fundamentally shaped by contested claims of legitimacy across law, politics, and religion. This article argues that the prohibition on the use of force under Article 2(4) of the UN Charter has operated asymmetrically, privileging state authority while marginalizing internal struggles for justice. Although Article 1(4) of Additional Protocol I recognized wars of national liberation, it entrenched hierarchies that legitimize some forms of violence while delegitimizing others. In parallel, religious narratives have been mobilized to both sanctify resistance and justify coercion by state and non-state actors. Drawing on African philosophical traditions, particularly ubuntu, and the African human rights framework, the article advances a reconstructive vision of legitimacy grounded in relational dignity, responsibility, and the preservation of life, challenging the enduring sanctification of violence in law and theology.

key: electoral violence in cross river and akwa ibom states
title: Electoral Violence in Cross River and Akwa Ibom States
venue: International journal  of research and innovation in applied science
abstract: Electoral violence remains a major threat to democratic stability in Nigeria, particularly in the South-South where political competition is tied to access to state resources. This study examines the causes and manifestations of electoral violence in Cross River and Akwa Ibom States, and assesses how institutional weaknesses, party rivalry, and socio-economic pressures shape recurring conflict. Using a mixed-methods design, quantitative data were obtained from the Nigeria Election Violence Tracker and INEC records (2011–2023), while qualitative insights came from interviews, newspaper archives, community reports, and civil society documents. Descriptive statistics, trend analysis, and thematic coding were applied to patterns across LGAs including Calabar South, Akpabuyo, Odukpani, Uyo, Ikot Ekpene, and Oron. Findings show that violence is driven by intense political competition, monetized elections, cult-group mobilization, weak law enforcement, and youth manipulation. The study recommends strengthening electoral security, enforcing sanctions, expanding civic education, and enhancing INEC’s capacity to reduce future electoral violence.

key: repression as an instrument of poverty management the bolivarian national guard between pr
title: Repression as an instrument of poverty management: the bolivarian national guard between protest suppression and control of the informal economy under conditions of mass UN-employment (2014–2026)
venue: Military Studies: Journal for Strategy, Technology and Defense Sciences
abstract:
Between 2014 and 2026 Venezuela combined the deepest peacetime economic collapse
in the modern history of the Western Hemisphere with one of its most intensive deployments of
state coercion: income poverty reached 73.2% of households and informality approximately half
of all employment (UCAB, 2025), while a United Nations fact-finding mission documented se-
curity-force conduct amounting, in its assessment, to crimes against humanity — with the Boli-
varian National Guard (GNB) responsible for the largest number of politically motivated deten-
tions and for indiscriminate firing on protesters across the 2014, 2017, 2019, and 2024 protest
cycles (UN Human Rights Council, 2020; OHCHR, 2025). The aim of this review article is to
synthesize the fragmented scholarship on Venezuelan coercion, poverty, and informality into a
single analytical account of the GNB's role. The research applies a structured review methodol-
ogy: a corpus of 53 peer-reviewed studies published 2019–2026, assembled through systematic
database searches and verified item by item, is coded by the state function each study documents,
and triangulated against United Nations, survey, and observatory sources. The original contribu-
tion of the article is the concept of coercive poverty governance and its operationalization as a
three-function typology of GNB activity — protest suppression, regulation of the informal sur-
vival economy, and enforcement of extractive rents — which reorganizes a literature convention-
ally split between “repression” and “informality” studies into a single governance logic. Key find-
ings: the reviewed literature's center of gravity shifts after 2019 from protest suppression toward
economic and extractive coercion, tracking the regime's own reallocation of the GNB; repression
functions not as a response to poverty's disorders but as the principal instrument by which an
insolvent state manages a population it can no longer pay; and lethal escalation produced exit
rather than voice — mass emigration of 7.9 million — consistent with cross-national repression
theory (Congressional Research Service, 2025; Curtice & Behlendorf, 2021; Weitzman & Huss,
2024). The typology is transferable to other cases where security forces govern survival econo-
mies under fiscal collapse.

key: on contrafacta transgression and the new right in brazil
title: On Contrafacta, Transgression, and the New Right in Brazil
abstract: This article examines the New Right’s stagings of transgression during Jair Bolsonaro’s 2018 presidential campaign. It takes as an entry point the campaign’s adoption of ‘O Proibidão do Bolsonaro’ (Bolsonaro’s Prohibited Funk), a contrafact of the funk hit ‘Baile de Favela’ (Favela Funk Party). The article then situates the song within a constellation of other contrafacta circulating on social media platforms and on the streets of São Paulo to reflect on the New Right’s transgressive performances and controversial claims to facticity. It demonstrates how the New Right deploys this sensibility to signal its alternativity to the liberal ‘mainstream’, a strategy that distances the movement both from neoliberal promises of tolerance and from the aesthetic canon of the traditional right. In a context marked by political corruption, economic crisis, and post-truth politics, this performance of transgression falsely constructs New Right leaders as truth-tellers.

key: managing conflicts in india
title: Managing Conflicts in India
abstract:
Bidisha Biswas explores the question of how a democratic state chooses between policies of coercion and accommodation when dealing with political violence by addressing an important, yet under examined, topic—India’ approach to internal conflicts. In Managing Conflicts in India, Biswas selects three cases of conflict: the separatist campaign in Punjab during the 1980s; the protracted insurgency in Kashmir; and attacks on the Indian state by left-wing extremists, also known as Maoists and Naxalites, a campaign that has existed in different forms since the 1960s. Using archival research and fieldwork, Biswas shows that the Indian state has chosen a mix of tactics in dealing with these insurgencies. She argues that the government’s responses have often been dictated by immediate political concerns, rather than a strategic vision. While the integrity of the Indian state remains intact, its democratic quality and credibility have been seriously compromised. By focusing on the choices—and missteps—that the Indian government has made, Biswas sheds light not only on the insurgencies themselves, but also on the overall processes that impact effective conflict management.

key: exploring the eu perspective on the organised nature of the trafficking in cultural goods
title: Exploring the EU Perspective on the Organised Nature of the Trafficking in Cultural Goods
abstract: In recent years the characterisation of the trafficking of cultural property as a form of organised crime has gained prominence in EU policies on the protection of cultural heritage. This article analyses how the EU has conceptualised and operationalised this link in terms of describing the phenomenon and designing countermeasures. Through a content analysis, we evaluate this connection in EU policy documents published from 1993 to 2023 that include both “organised crime” and “trafficking of cultural property” or similar terms (n=58). The analysis demonstrates conceptual deficits and a correspondingly weak foundation for EU policy, since misunderstandings related to the organised nature of trafficking of cultural property and its overlaps with other forms of organised crime, particularly terrorist financing, may result in misguided policies with the potential to undermine law enforcement efforts. We also address the addition to the list of obliged entities and persons in the anti-money laundering framework of persons trading or acting as intermediaries in the trade of cultural goods, because it opens new opportunities to disrupt the illicit financial flow in the art market. This paper is one of the results of the EU project Research, Intelligence and Technology for Heritage and Market Security (RITHMS).

key: beyond legal protection the institutional protection gap in addressing sexual and gender b
title: BEYOND LEGAL PROTECTION: THE INSTITUTIONAL PROTECTION GAP IN ADDRESSING SEXUAL AND GENDER-BASED VIOLENCE IN INDONESIA
abstract: Violence against women continues to challenge local governance even where formal protection policies exist. This study examines why legal and policy commitments do not automatically translate into substantive protection for women, using Tasikmalaya City, West Java, Indonesia, as an explanatory qualitative case. The article re-analyses interview, observation, documentary, and local administrative data originally collected for a study of the implementation of Local Regulation No. 8 of 2015 on the protection of women and children. The empirical material includes local government agencies, the Integrated Technical Implementation Unit for the Protection of Women and Children (UPTD PPA), and civil society actors including PUSPA and Taman Jingga. Reported cases in the administrative series supplied for this manuscript increased from 42 in 2020 to 164 in 2024, but qualitative evidence indicates that rising reports can reflect both persistent violence and greater willingness to report. The study identifies five connected constraints: delayed institutionalization, limited human and financial resources, incomplete survivor-service infrastructure, weak preventive outreach, and persistent patriarchal norms. It also finds that civil-society advocacy and cross sector collaboration were important in strengthening local response capacity, including the establishment of UPTD PPA. Building on policy-capacity, feminist institutionalist, collaborative governance, and survivor-centered perspectives, the article proposes the concept of an Institutional Protection Gap: the distance between formal recognition of women’s rights and the institutional and societal capacity to make protection accessible, coordinated, preventive, survivor centered, and sustainable. The study contributes a post-adoption perspective to research on violence against women policy in decentralized settings and develops the related concept of a reporting paradox for evaluating local policy outcomes.

key: after the caravels sailed continuing wrong state responsibility and the united nations res
title: ‘AFTER THE CARAVELS SAILED’: CONTINUING WRONG, STATE RESPONSIBILITY, AND THE UNITED NATIONS RESOLUTION ON THE SLAVE TRADE
venue: Journal of Advanced Research in Social Sciences and Humanities
abstract: This article examines whether the United Nations General Assembly’s Resolution 80/250, which declares the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans and the racialised chattel enslavement of Africans the ‘gravest crime against humanity’ and identifies claims for reparations as ‘a concrete step towards remedying historical wrongs’, can be grounded in the law of state responsibility. The states that opposed the Resolution, and most of those that abstained, did not dispute the gravity of the trade. Rather, they denied that it could ground a present legal remedy, invoking the intertemporal principle of the Island of Palmas award. This article argues that this objection does not withstand scrutiny. It rests on a partial reading of Island of Palmas, which distinguishes the creation of a legal situation from its continued existence; it assumes a uniform lawfulness which the nineteenth-century treaty record contradicts; and it overlooks the distinction between Article 13 and Articles 14(2) and 15 of the Articles on State Responsibility. The article then develops a ‘doctrine of living harm’, according to which a situation originating in the trade is a continuing wrong only where a determinate obligation binds the state now, the state presently controls the situation, and its present conduct fails to conform to that obligation. Drawing on the case law of the Inter-American Court of Human Rights, the European Court of Human Rights, and the International Court of Justice, the article identifies three modes of continuing wrong (persisting illicit possession, composite wrong, and inherited structural injury) and the five obligations that follow from them.

key: beyond compliance corporate environmental crimes and the quest for environmental justice i
title: Beyond Compliance: Corporate Environmental Crimes and the Quest for Environmental Justice in India.
abstract: Globalization and industrialization have no doubt assisted in improving the standard of living of the people. At the same time, it has also assisted corporations and business entities to expand their business operations, who were running their business at small scale and limited to a particular market of customers. This has made these entities to earn more revenue and wealth by supplying their products and services across the boundaries of the nation. However, for becoming a successful business entity in a globalized world, companies have started exploiting the ecological resources at an enormous rate. Natural resources like forest and rivers are being degraded at the whims of these corporations. Not afraid by the environmental laws and legal framework, these corporations become actively involved in venturing into environmental crimes in India like poaching of endangered wildlife, illegal trade of forest resources, illegal logging and polluting water resources. The minting of revenue from such crimes often leads to environmental injustice to forest dwellers and other individuals whose environment is being encroached upon. The present paper explores the corporate environmental crimes being committed in India, the impact of such crimes on the environment and the lives of the people. It also explores the existing Indian legal structure in preventing such crime, challenges being faced and possible remedies for preventing such crimes.

key: acculturation as a theory of value the circulation of goods among the korubo
title: Acculturation as a Theory of Value: The Circulation of Goods Among the Korubo
venue: Journal of Latin American and Caribbean Anthropology
abstract:
This article analyzes the
 Regime de Circulação de Bens
 (Regime for the Circulation of Goods), a document created by Funai in 2011 to standardize the transactions of the Korubo of the Vale do Javari Indigenous Land, in the Brazilian state of Amazonas, with non‐Indigenous people. I argue that this Regime projects the commodity‐form onto the Korubo through equivalence tables, differential pricing, and a prohibition on debt, all presupposing autonomous and mutually foreign transactors. This mercantile ontology revives the premises of acculturation, now obsolete in anthropology yet still operative in contemporary indigenist policy directed at Isolated and Recently Contacted Indigenous Peoples. The Korubo, however, conceive of the Regime as a “project” that enacts the logic of asymmetrical relations between predation and sharing. The article shows how the Brazilian state seeks to institute a regime of commerce among people who have historically related to non‐Indigenous society through warfare.

key: from criminalisation to human rights law and urban poverty in africa
title: FROM CRIMINALISATION TO HUMAN RIGHTS: LAW AND URBAN POVERTY IN AFRICA
abstract: This article examines the relationship between law and poverty in three African urban contexts: Nairobi, Lagos, and Johannesburg. The central theme concerns the criminalisation of survival strategies adopted by homeless persons and informal street traders. The objective is to analyse how legal frameworks, municipal by-laws, and police practices converge to penalise poverty despite constitutional guarantees of dignity and equality. The methodology adopts a qualitative, multi-jurisdictional case study design. Data were collected through doctrinal analysis of statutes, municipal by-laws, and judicial decisions from Kenya, Nigeria, and South Africa, complemented by 42 semi-structured interviews with street traders, homeless individuals, police officers, and legal advocates. The results reveal a consistent pattern of punitive governance. Colonial-era vagrancy laws are actively revived and repurposed. Municipal by-laws grant broad discretion to enforcement officers, creating legal grey zones where harassment and extortion thrive. Judicial interpretation frequently defers to executive notions of public order, limiting the protective reach of constitutional rights. The conclusion argues for a rights-based approach to urban governance. The criminalisation of poverty represents a fundamental failure of constitutionalism and undermines the project of building just and equal societies. The study contributes a novel analytical framework, the jurisprudence of precarity, to illuminate the legal logics that perpetuate urban marginalisation.

key: corrupting eu citizenship through the anti corruption smoke screen eurowhiteness solidarit
title: Corrupting EU Citizenship through the “Anti-Corruption” Smoke-Screen: Eurowhiteness Solidarity vs Investment Naturalisations
abstract: The EU chose “anti-corruption” to target a particular mode of citizenship acquisition: citizenship by investment. The fact that no other mode of acquiring citizenship has been actively stigmatised through “corruption” rhetoric, including discretionary naturalisations based on economic contributions, suggests that corruption was by no means the European Commission’s main concern. The high importance of citizenship could indeed carry corruption risks associated with it. This, however, cannot be the sole ground for closing particular avenues for naturalisation. Improving the enforcement of the rule of law and the effective implementation of anti-corruption mechanisms are more suitable approaches. Fighting “corruption” served as a rhetorical device deployed by the Commission to stop the supposedly corrupting effects of investment naturalisations on the ethno-nationalist Eurowhiteness model, which this institution, together with the Court of Justice, has chosen for Europeans in direct departure from the law in force. “Anti-corruption,” thus, helped achieve institutional ends unrelated to either fighting corruption or reinforcing the rule of law and other values in the EU.

key: policing intimacy a critical analysis of commissionerate police powers and same sex relati
title: Policing Intimacy: A Critical Analysis of Commissionerate Police Powers and Same Sex Relationships in Urban India
venue: International Journal of Law Management & Humanities
abstract: The decriminalisation of consensual same-sex conduct in Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018) removed the primary formal instrument through which police targeted sexual minorities in India. What it did not remove was the institutional architecture that had enabled that targeting for over a century and a half. This article examines how Commissionerate police structures in major Indian cities continue to exercise a range of executive powers, including preventive detention, public nuisance regulation, licensing authority, and extern orders, in ways that reproduce the practical effects of criminalisation without engaging its formal language. Drawing on constitutional doctrine, legal sociology, and ethnographic accounts from urban queer communities, the article argues that the persistence of this regulatory harassment reflects a deeper conflict between the transformative potential of constitutional privacy and dignity guarantees and the colonial-era administrative DNA of urban policing in India. The article concludes with a framework for institutional reform oriented toward accountability rather than aspiration.

key: an overview of corruption challenges and the african continental free trade area
title: An overview of corruption challenges and the African Continental Free Trade Area
abstract:
For decades, African leaders have committed themselves to
fighting corruption, but due to a lack of transparency and
accountability in governance, it continues to thrive and infiltrate
the social, economic and political spheres. Corruption undermines
the fundamental values of African unity grounded in socioeconomic development. Notwithstanding the prospects of the
African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), economic
integration will be in vain in the presence of corruption. In
recognising that corruption hinders Africa’s economic, political
and social development, the African Union enacted the Convention
on Preventing and Combating Corruption. Regrettably, the
Convention falls short of establishing a continental independent
anti-corruption institution. In its stead, article 22 of the Convention
provides for an Advisory Board on Corruption established within
the African Union. This article argues that the Convention
necessitates an independent investigative anti-corruption
institution aimed at promoting justice by holding perpetrators
accountable, promoting the rule of law, and minimising corrupt
opportunities and perpetration. The article begins with an
overview of the corruption conundrum and its effect on Africa
amidst economic integration efforts. This discussion is followed by
a synopsis of the AfCFTA. The article probes existing anticorruption mechanisms in Africa and argues that the absence of an
independent African anti-corruption investigative institution to
implement the Convention is a deficiency that could hinder the
effectiveness of the AfCFTA.

key: narrativizing a context of genderbased violence the possibility of justice in argentina s
title: Narrativizing a Context of Gender‐Based Violence: The Possibility of Justice in Argentina's Femicide Law
abstract: Latin American governments have enacted some of the most progressive laws against femicide in the world. Yet data show these laws have not prevented or mitigated the high rates of femicide. In this article, I conduct an analysis of four sentences tried under the Argentine femicide law that present a more nuanced assessment of the effects of this legislation. By analyzing rulings made by judges in different Argentine jurisdictions, I show that the law—when applied—can produce more gender‐equitable decisions because it challenges the historic sociolegal notions of the “crime of passion” and the “violent emotion” defense for cases of intimate femicide. However, I also posit that the law favors instances in which the victim was killed in the context of a heterosexual, monogamous relationship and underserves women who were killed in the context of sexual violence and under the influence of drugs and alcohol. By focusing on the utilization of testimony about the victim and her relationship to the perpetrator, I show how judges construct a narrative “context of gender‐based violence”—a condition that must be met for the femicide law to be applied. I argue that these sentences offer evidence that the femicide law—when applied—can (and has) countered misogynistic ideas about women's lives and deaths and contribute to a profound sense of gender justice for victims.

key: documentary erasure sexual violence the politics of counting and the gendering of ethnic c
title: Documentary Erasure: Sexual Violence, the Politics of Counting, and the Gendering of Ethnic Conflict in Manipur
venue: International Journal of Science and Social Science Research
abstract: Feminist scholarship on ethnic conflict has established that women’s bodies carry the symbolic weight of communal boundaries, and that wartime sexual violence operates as a strategy of collective humiliation rather than as private criminality. This article argues that symbolic analysis alone cannot explain how gendered harm survives its own public exposure. Drawing on the conflict between the Meitei and Kuki-Zo communities in Manipur since May 2023, it identifies a second mechanism: the documentary regime through which the state records, classifies, and compensates for violence. Of the 6,523 First Information Reports registered by August 2023, eleven concerned crimes against women and children. Ex gratia lists count the dead but hold no category for rape. A 142-day communications blackout removed the channels through which survivors reach police, lawyers and journalists. India appears in no United Nations register of conflict-related sexual violence. The article also reads the May 2023 stripping of two Kuki-Zo women against the Kangla Fort protest of 2004, arguing that perpetrators expropriated a repertoire Manipuri women had themselves built for resistance. It closes with proposals for disaggregated conflict data, gender-specific compensation categories and shutdown exemptions for reporting infrastructure.

key: arming the conflict united states complicity in mexicos war on drugs
title: Arming The Conflict: United States’ Complicity in Mexico’s War on Drugs
abstract: Mexico’s ongoing human rights crisis during the war on drugs has been driven not only by domestic factors, such as political corruption and organized crime, but also by decades of United States (U.S.) policy and strategy. The U.S. has played a central role in shaping the policy framework governing the drug war, often unilaterally, while overlooking significant drivers of the crisis within its own control. Through sustained support for militarized strategies and permissive domestic firearm regulations, the U.S. has exercised significant influence over the conditions under which violence and human rights abuses have proliferated in Mexico. Against this backdrop, this Comment examines U.S. conduct which has played a consequential role in shaping Mexico’s War on Drugs and assesses whether those actions give rise to international responsibility for the resulting infringements of fundamental rights. Applying the contemporary international legal framework governing state responsibility and human rights obligations, this Comment analyzes whether U.S. conduct that contributes to the perpetuation of human rights violations associated with the drug war gives rise to international responsibility. Ultimately, this Comment suggests that U.S. policies satisfy the legal thresholds for attribution and breach, thereby supporting a finding of international responsibility for contributing to systemic human rights violations associated with Mexico’s War on Drugs.

key: indigenous feminicide and the global politics answer the cases of canada and brazil
title: Indigenous feminicide and the global politics answer: the cases of Canada and Brazil
abstract: This article analyzes the political and legal responses to Indigenous feminicide in the global arena, understanding it as a continuous manifestation of postcolonial violence. Globally, Indigenous women and girls remain among the groups at highest risk of lethality, although the systemic lack of data and criminal under-reporting hinder an exact assessment of the phenomenon's prevalence. To ground these global dynamics, this study adopts Canada and Brazil as comparative case studies. This choice is justified because, despite occupying distinct geopolitical and economic positions in the Global North and South, both nations share a historical foundation of settler colonialism. This heritage perpetuates intersectional vulnerability through land expropriation, marginalization, and evident State complicity and impunity. It intersects decolonial feminist perspectives, ranging from the debate on "colonial femicide" and police negligence in Canada to the consolidation of the concept as a State crime in Brazil. The article concludes that tackling this epidemic requires a coordinated response in international relations that recognizes and integrates Indigenous struggles for self-determination and sovereignty.

key: exploring the symbolic erosion of the nigerian state security a case study of elite victim
title: Exploring the Symbolic Erosion of the Nigerian State Security: A Case Study of Elite Victimizations in the Northwest
venue: Australian Journal of Business and Social Science
abstract: Northwest Nigeria has emerged as the epicenter of a deepening security crisis, with armed banditry and kidnapping-for-ransom evolving from rural criminality into a sophisticated political economy of violence. While the human toll on farming communities has been extensively documented, less attention has been paid to the symbolic dimensions of elite victimisation the abduction of retired generals, traditional rulers, politicians, and religious leaders. This study examines how the targeting of high -status ind ividuals constitutes a symbolic erosion of state security, undermining the state’s monopoly on legitimate force and its claim to protect its most privileged citizens. Qualitative case study methodology was adopted; the research focuses on the abduction and death of retired Major General Rabe Abubakar in Katsina State in May-June 2026 as a critical incident. The study integrates primary documentary sources, media reports, and secondary scholarly literature to analyse four dimensions of symbolic erosion: the collapse of coercive deterrence, the inversion of state -society protection relations, the commodification of elite status as ransom value, and the legitimization of bandit governance. Findings indicate that elite victimization operates not merely as opport unistic criminality but as a strategic signal that accelerates capital flight, fiscal reallocation toward defensive spending, and the retreat of elite citizens into privatized security enclaves. The study concludes that sustainable peace requires rebuilding state legitimacy through inclusive governance, rural economic revitalization, and the reintegration of traditional institutions, rather than through military-centred countermeasures alone.

key: necropolitics of ntimacy family violence and trans lives in turkiye
title: Necropolitics of ıntimacy: family violence and trans lives in Türkiye.
abstract: This article examines the violence experienced by trans individuals in Türkiye within family and intimate relationships, treating it as a structured, enduring regime rather than a series of isolated acts. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with 17 trans individuals, the study uses reflexive thematic analysis to trace how violence originates within the family and extends into intimate relationships, public spaces, and institutional encounters. The analysis brings together Agamben's state of exception and bare life with Mbembe's necropolitics and politics of enmity to show how trans individuals are excluded from legal and moral protection and governed through abandonment, exposure, and slow death. Relocating Agamben's concepts from the concentration camp, his paradigmatic site of exception, to the family, the article distinguishes domination within family membership from the revocation of membership itself and treats bare life as a negotiated asymptote rather than an inhabited condition. The findings show that violence is normalised through discourses of love, protection and morality, while state institutions often withdraw from their protective role or become sites of secondary harm. Preventing violence against trans individuals requires political interventions that simultaneously address familial relations, intimate life, and institutional responsibility.

key: effectiveness of the east african court of justice as a vanguard for regional integration
title: EFFECTIVENESS OF THE EAST AFRICAN COURT OF JUSTICE AS A VANGUARD FOR REGIONAL INTEGRATION
venue: International Research Journal of Rongo University
abstract: This Paper seeks to navigate the exactitude of compliance and enforcement mechanisms taking place in the East African Community (EAC) through the lens of the East African Court of Justice (EACJ), with a particular focus on the efficiency of its authority and functionality. The paper extrapolates thoughts on the perceptions of legal mirages, myths and realities and the extent to which existing regional institutional frameworks shift to practical enforcement and adherence to EAC Treaty obligations. By borrowing from a deep analysis of regionalism and relevant case material, this Paper sets to and finds a gaping disconnect involving regulation and their operationalization. While the EAC Treaty provides an imperfect policy framework for operationalization and judicial enforcement, Partner States repeatedly exhibit a regular pattern of selective compliance; brushing off legal obligations by consistently bypassing mandatory regional requirements either in favor of international pursuits or jingoist alternatives seen in Globalisation agendas and which have in turn led to the weakening of the effectiveness, legitimacy and authority of the EACJ and which in turn ends up limiting institutional credibility. The paper then concludes by arguing that without stronger community enforcement, outright political commitment and sweeping community law reforms, the EACJ’s role as a safeguard of regional integration will remain constrained. Lastly, the Paper goes on to recommend a few insights that seek to contribute towards a broader debate on the effectiveness of the mandates of Regional Integration.

key: law and political violence against women in central america
title: Law and Political Violence against Women in Central America
abstract:
Cristiana Chamorro Barrios is a Nicaraguan journalist and founder of the Nicaraguan Foundation for Freedom of the Press, a nonprofit focused on promoting freedom of expression and public access to information, as well as providing training and support to local journalists. Cristiana was arrested on June 2, 2021, in Managua, Nicaragua, on accusations of tax evasion (International Society for Human Rights 2025). At the time of her arrest, Cristiana, a member of a prominent Nicaraguan family, had recently announced her intention to challenge Daniel Ortega in the November 2021 presidential election and was widely considered the favorite in the race. The charges against Cristiana
 1
 — including the vague claim of “abusive management and ideological falsehood” — though made with no evidence, disqualified her from running for office. She was later tried in sham proceedings and sentenced to eight years in prison. In 2023, Cristiana was one of hundreds of political prisoners forcibly expelled from the country and later stripped of their citizenship (Abi-Habib 2023; Confidencial 2021).

key: illicit drug use and street violence in aba metropolis nigeria a decade analysis 2015 2025
title: Illicit Drug Use and Street Violence in Aba Metropolis, Nigeria: A decade analysis, 2015 -2025
venue: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF SOCIAL SCIENCES AND MANAGEMENT RESEARCH
abstract:
This study investigates hard drug use and street violence in Aba metropolis, Abia State, from 2015 
to 2025, drawing exclusively on evidence from Aba and its immediate metropolitan area. The 
objectives are to examine the correlation between hard drug use and street violence, identify 
commonly abused hard drugs, assess the role of unemployment as a driver of drug-related 
violence, and analyse the challenges in addressing drug abuse and street violence. The research 
is grounded in the Availability-Proneness Theory. A case study design was employed, relying on 
qualitative secondary data from thirty-five sources, including journal articles, a preprint, official 
statistics, National Drug Law Enforcement Agency operational disclosures, government 
statements, and press reports of specific raids and incidents, all analyzed through content analysis. 
Findings indicate that drugs and violence converge at specific locations, such as York Street, a 
drug bunk on Ngwa Road, a section of Ahia Ohuru market, Cemetery Barracks, and the abandoned 
Enyimba Hotel at Ogbor Hill. A significant portion of reported violence in the city lacks drug 
attribution. Cocaine, heroin, methamphetamine, tramadol, and codeine syrup were identified, 
though only some were linked to violent locations. Unemployment was identified as necessary but 
insufficient, as disputes over levies and control of trading spaces independently drive 
confrontations. The response to these issues has been characterized by raids without sustained 
occupation, arrests without convictions, and treatment efforts lacking adequate capacity. 
Recommendations include occupying raided sites and establishing permanent outposts, 
implementing joint enforcement against concealed supply chains, publishing a schedule of lawful 
levies with formal apprenticeship, and aligning courts, treatment capacity, and command 
locations with identified flashpoints.

key: countering illegal migration features of k starmers cabinet approach
title: Countering Illegal Migration: Features of K. Starmer’s Cabinet Approach
abstract: The article explores the Labour government’s approach to illegal migration through the lens of migration diplomacy concept across several parameters (border control, asylum policy, return migration, externalization policy). The author analyzes new legislation (Border Security, Asylum and Immigration Act 2025), restrictive measures against smugglers, and the foreign policy dimension of the UK’s asylum policy. Although K. Starmer’s Cabinet, guided by the thesis of “moral superiority” over its predecessors, declared the primacy of international law and human rights in countering illegal migration, the rise of right-wing sentiment is pushing the government to tighten asylum legislation (while repealing only a few high-profile Conservative measures, such as the Rwanda plan). Labour government is seeking to compensate for the failure of negotiations with the EU on migration through bilateral agreements with European countries (France, Germany, etc.) and has strengthened international measures to combat organized crime. It is concluded that Labour’s flagship project of countering smugglers internationally is intended to compensate for the lack of an effective and coherent strategy. As a result, the halfhearted policy has drawn criticism from both the general public for its lack of rigor and human rights activists for its anti-migrant approach.

key: from mills to latifundios a reflective essay on brazilian agribusiness as a continuation o
title: From Mills to Latifundios: A Reflective Essay on Brazilian Agribusiness as a Continuation of the Colonial System of Expropriation of the Black Body
abstract: This article presents a reflective essay on racial capitalism as a mechanism for the expropriation of Black bodies. Through contributions from activist thinkers from the Black movement, combined with the account of Olaudah Equiano, a young Nigerian sold into slavery, it argues that Brazilian agribusiness represents the continuation of colonial structures, particularly in its alignment with policies implemented during the Bolsonaro administration, marked by increased land concentration and the legitimacy of violence. The analysis is conducted in light of Rosa Luxemburg’s critique of militarism as a tool for the expansion of capitalism. The work then examines the myth of racial democracy, highlighting its ideological role in maintaining racial inequalities in Brazil. Finally, it articulates an analysis of W.E.B. Du Bois’s studies on “color lines” in processes of exploitation. Thus, the article proposes identifying the persistence of colonial structures in the Brazilian agro-export system and its naturalization of racial violence. Keywords: Agribusiness. Colonialism. Slavery. Expropriation. Racial Democracy.

key: when protection becomes predation militarized masculinity and sexual violence in northeast
title: When Protection Becomes Predation: Militarized Masculinity and Sexual Violence in Northeastern Nigeria
venue: Dignity: A Journal of Analysis of Exploitation and Violence
abstract: The study investigates the structural and situational drivers of conflict-related sexual violence (CRSV) perpetrated by state security actors in the context of Nigeria’s counterinsurgency campaigns in Borno State. Drawing on militarized masculinity and strain and deprivation theories, and using a qualitative, interpretive research design, the study argues that CRSV is not an isolated or episodic form of deviance by individual soldiers and security personnel but is embedded in routine military–civilian interactions. Advancing an interactionist explanation of CRSV in Nigeria’s Islamist counterinsurgency operations, the study demonstrates that the likelihood of sexual violence increases through the interaction of gendered institutional norms, operational pressures, and permissive institutional environments. It further highlights the strategic implications of such abuses, including their potential to undermine state legitimacy and contribute to insurgent recruitment. The paper concludes that preventing CRSV requires addressing not only individual misconduct but also the structural and institutional conditions, including gendered organizational norms, operational strain, and weak accountability mechanisms, that enable and sustain such violence.

key: coerced labor caste and aspirations for liberty in early nineteenth century bengal revisit
title: Coerced Labor, Caste, and Aspirations for Liberty in Early Nineteenth-Century Bengal: Revisiting the Antislavery Debate from South Asia
venue: Comparative Studies in Society and History
abstract: This article revisits the debate on the relationship between capitalism and abolition from the perspective of South Asia. It argues that bringing the antislavery debate into conversation with the extensive literature on caste opens up new comparative possibilities. Commercial slavery in the early modern Indian Ocean world is now well established, but global histories of slavery have rarely inspired global histories of antislavery. The dominant interpretation of abolition in South Asia remains focused on the contingent requirements of colonial governance. Through an analysis of legal conflicts over the status of slavery in the eastern Indian province of Bengal in the 1820s and 1830s, I argue that this approach obscures the ethical-political significance of abolition in a context shaped by caste and agrarian slavery. The emancipatory potential of abolition, however, was undermined by a colonial state committed to revenue extraction and social order, as well as by the global capitalist context of counter-revolution. By situating the colonial archive within this wider historical conjuncture, the essay shows how both the possibilities and limits of abolition emerged from the contradictions of liberalism and global capitalism. It thereby puts the South Asian case in conversation with broader histories of revolution and counter-revolution.

key: divergent legacies how the local instantiation of national conflict conditions postwar pol
title: Divergent Legacies: How the Local Instantiation of National Conflict Conditions Postwar Political Engagement
abstract:
Under what conditions does violence generate legacies of political [dis]engagement? Victimization is frequently linked to higher rates of political engagement – voting, protesting, attending meetings, etc. Often, however, victims withdraw from politics. These initial responses are evident generations later. I reconcile these disparate trends by analyzing the materialization of national conflict at the local level. When a community experiences violence perpetrated by non-local factions, victimization is more likely to politicize. By contrast, when perpetrated by members of one’s community against other local members, violence is more likely to depoliticize. To test these arguments, I leverage an original survey, archival material, and interviews from the understudied case of Cameroon. From 1956 to 1971, the
 Union des Populations du Cameroun
 (UPC) fought against French and Cameroonian state and paramilitary forces. Civilians were heavily targeted by the state, militias, and UPC guerillas. Today, variation in those local experiences is associated with differences in political behavior and socialization practices.

key: absence of strict gate keeping in the new media implication in fighting corruption in nige
title: Absence of Strict Gate-keeping in the New media: Implication in Fighting Corruption in Nigeria
abstract: This academic work makes an inroad into the place of the new media as part and parcel of today’s information society to examine if it is making some noticeable impact in the societal war against corruption. The new media which has become significant in effecting change and transforming lives all around the world seems to be emerging as a highly powerful developmental tool used across generations for several purposes including to fight against corruption. This paper therefore through its analytical and descriptive approach buttresses the argument that the new media have inherent potentials of easier accessibility in reporting corruption which may likely suffer some setback in the traditional settings as a result of institutionalized gate-keeping and stringent censorship. Through literature review and theoretical perspective, the paper acknowledges that the traditional mass media, due to their inherent ties with government ownership and control, institutionalized gate-keeping practices via editors and editing, various economic and political forces in the society, are somewhat incapacitated from rising above board in challenge of reporting corruption more effectively. The paper goes further to assert that the new media has offered a viable alternative, arguing that social media tools have what it takes through serving as a platform for the citizenry to point out loopholes that may make the system vulnerable to corruption. Nevertheless, given their perceived anonymous nature and free internet access and easy ownership of information platforms, the new media have established a portion for itself even though it still battles with some credibility challenges because of its unfettered access even to the goon for all kinds of narratives that could hinder its effective use in the anti-corruption fight and could as well pose the risk of malicious slander of character of innocent people.

key: privatized violence and the making of public concern the 1922 fuyang bandit crisis in repu
title: Privatized violence and the making of public concern: the 1922 Fuyang bandit crisis in Republican China
venue: The International Journal of Asian Studies
abstract: The 1922 seizure of Fuyang, Anhui Province, by the “Old Foreigner” (Laoyangren) bandit clique exposed the catastrophic consequences of localized military privatization during the Beiyang era (1912–1928), a period marked by rapid shifts in provincial control and the absence of consolidated state authority. This article reconstructs the collapse of Fuyang’s system of defense, hollowed out by the predatory kinship-military structure of the Ni clan, to argue that the boundary between state protection and banditry had effectively dissolved. Building on debates over the Chinese public sphere, the study demonstrates how the administrative paralysis that followed the sacking of the city inadvertently catalyzed a transregional civic mobilization. Drawing on press reports and historical memoirs, it traces how Anhui natives in Shanghai utilized modern media not merely as a channel for public opinion but as an alternative mechanism of political contestation to check warlord impunity. The Fuyang case reveals a paradox: state fragility did not simply atomize society, but compelled temporarily disarmed revolutionary and civic elites to forge new, if ultimately constrained, networks of political accountability across regional boundaries. In doing so, they transformed the public sphere into both a humanitarian arena and a strategic instrument against warlord rule.

key: home at the margins police violence evictions and the resistance to belonging in sao paulo
title: Home at the Margins: Police Violence, Evictions, and the Resistance to Belonging in São Paulo's ‘Cracolândia’
venue: PoLAR: Political and Legal Anthropology Review
abstract: In São Paulo's Cracolândia—one of the world's largest open‐air drug scenes—urban transformation operates not through direct expulsion but through the systematic erosion of territorial bonds. Drawing on twenty months of ethnographic research with unhoused crack users, NGO workers, and state officials, this article examines how interactions with the state—entangled with commercial and legal pressures—dismantle the survival infrastructures that enable marginalised populations to remain: work opportunities, social networks, housing access, and community ties. Home, we demonstrate, is not merely space but a political claim to stability, community, and the right to remain—a claim constantly under erasure yet persistently reinvented at the margins. Through two extended ethnographic vignettes, we trace how deterritorialisation unfolds in individual lives: one trajectory ending in departure after years of cyclical displacement; another sustained only through alliances with neighbours and outsiders as the condition for conditional belonging. We argue that anthropological attention to these trajectories reveals mechanisms invisible to urban studies focused on physical removal or state action alone. Deterritorialisation operates through making people's identities with territory untenable—severing the relationships, routines, and survival infrastructures that constitute home—even as physical presence remains technically possible.

key: illegal logging routes and transnational crime in africa
title: Illegal logging routes and transnational crime in Africa

key: between resistance and reproduction the brazilian supreme court under authoritarian pressu
title: Between Resistance and Reproduction: The Brazilian Supreme Court Under Authoritarian Pressure
abstract: For upholding evidence-based policymaking during the COVID-19 crisis and prosecuting antidemocratic actors, the Brazilian Federal Supreme Court (STF) has been widely portrayed as a bulwark of democracy. This article challenges this celebratory narrative by examining the Court’s jurisprudence through the lens of fundamental rights. It argues that the STF’s democratic protagonism coexists with a pattern of ambivalent adjudication in which boldness in defending institutional order is coupled with caution and avoidance in areas such as labor rights, gender equality, and reproductive rights. The article shows how these strategies produce hybrid rulings that advance democratic goals while limiting their transformative reach, often with disproportionate effects on marginalized groups. The analysis shifts the focus from the role of courts as arbiters of institutional conflict to their role in shaping the distributive and substantive dimensions of democracy. It demonstrates that judicial responses to authoritarianism are structured not only by external political pressures but also by internal constraints and longer-standing commitments to market-oriented and exclusionary legal frameworks. The article advances the concept of selective constitutionalism to capture this dual dynamic, arguing that courts may simultaneously resist authoritarian threats while reproducing structural inequalities. The Brazilian case offers insights into how courts operate in contexts of democratic erosion, showing that the preservation of democracy may coexist with, and sometimes depend on, the containment of substantive equality.

key: reconstructing trading in influence as a corruption offense in indonesian criminal law ref
title: Reconstructing Trading in Influence as a Corruption Offense in Indonesian Criminal Law Reform and UNCAC Perspectives
abstract: Trading in influence is a form of modern corruption that develops along with the complexity of power relations within governance systems. The main issue addressed in this research is the absence of explicit regulation of trading in influence in Indonesian positive law, despite its recognition under the United Nations Convention Against Corruption (UNCAC). This study aims to analyze the regulation of trading in influence in UNCAC, examine the legal vacuum in national law, and formulate the reconstruction of such offense within the framework of criminal law reform. This research employs a normative juridical method with statutory, conceptual, and comparative approaches. The findings reveal that the absence of trading in influence regulation limits law enforcement in addressing corruption practices, particularly those involving abuse of influence that do not meet the elements of bribery or gratification. Therefore, reconstruction of the trading in influence offense is necessary by adopting UNCAC principles to ensure legal certainty and enhance the effectiveness of corruption eradication in Indonesia.

key: how not to address the problem of gender based violence the political uses of restorative
title: How (Not) to Address the Problem of Gender-Based Violence: The Political Uses of Restorative Justice
venue: Canadian Journal of Law and Society / Revue Canadienne Droit et Société
abstract: This article investigates why restorative justice in France—legally recognized since 2014 and broadly endorsed by political actors—remains only marginally implemented, particularly in cases of gender‑based violence (GBV). Drawing on qualitative research, including interviews, observations, and parliamentary debate analysis, the study shows that limited uptake cannot be explained primarily by feminist resistance or public reluctance. Instead, restorative justice has been shaped by blame‑avoidance strategies, institutional ambivalence, and the downward delegation of responsibility to under‑resourced local actors. Presented as a right but maintained in a quasi‑experimental mode, it relies heavily on the discretionary, often overtime labour of frontline practitioners. This governance configuration reframes, a statutory right into an optional service, preserves existing penal hierarchies, and obscures the structural nature of GBV. The article highlights how symbolic reforms may be neutralized through managerial practices and calls for comparative research on institutional designs that enable more consistent implementation.

key: colombias war economy an obstacle to peace
title: Colombia’s War Economy – An Obstacle to Peace?
abstract:
War economies are frequently seen as a main hindrance for peacebuilding. Over the last ten years, the persistence of the drug economy has been an important element of the Colombian narrative to explain postwar violence. However, high levels of variation at the sub-national level suggest there is no deterministic relation between war economies and postwar violence. While they all rank high in terms of illicit crop density, violence levels (in terms of homicide rates) differ among Catatumbo and Montes de María region. We argue that patterns and levels of postwar violence depend on the interaction between war economies and dynamic combinations of political regime, economic state capacities and territorial control, which operate as intermediating variables in the production of violence. In brief, we argue that violence increases when this relationship is weak and decreases when strong.
 Las economías de guerra frecuentemente impiden el avance hacia la construcción de la paz. A lo largo de los últimos diez años, la persistencia de la economía de las drogas ilícitas ha sido un elemento importante de la narrativa colombiana para explicar la violencia postguerra. Sin embargo, elevados niveles de variación sub-nacional sugieren que no existe una relación determinada entre economías de guerra y violencia postguerra. A pesar de que presentan elevados niveles de densidad en cultivos ilícitos, los niveles de violencia (en términos de tasa de homicidios) difieren entre la región del Catatumbo y la de Montes de María. Argumentamos que los patrones y niveles de violencia postguerra dependen de la interacción entre economías de guerra y una dinámica combinación de capacidades políticas y económicas del Estado y control territorial. En breve, argumentamos que la violencia aumenta cuando esta relación es débil y disminuye cuando es fuerte.

key: its still about race assessing sources of public opinion on immigration and its ties to cr
title: It’s Still About Race: Assessing Sources of Public Opinion on Immigration and Its Ties to Crime, Gangs, Drugs, and Border Control
abstract:
There is a divide between political rhetoric and academic research on the topic of immigration and crime. Political rhetoric often claims that immigrants are dangerous and deportation is necessary to decrease crime. In contrast, empirical research demonstrates lower criminality among immigrants and little effect of deportation on crime. In light of these competing narratives, it is unclear where public perception stands on this issue. Some recent research has demonstrated that more American’s may be buying into political claims that immigration increases crime, however, recent research has not explored
 why
 the public has grown to accept these claims, and
 what factors
 drive these beliefs. To address these gaps, this study investigates the factors that are associated with endorsement of the four core pillars of contemporary political rhetoric concerning immigration’s effects on (1) crime, (2) gangs, (3) drugs, and (4) the need for immigration enforcement. Using a nationally benchmarked sample (
 n
 = 1139) from Lucid Theorem collected in May–June 2025, the analysis assesses multiple theorized predictors of support for these narratives about immigration, including support for Trump, White nationalist sentiment, and Latino punitiveness, alongside other relevant correlates. The findings suggest Latino punitiveness is the strongest and most consistent predictor of these beliefs.

key: legal limits and enforcement challenges of ecowas in addressing military coups in west afr
title: Legal Limits and Enforcement Challenges of ECOWAS in Addressing Military Coups in West Africa
venue: Journal of International Law and Jurisprudence
abstract: Military coups d’état occurring repeatedly in West Africa are a great setback to the regional efforts to consolidate democracy and good governance. This paper examines the legal and political dimensions of the recent military seizures of power in member states of the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS). It evaluates the interaction between internal governance failures and regional security crises that have created a fertile ground for the erosion of constitutional order. Although ECOWAS has established a strong normative framework through the Protocol on Democracy and Good Governance, reliance on punitive enforcement mechanisms and economic sanctions has revealed significant legal and practical constraints. The paper shows that the ECOWAS Authority's enforcement mandate is limited by the principle of state sovereignty, ambiguities in Community law on the use of force, and a legitimacy crisis stemming from its inability to address so-called constitutional coups by civilian elites. A comparative analysis of the African Union’s zero tolerance policy and the European Union’s Article 7 Treaty of European Union (TEU) procedure underscores the need for ECOWAS to adopt clearer legal tools, apply targeted sanctions, and strengthen institutional and judicial capacity. The paper concludes that restoring civilian rule over the long term requires not only condemning military interventions but also proactively promoting democratic accountability, judicial independence, and effective governance at the national level.

key: an analysis of murder cases in indonesia and the evidence used in criminal proceedings
title: An Analysis of Murder Cases in Indonesia and the Evidence Used in Criminal Proceedings
venue: TOFEDU: The Future of Education Journal
abstract: In contemporary society, both individuals and groups may engage in conduct that deviates from prevailing social norms, particularly legal norms. The increasing incidence of criminal activity in Indonesia remains a significant concern, with criminal offenses ranging from seemingly minor acts of theft to robbery, sexual violence, and homicide. Homicide is a particularly serious criminal offense because it results in the loss of human life. In 2021, at least 1,076 homicide cases were recorded in Indonesia, involving victims of different ages and genders. This situation raises important questions regarding how homicide cases can be identified and distinguished and why evidence discovered at crime scenes can serve as a basis for identifying the perpetrator. This study employs normative legal research using statutory, case, and historical approaches. Homicide cases often originate from minor conflicts that escalate and persist over time. Under Article 184 of the Indonesian Code of Criminal Procedure (KUHAP), recognized forms of evidence include witness testimony, expert testimony, documentary evidence, indications, and the defendant’s statement. Factors contributing to premeditated and non-premeditated homicide include family circumstances, economic conditions, and environmental factors. Therefore, greater public awareness is needed regarding criminal offenses and the legal sanctions applicable under Indonesian law.

key: desecuritizing cannabis the role of local political and social actors in californias polic
title: Desecuritizing Cannabis: The Role of Local Political and Social Actors in California’s Policy Reform
abstract: Abstract The United States has been the driving force behind the establishment of the international drug control regime and has historically served as its principal enforcer. What impact have domestic policy changes had on federal authorities in the case of the state of California? We argue that growing civil and political support for reform led to significant changes in the policy landscape, with legislation gradually turning California “green” for the recreational use of marijuana. From a methodological perspective, this study employs detailed historical process tracing to examine a single case study: the state of California. We explore how the drug issue has been perceived, how drug-related laws have been developed, and the role played by local political and social actors in shaping these changes. To understand this process, we draw on the theories of securitization and desecuritization. We ask: how is the leader of the global prohibition regime rearticulating the drug issue from a process of securitization to one of desecuritization? Our findings suggest that the securitization of drugs in California was driven primarily by governmental actors through a top-down process, whereas desecuritization has been led largely by civil society through a bottom-up dynamic.

key: thirty grand for a mac 10 revealing the factors that influence illicit firearm prices
title: “Thirty grand for a MAC-10”: revealing the factors that influence illicit firearm prices
abstract: Illicit firearm markets constitute a significant component of global illicit economies and assume a central role in facilitating violent and organised criminal activities. Despite restrictive legislation across many jurisdictions that aim to limit access to firearms, criminal actors continue to access firearms through a range of channels, particularly via criminal networks and informal social connections. However, little is currently known about the factors that influence the prices of firearms in these illicit contexts. Building on the existing literature and drawing on interviews with 75 prisoners incarcerated across sixteen correctional centres in two Australian states—South Australia and New South Wales—this paper examines the factors that influence the prices of illicit firearms. In doing so, this paper contributes new empirical insights into how illicit firearms prices are structured and negotiated, as well as the social and market forces that influence illicit firearm pricing. Overall, participants’ accounts suggest that illicit firearm prices were affected by a combination of restrictive policy environments, supply and demand dynamics, perceived risks of buying and selling illicit firearms, distinctions between firearms perceived to be “clean” and those associated with previous criminal activity and how these affect pricing, the unique characteristics of specific firearms, and social dynamics including closed social networks and interpersonal trust. We conclude by reflecting on the implications of empirical findings of this paper on policy and practice.

key: a constitutional evaluation of the legal standing of the zimbabwe patriotism law under zim
title: A constitutional evaluation of the legal standing of the Zimbabwe patriotism law under Zimbabwe’s 2013 constitution
abstract: Freedom of expression enhances individual autonomy and self-fulfilment, providing a guiding light towards discovering truth in the marketplace of ideas. This qualitative contribution argues that Zimbabwe’s new Criminal Law Codification and Reform Amendment Act, 2023 (also referred to as the patriotism law), carries provisions that limit freedom of expression. This is particularly during the country’s often robust and conflict-ridden electoral contestations. Legislating patriotism presents manifold constitutional complications. These complications tend to obscure state or government-citizen relationships. While the attempt to use the patriotism law to create a cohesive social community with a sense of belonging is important, it ignores the complexities related to drawing a line between harming national sovereignty, with robust engagement from active citizenship, and constructive patriotism, especially in Zimbabwe’s often belligerent electoral processes. The contention made in this study is that patriotism manifests in affection, pride and sense of love for one’s motherland, but such ingrained sociological affections cannot be inculcated through coercive legislation. The confluence of criminal law and foreign policy relations is a delicate area, and the Act discounts that future foreign affairs or national policies may run contrary to enlightened public opinion and values, which may result in the law inadvertently restricting interactions and genuine vigorous democratic discourse. The main point of this contribution is that, if subjected to potential judicial review, the substantive constitutional validity of the Act’s provisions may be found wanting, because they violate the principle of legality, proscribe false information, and carry disproportionate criminal sanctions that impermissibly restrict free speech.

key: whistleblowers as agents exposing systemic criminality a study of two south african period
title: Whistleblowers as Agents Exposing Systemic Criminality: A Study of Two South African Periods
abstract: The Republic of South Africa’s recent history, and contemporary period, has fallen victim to systemic criminality, which this article argues has transpired across two periods, namely state capture under Jacob Zuma’s presidency and the contemporary period encompassing the capture of the policing apparatus. The full extent of both cases of capture emerged because of disclosures by whistleblowers. Across both periods, whistleblowers have faced retaliation. This article, however, contends that an observable pattern of escalation in retaliation has transpired. It determines that state capture whistleblowers were largely subjected to social and legal retaliation, while policing apparatus whistleblowers have been frequently subjected to physical retaliation (assassinations). This is the result of inadequate measures taken to address previous instances of systemic criminality, thereby setting a precedent in which wrongdoers seldom face meaningful punitive consequences. The recommendation is that the South African state authorities need to react quickly to reverse the trend.

key: parallel governance in a negotiated peace the agc and state displacement in rural colombia
title: Parallel Governance in a Negotiated Peace: The AGC and State Displacement in Rural Colombia
venue: North Texas Journal of Undergraduate Research
abstract: In the rural areas of Colombia, there are various areas where institutional weakness of the state has created a power vacuum that has been filled by non-state actors involved in the internal conflict in Colombia. One of those is the Autodefensas Gaitanistas de Colombia (AGC)- also known as the Clan de Golfo, the largest drug cartel in South America, a group of several armed organizations, including regional criminal structures, drug traffickers, and collection officers that control illicit economies involving narco trafficking, illegal mining, and extortion. The AGC takes advantage of weakened institutions to provide public services and regulate matters concerning civilian life. This is particularly significant because state authority is replaced; local power relations are reshaped and parallel forms of rule are legitimized. The historical context for the AGC can be traced back to the 1980's from the coming together of large landholders and business leaders, drug cartels, and the Colombian army to form paramilitary structures to combat leftist guerilla groups. Overlapping paramilitary groups would come in 1977 to form one national structure called the Self Defense Forces of Colombia (AUC), which would eventually demobilize in 2005. Disparate groups would then form, the most prominent being the AGC. The core argument of this paper is that the AGC estabished a durable parallel governance in rural Antioquia through selective violence, social regulation, insitutional co-optation and economic control, ultimately legitmized by a negotiated peace. Rather than functioning soley as a drug cartel or insurgency, the AGC derives legitimacy from governing everyday life where the state is absent or ineffective. Focusing on post-FARC rural Antioquia, the study traces how territorial control evolves into adminstrative influence, economic dominance and political leverage, revealing why conventional secuirity-centered responses fail to dismantle the AGC's negotiated peace and flaws with other implementations to upset the negotiated peace.
