key: modus operandi and trends of high risk criminal networks for illegal immigration operating
title: Modus Operandi and Trends of High-Risk Criminal Networks for Illegal Immigration operating in Republic of Bulgaria
abstract: The manuscript aims to explore and represent the currently exploited trends and strategies of organized criminal groups active in the Republic of Bulgaria, involved in smuggling of illegal migrants across Europe as part of a larger high-risk criminal networks. It details the prevailing trends and specific mechanisms employed in these criminal activities over the past three years, relying on a methodology of data analysis from different text sources and the professional experience of the author.   The topic of the paper is researched from the perspectives of criminology, law enforcement, and intelligence.  The study identifies five key findings as primary factors—the geo-social factor, the local factor, the foreign factor, the factor of criminal and non-criminal actors, and the geopolitical factor—that influence the characteristics of criminal groups engaged in illegal immigration, as observed in Bulgaria.   These factors offer insights for enhancing operational and strategic responses to counter emerging threats posed by high-risk criminal networks of illegal immigration.  The research emphasizes the different organizational levels and operational functions of these criminal groups and their networks. It examines specific patterns of criminal activity over the past three years, including the roles of illegal migrants, their drivers, guides, field captains, middlemen, and the leaders of the criminal organizations.

key: socio environmental impact of mining concessions in mexico a spatial analysis
title: Socio-environmental impact of mining concessions in Mexico: a spatial analysis
abstract: Abstract Mexico is globally recognized for its rich mineral resources. While mining is often seen as a driver of economic development, it is crucial to consider its short-, medium-, and long-term impacts on biodiversity, as well as on the surrounding rural and Indigenous communities that are frequently overlooked. Information on mining projects in Mexico is fragmented and incomplete within official institutions, complicating access. A significant lack of transparency in mining operations further obscures their effects on biodiversity. Therefore, this study aimed to analyse, using geographic information systems, the distribution of current mining concessions in Mexico and their spatial overlap with environmental and social variables in order to identify areas potentially vulnerable to the impacts of mining activities. Research was conducted on mining concessions in Mexico to assess their spatial relationship with eight environmentally and socially significant variables. The findings indicated that 8.24% of the national territory is under concession. The regions classified as Priority Land Regions and Priority Hydrological Regions exhibited the highest overlap with mining concessions, at 84% and 75%, respectively. Moreover, Protected Natural Areas designated as Biosphere Reserves were identified as the most potentially affected by these activities. Additionally, there was a 10.37% overlap of concessions within communities characterized by a high to very high degree of social vulnerability, including Indigenous communities of 39 ethnic groups. This analysis highlighted specific sites that could be particularly susceptible to the detrimental impacts of mining due to their environmental or social conditions.

key: technology and cross border financial crimes
title: Technology and Cross-Border Financial Crimes
venue: Journal of Law and Global Policy
abstract:
This paper, explores how technology facilitates cross-border financial crimes and underscores
the importance of international collaboration in curbing these activities. It further examines
the role of shared intelligence, harmonized legal frameworks, and the adoption of advanced
technology in building a united front against global financial crime. This study is guided by
Robert K. Merton’s strain theory and McClelland’s Needs Theory. The study utilized secondary
research methodology. In the 21st century, the rapid advancement of technology has
revolutionized financial systems, improving efficiency and connectivity but simultaneously
creating new avenues for criminal tendencies such as financial crimes. Crimes under the
category of money laundering include cyber fraud and tax evasion has transcended national
borders, making them increasingly complex to tackle. The intersection of that technology and
cross-border financial crime has continued to poses a significant challenge to global security
and economic stability. Therefore, as financial criminals exploit advances in technology;
international collaboration becomes essential for effective enforcement. Harmonizing legal
frameworks, sharing intelligence, and leveraging emerging technologies are key to curbing
financial crime. The mandatory collaborative effort of international organizations and
governments continuity is to stay strong ahead of these threats, ensuring that the global
financial system remains secure and resilient in the face of evolving challenges. On this note,
this paper among other recommendations proposed that there should be collaborative efforts
to strengthen the independence of anti-money laundering (AML) and anti-corruption agencies
and increasing their collaboration with similar agencies in other jurisdictions. This will
improve their ability to collect evidence to be used in foreign criminal prosecutions and foreign
forfeiture cases.

key: criminal policy on illegal logging in indonesia in the aftermath of the job creation law a
title: CRIMINAL POLICY ON ILLEGAL LOGGING IN INDONESIA IN THE AFTERMATH OF THE JOB CREATION LAW: A REFORMULATION OF ENVIRONMENTAL CRIMINAL ENFORCEMENT
abstract: Illegal logging remains one of the most damaging environmental crimes in Indonesia, and the enactment of Law Number 11 of 2020 on Job Creation, together with its perpetua form under Law Number 6 of 2023, has substantially reshaped the criminal-policy landscape governing Law Number 18 of 2013 on the Prevention and Eradication of Forest Destruction (P3H Law). This study aims to examine the reformulation of illegal-logging criminal policy after the Job Creation Law and to evaluate its coherence with the constitutional obligation to protect the environment. The research employs a doctrinal legal method, combining statutory, conceptual, and case-based approaches, supported by content analysis of P3H Law provisions amended by the Job Creation Law and by policy documents issued between 2020 and 2026. The findings show that the amendments have narrowed the operational reach of several core offences, shifted a significant portion of enforcement toward administrative sanctions, and introduced ambiguities that weaken the deterrent function of criminal law, particularly for corporate offenders operating in Kalimantan, Sumatra, and Papua. The study concludes that the current formulation reflects an incomplete transition from a punitive to a restorative model, and that a hybrid accountable-restorative framework, complemented by strict corporate liability, is required to restore proportionality. The academic contribution lies in offering an integrated formulative-applicative-executive matrix that scholars, legislators, and enforcement agencies can use to reconstruct environmental criminal policy in the post-Job-Creation-Law era.

key: the economic consequences of conflict in nigeria
title: The Economic Consequences of Conflict in Nigeria
venue: Journal of Business and Economic Insights
abstract: In Nigeria, the past decade has been characterized by conflict, insecurity, banditry and kidnapping, which have led to significant losses of lives, property, agricultural output, foreign direct investment and economic stability; the losses to GDP are estimated at tens of billions of dollars and outright displacement of millions of Nigerians. This research appraises the effect of conflict on the economic development of Nigeria by studying the relationship between Gross Domestic Product (GDP) and three proxies for conflict and insecurity such as Global Peace Index (GPI), Corruption Perception Index (CPI) and Annual Defence and Security Allocation (ADSA) covering the period of 2015-2026 in Nigeria. The analysis using time series regression model (ARDL) on log-transformed variables shows that there is a strong, positive and statistically significant relationship between ADSA and GDP, and a positive but statistically insignificant relationship between GPI and GDP, whereas the coefficient of CPI is negative but statistically insignificant. The overall level of significance of the model is high, and it accounts for about 90 per cent of the variation in GDP. The results suggest that the influence of defence and security budget on economic performance is related and the relations between the peace levels and perceived corruption are more complex in nature. The study highlights the importance of security investments that can be focused on specific areas, and an overall institutional overhaul, to reduce the economic costs of conflict and promote sustainable economic growth in Nigeria.

key: economic dimension of security in africa
title: Economic Dimension of Security in Africa
venue: Journal of Law and Global Policy
abstract:
This study examines the Economic Dimension of Security in Africa. Africa is endowed with several
rich natural resources like petroleum, gold, diamond, timber, rivers and so forth, and yet Africa
is part of the poorest countries in the world, and the indicators of measuring economic
development are declining in this area. The African region is faced with a myriad of security
challenges, which range from terrorism, political instability, conflicts, infrastructural deficit,
poverty, and unemployment, among others, which have grave implications on the economic
development of the continent. Issues bordering on security are very critical for the material
progress of any polity. Secondary source of data was deployed for the study; it involves the
collection of data from textbooks, journals and seminar papers, among others. The adopted theory
for this study is the Marxian political economy theory. This study found that insecurity has been
the major problem that the continent is still struggling to defeat owing to the increase in terrorism,
conflict, political instability, unemployment, poverty, inequality, infrastructural deficit and other
developmental problems in the region. The study recommended that African leaders should ensure
the provision of a good life for their citizens. Provision of basic social amenities like health care
facilities, schools, electricity and very importantly security will go a long way in ensuring social
stability and economic development.

key: responsibilities of mining companies in the relaxation of mining exports according to indo
title: Responsibilities of Mining Companies in the Relaxation of Mining Exports According to Indonesian Positive Law
abstract: This study aims to analyze the regulation of export relaxation of mining products in Indonesian positive law and examine the form of responsibility of mining companies in implementing this policy. This study uses a normative legal method with a statutory approach, which systematically examines primary and secondary legal materials. The results show that export relaxation is a dispensative and transitional administrative policy, which provides relaxation of the obligation to process and refine mining products. However, this policy creates normative ambiguity because it has the potential to conflict with imperative legal norms, thus impacting legal certainty and regulatory consistency. Mining companies' responsibilities under export relaxation remain fully attached, encompassing administrative, civil, and criminal responsibilities. Relaxation does not eliminate the company's legal obligations, but only provides limited leniency in their implementation. The implications of the relaxation policy indicate a potential weakening of the enforcement of legal obligations, particularly regarding downstreaming, environmental protection, and state revenue. Therefore, strengthening regulations, supervision, and law enforcement is needed to ensure that the relaxation policy remains within the corridor of the principles of the rule of law and in line with the goal of managing natural resources for the greatest prosperity of the people.

key: appraising the implication of book piracy on national development in nigeria
title: Appraising the implication of book piracy on national development in Nigeria
abstract: Development is a progressive process of change and transformation through which a nation enhances the quality of life of its citizens, making it more efficient and desirable. No nation can afford to neglect this vital aspect of national growth. National development, therefore, facilitates a reduction in poverty, unemployment, insecurity of lives and property, corruption, inequality and some other indicators achievable through national development. However, piracy in all its forms has become a major threat to the economic well-being of Nigeria. This problem is not peculiar to Nigeria alone but affects many nations around the world, including developed countries. Piracy is a criminal act that undermines the intellectual property industry in Nigeria and poses serious risks to education, government, and society at large. This paper therefore examines the concept of national development, the nature and forms of piracy, and its implications for national development. These implications include low levels of economic growth, job losses and unemployment, tax evasion, discouragement of foreign trade and tourism, and the proliferation of counterfeit products. The paper concludes by proposing possible ways forward, such as providing grants to intellectual property industries, enforcing relevant laws and prosecuting offenders, generating employment, and promoting intellectual property literacy among creative individuals and the general public

key: the global scale of gold precious mineral and metal crime
title: The global scale of gold, precious mineral and metal crime
abstract: The illegal trafficking, theft and trade in precious metals is a widespread global problem. Illicit precious metals may become legitimized and enter the supply chain usually at a different geographical location to their origin. The beneficiaries are often well‐organized syndicates, criminal gangs, cartels or terrorist organizations. These crimes involve precious metals such as gold and platinum group metals (PGM), and take place at all stages in the supply chain including exploration, mining, processing, transportation, storage, smelting, refining and commodities trading. Minerals and precious metals can have inherent variability in terms of their physical, chemical (e.g. isotope ratios), morphological (surface), textural and mineralogical characteristics. This variability can be attributed to a number of factors including, for example, their geological origin, post mining mineral processing, beneficiation or the blending of different ore or processing streams. Methods are now available (or being developed) to enable provenance determination and to identify the geographical location or geological origin from where a mineral or metal sample was derived or refined. These can also be used to verify whether or not a mineral originated from an illegal or conflict source or from a mine or processing plant aligned with criminal activities. These methods aid traceability, facilitating the systematic recording and tracking of precious minerals and metals as they move through the supply chain from the mine to the refiner and finally to the market.

key: the impact of organized crime on climate change in nigeria an exploratory study
title: The Impact of Organized Crime on Climate Change in Nigeria: An Exploratory Study
venue: Journal of Law and Global Policy
abstract:
This exploratory study examines the intricate relationship between organized crime and climate
change in Nigeria, a nation highly vulnerable to environmental degradation. Organized criminal
activities such as illegal logging, oil theft, illegal mining, and wildlife trafficking operate within
weak governance structures, exploiting systemic vulnerabilities to sustain their operations. These
illicit activities significantly contribute to environmental harm by accelerating deforestation,
water pollution, and greenhouse gas emissions, thereby exacerbating climate change impacts. The
study employs a qualitative research approach, analyzing secondary data from government
reports, environmental audits, and international organizations spanning 2013 to 2024. Findings
reveal a persistent upward trend in illegal logging, oil spills, and emissions, closely linked to
organized criminal enterprises. Theoretical frameworks such as environmental criminology and
resource curse theory elucidate how systemic weaknesses, corruption, and socio-economic
disparities facilitate these crimes. Empirical evidence underscores that organized crime not only
undermines Nigeria’s environmental sustainability but also hampers climate resilience efforts.
Addressing these challenges requires integrated strategies encompassing law enforcement,
community engagement, and policy reforms aimed at strengthening institutional capacity and
disrupting illicit networks. This study highlights the urgent need for targeted interventions to
mitigate the compounded effects of organized crime on Nigeria’s climate stability and sustainable
development goals.

key: operationalising the ultimum remedium principle in indonesian mining law administrative sa
title: Operationalising the Ultimum Remedium Principle in Indonesian Mining Law: Administrative Sanctions, Mining Work Plan and Budget Compliance, and Criminal Enforcement Thresholds
abstract: This study examines how the Ultimum Remedium principle is operationalised in Indonesian mining law enforcement, particularly with respect to administrative sanctions, compliance with the mining Work Plan and Budget (Rencana Kerja dan Anggaran Biaya, RKAB), environmental restoration, and criminal enforcement thresholds. Although the principle is widely recognised as requiring the use of criminal law as a last resort, its practical application in the mining sector remains unclear. This study adopts a socio-legal research design combining semi-structured interviews, questionnaire data, regulatory review, and comparative legal analysis. The empirical data consist of interviews with 24 informants and questionnaire responses from 68 respondents representing government officials, mining company representatives, civil society organisations, and affected communities. The comparative analysis examines selected materials on mining and environmental enforcement from Australia, Canada, Chile, and Indonesia. The findings show that stakeholders generally accept the Ultimum Remedium principle, but they attach different operational meanings to it. Government officials frame it as a proportional enforcement procedure, mining companies associate it with legal certainty, civil society organisations emphasise accountability, and affected communities evaluate it through environmental restoration outcomes. The PT GMS case further illustrates weak sequencing between RKAB-related non-compliance, administrative correction, restoration obligations, and possible criminal escalation. Comparative legal findings indicate that Australia, Canada, and Chile situate punitive enforcement within broader systems of compliance supervision, administrative correction, restoration, and documented escalation mechanisms. The study implies that Indonesian mining enforcement requires a staged but flexible model that distinguishes correctable administrative non-compliance from serious, repeated, fraudulent, corrupt, obstructive, or environmentally harmful conduct. The originality of this study lies in its integration of stakeholder perceptions, RKAB compliance, an illustrative mining case, and comparative enforcement models to operationalise Ultimum Remedium as an institutional sequencing framework rather than merely a criminal law doctrine.

key: corruption and national development in nigeria 1999 2024
title: Corruption and National Development in Nigeria: 1999 - 2024
venue: JOURNAL OF POLITICAL SCIENCE AND LEADERSHIP RESEARCH
abstract:
Corruption remains a persistent global challenge and a major obstacle to national development 
in Nigeria. Despite repeated efforts by successive civilian and military governments and the 
establishment of anti-corruption institutions, corruption continues to be deeply embedded in the 
country’s political and administrative structures. This study examined the effects of corruption 
on Nigeria’s national development and the consequences it has produced for the country. The 
study was anchored on the Theory of Prebendalism and adopted a qualitative approach based 
entirely on secondary sources, including academic journals, government reports, official 
statistics, newspaper articles, historical records, and credible internet sources. The study found 
that corruption has significantly undermined Nigeria’s economic growth and sustainable 
development, particularly since the return to democratic governance in 1999. Persistent 
challenges such as lack of political will, weak accountability, limited transparency, electoral 
malpractice, godfatherism, abuse of office, insecurity, and mismanagement of public resources 
have contributed to widespread poverty, unemployment, inequality, inadequate education, and 
poor social infrastructure. Corruption has also negatively affected critical sectors including 
healthcare, education, transportation, electricity, infrastructure, and security, while encouraging 
inefficient resource utilization, weak policy formulation and implementation, misappropriation 
of public funds, and reduced foreign direct investment. The study concludes that corruption 
remains a fundamental threat to Nigeria’s national development and that meaningful progress 
requires stronger political commitment, transparency, accountability, effective institutions, and 
sustained anti-corruption reforms.

key: money laundering proceeds of forestry crimes in the perspective of the national criminal c
title: Money Laundering Proceeds of Forestry Crimes in the Perspective of the National Criminal Code: Follow the Money Approach
venue: International Asia Of Law and Money Laundering (IAML)
abstract: Forestry crimes such as illegal logging are often accompanied by money laundering efforts  through the formal banking system to disguise the origin of the proceeds of crime. The enactment of Law Number 1 of 2023 concerning the National Criminal Code, which integrates money laundering provisions into the general criminal codification, raises academic urgency to examine the relevance of the follow the money approach  to money laundering crimes originating from forestry crimes. This research aims to analyze legal arrangements, the application of the follow the money approach, and the obstacles to law enforcement after the enactment of the National Criminal Code. The research uses a normative juridical method  with a statute approach and a conceptual approach, sourced from primary, secondary, and tertiary legal materials that are analyzed descriptive-analytically. The results of the study show that forestry is still maintained as  a predicate crime in Article 2 paragraph (1) letter w of the TPPU Law and Article 607 paragraph (2) letter w of the National Criminal Code. The follow the money approach  has proven to be effective in tracing the flow of funds from illegal logging, but its implementation is still hampered by sectoral egos, lack of transparency of beneficial ownership, and weak coordination between institutions such as PPATK, MoEF, and the police. It was concluded that the optimization of Article 607 and Article 608 of the National Criminal Code requires harmonious derivative regulations, strengthening the capacity of investigators, and institutional synergy so that the eradication of money laundering from forestry crimes runs effectively and sustainably.

key: a criminalistic model of economic crimes investigation in the housing and utilities sector
title:
A CRIMINALISTIC MODEL OF ECONOMIC CRIMES INVESTIGATION 
IN THE HOUSING AND UTILITIES SECTOR: ALGORITHMIZATION 
OF INVESTIGATIVE ACTIONS AND SPECIFICS OF PROOF
venue: Bulletin of the Institute of Law of the Bashkir State University
abstract: The relevance of this study lies in the fact that economic crimes in the housing and utilities sector are characterized by great secrecy and a complex structure of implementation. The embezzlement of budget funds or residents’ payments is disguised as civil law transactions. The scientific novelty consists in the creation of a criminalistic approach to conducting an investigation that combines criminal procedures with the special features of the housing and utilities industry, the specifics of electronic trace formation and the tactics of deferred prosecution. The purpose of the article is to create a scientifically grounded typical algorithm for conducting investigative actions to detect a fictitious transaction and determine the actual route of movement of stolen property. The following methods are used in developing this algorithm: systemic-structural analysis of judicial and investigative practice materials, comparative legal analysis (study of norms), modeling of investigative action tactics to enhance their effectiveness in solving emerging tactical tasks. The empirical basis of the study comprised data from criminal cases concerning the theft of subsidies and thefts from homeowners during the period 2019–2026, on the basis of which an assessment of the dynamics of these types of crimes was made. Results: it is established that the effectiveness of proof depends on adherence to a certain logic of the inquiry process: it must begin with the collection of valuable documents and end with the systematization of materials by types of real estate objects and counterparties. When conducting the procedure of seizing electronic information, the participation of a specialist is required due to the automation of accounting. It is tactically advisable to bring charges only when an evidentiary base exists. This tactic makes it possible to exclude opposition from persons who do not want to establish the circumstances of the crime committed. Conclusions: the proposed investigation model makes it possible to uncover the document’s forgery by analyzing their metadata and requisites; the need to apply a set of economic and construction and technical expertise is conditioned by the fact that they mutually complement each other to establish the absence of counter-performance of obligations (financial data contradict technical data). Compliance with this scientifically grounded procedure ensures the independence of the investigator’s work, its expediency, prevents the loss of evidence and allows for comprehensive collection and analysis of all obtained information having evidentiary value.

key: comparative study of gold vs gold etfs during geopolitical crisis
title: Comparative study of Gold vs Gold ETF’s during geopolitical crisis
abstract: The tradition in gold is that it serves as a safe haven in times of financial and geopolitical crisis. The latest trend is the Gold Exchange Traded Fund (Gold ETFs) as an alternative investment vehicle which follows the physical gold prices, however, it is differentiated by the liquidity, transparency and convenience of investing. The paper compares the performance, risk-return profile and market efficiency of physical gold, and Gold ETFs, in both the stable and crisis periods between the period 2021 and 2023. The two periods are analysed, pre-crisis period (2021-2022) and the period of geopolitical crisis (2022-2025) connected with the war in Russia and Ukraine. This paper evaluates the validity of gold ETFs to the price of physical gold and characteristics of a safe haven in the times of geopolitical uncertainty, using risk-adjusted performance ratios of the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM) and correlation and regression analysis based on an Efficient Market Hypothesis (EMH). The result of this research will offer information to the investors, regulators and other financial institutions on the hedging ability and efficiency of Gold ETFs over time or whether the property of safe haven does actually anticipate higher returns.

key: differentiated geography of insecurity related agricultural losses in atacora alibori and
title: DIFFERENTIATED GEOGRAPHY OF INSECURITY-RELATED AGRICULTURAL LOSSES IN ATACORA, ALIBORI AND BORGOU (NORTHERN BENIN)
venue: World Journal of Advanced Research and Reviews
abstract: Armed violence spreading from the Sahel since 2021 has reached the farming systems of northern Benin, but we know little about where agricultural losses are heaviest and why. This study measures them at household level in three departments. A multisectoral survey interviewed 350 households in Alibori (116), Atacora (110) and Borgou (124) between 29 August and 4 September 2026: hosts, internally displaced persons (IDPs) and refugees. Fourteen binary indicators covering production, land, productive capital and markets were averaged into an agricultural loss index (ALI) running from 0 to 1. The index is 0.413 in Borgou, against 0.297 in Alibori and 0.297 in Atacora, and the average household reports 4.6 of the 14 losses. The gap is driven by land dispossession (45% of households in Borgou, 12% in Atacora and 7% in Alibori), by fields destroyed during violence and by productive assets lost. The share of households with an index above 0.5 is 35.5% in Borgou against 6.9% in Alibori and 10.0% in Atacora (χ² = 40.1, p < 0.001). Market disruption is more evenly spread. Within departments, Kalalé stands out, and mean ALI is higher for refugees (0.383) than for hosts (0.288). A Kitagawa decomposition shows that 91% of the Borgou–Alibori gap comes from differences within status groups and only 9% from the mix of statuses. Territory matters more than the legal situation of the household. Responses should therefore be designed by commune and by type of loss: land security in Kalalé, livestock and equipment replacement, and market support in the departments where it is the main loss.

key: money laundering from gambling in the perspective of the national criminal code criminal p
title: Money Laundering from Gambling in the Perspective of the National Criminal Code: Criminal Policy on Economic Crimes
venue: International Asia Of Law and Money Laundering (IAML)
abstract: This article analyzes the legal construction of money laundering from gambling in the perspective  of the National Criminal Code and the criminal policies built against these economic crimes. The purpose of this study is to examine the synchronization of norms between  the National Criminal Code and the Money Laundering Law, as well as evaluate the effectiveness of its criminal policies. The research uses normative legal methods  with a statutory and conceptual approach, sourced from primary legal materials in the form of two main regulations and secondary legal materials in the form of previous scientific journals. The results of the study show that gambling has been explicitly categorized as  a predicate crime in both regulations, so that the existing norms are textually harmonious. However, the effectiveness of its enforcement is still constrained because criminal policies tend to be reactive, oriented towards penal strategies  only, and have not yet reached new modus operandi and transnational character of this crime. The research recommends strengthening integrative criminal policies, combining penal and non-penal strategies, accompanied by strengthening cross-border legal cooperation so that the prevention of money laundering from gambling can be more responsive to the dynamics of digital-based economic crimes in Indonesia.

key: legislative support for regulating social impacts of the extractive industry
title: Legislative support for regulating social impacts of the extractive industry
venue: Population and Environment: Challenges and Perspectives - Book of abstracts - zbornik radova
abstract: Resource extraction induces a range of positive (economic progress) and negative impacts at the local, regional and even national level. The most dominant negative aspects include environmental degradation, as well as diverse social & community consequences of the development - forced resettlement, loss of agricultural land, construction of boom towns and company settlements, endangered indigenous rights, impoverishment, human rights abuse, forced and child labour, endangered health, gender dimension, physical cultural resources, and workforce migration. All those harmful consequences are very complex and demanding to direct and mitigate. Development of proper international and national legislation, along with institutional solutions and development planning, plays a crucial role in this regard. This research will analyze the international legislation regulating social impacts of resource extraction, including both hard and soft laws. Further, this will be followed by a critical analysis of the relevant national legislation of the Republic of Serbia, including the key strategies and national laws. The primary goal is to identify current issues and inconsistencies, and to propose improvements that would promote more sustainable and socially responsible development in mining regions. The findings related to Serbia indicate the following: (a) integration of international norms and standards, including the adoption of aquis communautaire, is incomplete; (b) social impacts are briefly acknowledged however without detailed mitigation strategies (a superficial approach); (c) several important strategies are outdated or have been abolished without suitable replacements; and (d) while environmental issues are prioritized, other social impacts are inadequately addressed or inconsistently considered. The introduction of a comprehensive law to regulate mining development would address these hierarchical and horizontal inconsistencies, fill gaps, and incorporate overlooked aspects, such as the social impacts of mining activities.

key: juvenile drops as a specialized criminal segment of modern russian crime
title: Juvenile “Drops” as a Specialized Criminal Segment of Modern Russian Crime
abstract:
The study is devoted to the criminal law assessment of the phenomenon of the involvement of minors in fraudulent schemes using electronic means of payment, which acquired a systemic character in the territory of the Russian Federation in 2023–2025. The urgency of the problem is due to the exponential increase in the number of cases of teenagers being used as “drops” for the transit and legalization of stolen funds through digital payment systems, which generates new victimological risks and requires a rethink of current criminal law norms.
The purpose of the study is to develop the theoretical and legal foundations for optimizing the preventive system for preventing the involvement of minors in digital fraud. The tasks include: identification of the socio‑legal determinants of the phenomenon under study; analysis of gaps and conflicts in the norms of Article 187 of the Criminal Code; assessment of the adequacy of existing criminal law measures; formulation of proposals for improving legislation.
The methodological base consisted of: content analysis of 224 closed Telegram channels specializing in illegal processing operations; legal linguistic expertise of communicative practices involving minors; comparative analysis of domestic and foreign doctrine; study of materials of law enforcement practice.
The analysis of closed Telegram channels revealed the formation of a specialized criminal segment focused on involving minors in schemes for the transit of stolen funds through access to bank cards of the “Junior” category. Key linguistic markers and communicative strategies for recruiting adolescents have been identified, the need for a comprehensive psychological and linguistic expertise in cases of illegal turnover of funds of payments involving minors has been substantiated, and a new type of compulsory educational measures has been proposed — “digital probation control”.

key: implementasi port state measures agreement 2009 dalam penanggulangan illegal fishing studi
title: Implementasi Port State Measures Agreement 2009 dalam Penanggulangan Illegal Fishing : Studi Komparatif Indonesia dan Thailand
venue: SEIKAT: Jurnal Ilmu Sosial, Politik dan Hukum
abstract: Illegal Fishing is a cross-border problem in fisheries management that requires strengthened monitoring of fishing vessels, including through port-based controls. The Port State Measures Agreement (PSMA) 2009 serves as an international legal instrument that strengthens the authority of port States to control access, conduct inspections, exchange information, and take measures against vessels suspected of engaging in Illegal, Unreported and Unregulated (IUU) Fishing. This study aims to analyze the implementation of the PSMA 2009 in combating Illegal Fishing in Indonesia and Thailand and to identify the similarities and differences in its implementation. This study employs a normative juridical method using statutory, conceptual, and comparative approaches. The results show that Indonesia and Thailand have incorporated the PSMA 2009 into their respective national legal frameworks and implemented port access controls, vessel inspections, information exchange, and law enforcement measures. The similarities lie in the use of ports as a mechanism for monitoring foreign fishing vessels, while differences are found in national legal frameworks, institutional mechanisms, supporting monitoring systems, and implementation challenges. These findings highlight the importance of strengthening institutional capacity and coordination to improve the effectiveness of PSMA 2009 implementation.

key: reframing oil pollution as a human rights violation and assessing the adequacy of availabl
title: Reframing Oil Pollution as a Human Rights Violation and Assessing the Adequacy of Available Legal Redress in Nigeria
venue: Journal of Law and Global Policy
abstract:
The petroleum industry has long sustained Nigeria’s economy, contributing significantly to
national revenue and energy supply. However, this growth has come with severe environmental
and human rights costs, particularly in the Niger Delta region. The problem lies in the persistent
degradation of land, water, and quality of air, which undermines fundamental rights such as the
rights to life, health, dignity, livelihood, and a healthy environment, as protected under both
international and regional human rights instruments. This research aims to assess the adequacy
of Nigeria’s legal redress mechanisms in addressing the human rights violations resulting from
oil pollution. As its objective, the paper specifically explores how environmental justice can be
strengthened through state accountability and legal reforms. Adopting a doctrinal methodology,
the research examines relevant statutes, international conventions, and case laws to evaluate the
extent to which the rights of victims are protected and enforced. The findings reveal systematic
failures, including weak enforcement, delayed justice, and lack of corporate accountability. These
shortcomings reflect a broader state failure to meet its positive obligation to protect citizens from
third-party corporate abuses. The research concludes that without serious structural reforms,
environmental harm and its attendant human rights violations will persist. Accordingly, the
establishment of environmental courts, more effective independent regulatory bodies, and greater
community participation in environmental governance are recommended as essential steps toward
accountability and sustainable development.

key: natures contributions to people and ecoprecarity in indias mining landscapes
title: Nature’s Contributions to People and Ecoprecarity in India’s Mining Landscapes
venue: The International Journal of Social Sustainability in Economic, Social, and Cultural Context
abstract: Mining reshapes ecosystems and affects communities that depend on land and forest resources for their survival. This study examines how mining alters human–nature relationships in India’s extractive regions, with a focus on Adivasi communities. It analyzes two documentaries—Agar Wo Desh Banati (2018), on coal mining in Chhattisgarh, and Behind the Glitter: Child Labour in Mica Mining (2023), on mica mining in Jharkhand—using a qualitative thematic approach. The study applies the Nature’s Contributions to People (NCP) framework, together with the concept of ecoprecarity, to examine how environmental disruption is represented and experienced in everyday life. The analysis shows that mining disrupts access to land, forest resources, clean air, water, and cultural relationships with places. These changes are linked to livelihood insecurity, health risks, and intergenerational vulnerability, particularly for women and children. The study argues that extractive development should be understood not only in economic terms but also through its ecological and social consequences for vulnerable communities.

key: two way crimes parallel economies and professional enablers dissecting corruption in the e
title: Two-Way Crimes, Parallel Economies and Professional Enablers: Dissecting Corruption in the EU’s Financial Sector
abstract: The European Union is in the midst of developing an Anti-Corruption Strategy to achieve the multi-part goal of preempting corruption, improving oversight, strengthening enforcement, and reducing the damage corruption causes to public institutions, companies, communities and citizens. To further this undertaking, we have identified areas and sectors that are especially prone to corruption. This entailed a three-step process of identifying a broad list of high-risk areas, narrowing these to six areas for in-depth study, and examining the character, causes and consequences of corruption in these six sectors. One of these areas is the financial sector. A significant portion of corruption in the EU either originates from the financial sector or is inflicted upon it; sometimes the line between perpretator and victim is blurred. As the most serious corruption-related crimes, money laundering and tax evasion involve many types of people and organisations including banks, investment advisors, wealth managers and organised crime groups (OCGs). With the help of professional enablers such as lawyers, notaries, accountants and real estate agents, OGCs have built a “parallel criminal economy” in the EU. This complex and overlapping landscape complicates interdiction, as the epicentre of any particular corrupt act is not always easy to pinpoint.

key: economic relations between mexico and romania trade security and development prospects
title: Economic Relations between Mexico and Romania: Trade, Security, and Development Prospects
venue: Bulletin of "Carol I" National Defence University
abstract: This paper analyzes the economic relations between Romania and Mexico from the twofold perspective of  bilateral trade and economic security, using geoeconomics, understood as the coordinated use of economic and geopolitical instruments to attain security-relevant objectives, as the organizing concept. Drawing on official Romanian, European, and Mexican data, the study shows that trade flows, although modest, follow an upward trajectory, run a strong surplus in Romania’s favor, and are concentrated in processed industrial goods, while questioning how far this structure reflects genuine domestic capacity for geoeconomic actionrather than the behavior of foreign-owned subsidiaries operating in Romania. It argues that the 2026 modernized EU-Mexico Global Agreement and Mexico’s membership in the Pacific Alliance open new channels for deepening these relations, including in defense, where dual-use cooperation is a more realistic avenue than the export of lethal armament. The paper proposes a strategy for increasing Romanian exports of services and technological capabilities in information technology, cybersecurity, and the aerospace industry, by leveraging the nearshoring phenomenon and the complementary position of the two states within their respective trade blocs.

key: economic and social implications of the 2023 petroleum subsidy removal on nigerias develop
title: ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL IMPLICATIONS OF THE 2023 PETROLEUM SUBSIDY REMOVAL ON NIGERIA’S DEVELOPMENT
venue: International Journal of African Research Sustainability Studies
abstract: Recently, the sudden increase in fuel price has often led to protests and social unrest, particularly among the low-income earners in Nigeria. This study therefore, examined the economic and social implications of the 2023 petroleum subsidy removal on Nigeria’s development, identifying the efforts of government toward addressing the issues and challenges of its removal. Expo-Facto research design was adopted, as well as secondary sources of data collection. The data collected were analyzed qualitatively through content analysis. The study is anchored on Social Contract Theory. Essentially, the study established that even when there were positive economic and social implications of petroleum subsidy removal, the negative aspects like (high cost of living, rising inflation, high unemployment rate and poverty margin, perceived public protests, etc.), and limited government efforts such as (inadequate financial support and wage awards, weak Presidential CNG initiative, poor support for businesses or palliatives, food insecurity and poor agricultural interventions, etc.) were significant, therefore, lacked the capacity to address the issues and challenges of its removal in Nigeria. The researchers recommended that the government at all levels should strengthen the policies and programmes to cushion the negative effects of petroleum subsidy removal, and identify the appropriate strategies to address the concerns like (poor investment on refineries, corrupt practices, etc.) against Nigeria’s development.

key: assessment of oil spillage and its control in the oil and gas industry in nigeria
title: Assessment of Oil Spillage and Its Control in the Oil and Gas Industry in Nigeria
venue: IIARD International Journal of Geography and Environmental Management
abstract:
This project set out to examine the compensation of oil spill victims in the Nigerian oil industry.
The compensation of these victims has become clumsy and dark in the wake of oil bunkering,
pipeline vandalism, sabotage, since in the past, oil spill was as a result of the activities of the oil
companies or operators. The object is to discuss who is responsible for payments of compensation
to oil spill victims who are entangled in a political system that lacks legislative and administrative
guidelines and framework that will effectively deal with the issue of petroleum compensations
arising from sabotage, bunkering and even activities of multinational oil companies. Nigeria has
become one of the most petroleum-polluted environments in the world. The impact of the oil spill
include habitat degradation, pollution from gas flaring and these are cumulative and have acted
synergistically with other environmental stresses to impair ecosystems and severely compromise
human livelihoods and health. These unfortunate incidents make the victims individuals and host
community, landowners, pond owners and other property owners to demand compensation. It is
hereby recommended that the Nigerian government should set up oil pollution compensation funds
that will make provision for compensation for oil pollution damage resulting from activities of not
only multi-national oil companies but that of oil thieves, saboteurs and pipeline vandals. More so,

key: laundering of dirty money and cashing in of money the legal side of the phenomena
title: Laundering of “Dirty” Money and Cashing in of Money: The Legal Side of the Phenomena
abstract:
Money is a key element of the financial system of any state that issues banknotes in the status of national currency in order to provide the sphere of economic exchange with reliable means of circulation and payment — legitimate means of payment. By definition, such funds should be used in the legal sector of the economy for the benefit of the state, society and citizens. At the same time, there have always been criminal activities that generate illegal income, which allowed criminals to satisfy their financial needs, develop criminal business, and bribe government officials. Such activities are socially dangerous at all times, as they contradict legal guidelines. This activity is invariably combined with tax evasion. In order to avoid prosecution by regulatory and law enforcement agencies, criminals commit targeted actions to launder and cash out money, form funds of “dirty” money and “black” cash. These funds are actually withdrawn from legal circulation and used in the interests of organized criminal groups. The transnational nature of financial transactions carried out by criminals has necessitated cooperation between States in countering money laundering and the adoption of a set of measures at the national level.
Based on the analysis of scientific publications by domestic and foreign authors, acts of international law and national legislation related to the problem of laundering dirty money and cashing in of money, the author’s vision of the current state of affairs in this area is presented.

key: dynamics and structure of criminal offenses related to illicit drug trafficking legal anal
title: Dynamics and structure of criminal offenses related to illicit drug trafficking: legal analysis for Kazakhstan
abstract: The paper provides a legal and criminological analysis of crimes related to the illicit trafficking of drugs in Kazakhstan. Based on statistical data, regulatory legal acts, and academic research, the main trends in the development of this category of crime are examined. It is established that a significant proportion of offenses consists of acts not related to the sale of narcotic drugs; at the same time, the role of organized groups and digital channels for the distribution of prohibited substances is increasing. Particular attention is paid to distinguishing the elements of crimes provided for in Articles 296 and 297 of the Criminal Code of the Republic of Kazakhstan, as well as to the problems of proving intent to sell and assessing digital evidence. The impact of subordinate regulatory acts, including lists of controlled substances and quantitative criteria for their determination, is analyzed. The importance of judicial clarifications for the uniform application of legislation is demonstrated. It is noted that improving the effectiveness of combating drug-related crime requires a combination of criminal law measures with preventive and rehabilitation activities, as well as consideration of new challenges associated with the digitalization of social relations.

key: blue crime human rights and constitutional governance of indonesian fisheries
title: BLUE CRIME, HUMAN RIGHTS, AND CONSTITUTIONAL GOVERNANCE OF INDONESIAN FISHERIES
abstract: Fisheries crime has moved beyond illegal harvesting and resource mismanagement to become a complex maritime governance problem in which illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing may intersect with forced labour, human trafficking, violence, document fraud, corruption and transnational criminal networks. This article asks how fisheries crime should be reframed as blue crime and what constitutional and human rights obligations arise for Indonesia as an archipelagic state. Using normative legal research, the study analyses international maritime, labour and anti-trafficking instruments, the 1945 Constitution of the Republic of Indonesia, relevant Indonesian legislation and recent fisheries governance regulations, together with policy materials from international organisations. The analysis shows that existing governance remains fragmented across fisheries regulation, labour protection, migration law, criminal enforcement and human rights accountability. Such fragmentation produces legal invisibility, especially for migrant crews working far from ordinary inspection and complaint mechanisms. The article argues that Indonesia should integrate maritime surveillance, fisheries enforcement, labour inspection, victim identification and protection, port-state measures, data sharing, network accountability, supply-chain due diligence and international cooperation. It concludes that a human-rights-based maritime governance model can strengthen constitutional state responsibility by treating fisheries enforcement as an entry point for protecting both marine resources and human dignity. The principal limitation is that the study is doctrinal and conceptual rather than based on field interviews or empirical case data.

key: mapping the discourses on seabed mining in south taranaki
title: Mapping the discourses on seabed mining in South Taranaki
abstract: For over a decade, the proposed seabed mining of the ironsands in South Taranaki Bight has generated sustained opposition from iwi, hapū, local communities, and several environmental NGOs. Despite multiple consent applications, litigation, and iwi assertions that they do not consent, the project has repeatedly returned to, and progressed through, the environmental regulatory system in Aotearoa. Most recently, the seabed mining proposal was advanced through the new fast-tracking process which was introduced by the 2023 elected coalition government[BU1.1][AO1.2]. The application was eventually rejected in a draft decision by the fast-track expert panel in February 2026, after which the mining company (Trans-Tasman Resources) withdrew their application. While existing research has examined legal struggles in the seabed mining litigation history, and examined multiple ontological meanings, narratives, and discourses about seabed mining, less attention has been paid to how parliamentary discourses construct, enable, or constrain dissent in lawmaking. This thesis analyses parliamentary debates on the Taranaki seabed mining with the understanding that dissent is integral to political debates. Through the lens of radical democracy, I map parliamentary discourses on the seabed mining from December 2023 to June 2025. This thesis contributes to Environmental Studies scholarship by critically analysing the discursive parliamentary landscape of the Taranaki ironsands showing how parliamentary debates both reproduce and destabilise colonial neoliberal capitalist logics through postpolitical practices of depoliticisation and repoliticisation.
