key: illegal sand mining
title: Illegal sand mining
abstract: The increasing global demand for sand, largely for construction, far exceeds natural sand supply via weathering. With increased demand has come illegal sand mining, where extraction is unregulated and its environmental impact not managed. This is a complex societal challenge; sand is perceived as freely available, is easily extracted and provides local populations a source of income and also benefits from development. However, the long‐term environmental impact on both the areas mined (e.g. rivers, lakes, coastlines and shallow seas) but also adjoining land areas is significant. In addition, alongside illegal mining there is criminality associated with exploitation of workers and environmental degradation. Globally, the scale of sand mining (both legal and illegal) is poorly quantified and regulated. Geoscience has a critical role to play in both aiding the assessment of the scale of sand mining, its monitoring and regulation but also in looking at how to reduce demand, through aggregate recycling and the increasing use of waste materials to substitute for primary aggregates.

key: analysis of land use detection between 1996 and 2024 in the central district of adiyaman s
title: Analysis of Land Use Detection Between 1996 and 2024 in the Central District of Adiyaman (Southeastern Türkiye)
venue: Bilge International Journal of Science and Technology Research
abstract: Land use change detection is critically important for environmental sustainability and resource management. This study investigates at the specifics of the methods used to identify changes in land use, their possible effects on ecosystems, and the causes of the decline in residential areas and rise in building on agricultural land after the February 6 earthquakes. According to the analysis results, it is seen that agricultural lands have decreased by 62.81% from 1996 to 2024. It is seen that there has been a partial increase in construction, especially after the earthquake with a magnitude of Mw 7.7 on February 6, 2023, there has been an increase in flat and bare areas and construction in these regions has increased by over 60%. According to the kappa statistics of land use maps made from satellite images of 1996, 2011 and 2024, the analysis results were calculated as 0.83, 0.82 and 0.89, respectively.

key: population growth and environmental impacts of changing land use and landcover in the fcc
title: Population Growth and Environmental Impacts of Changing Land use And Landcover in the FCC, Abuja, Nigeria
venue: IIARD International Journal of Geography and Environmental Management
abstract:
This study examined the trend in population growth in the Federal Capital City between 1994 and 
2024, as well as the environmental impacts of changing land use and landcover (LULC). 
Population datasets of the study area were acquired from the National Population Commission 
(NPC) and used to examine population trend in the last thirty (30) years using quantitative 
techniques. Questionnaire was used to elicit the perceived environmental impact of changing 
LULC in the the study area. The study established that FCC in 1994 had a population of 125,125 
people with 11.55% at the growth rate of 3.68%. In 2004 the population was 198,866 at the rate 
of 3.70% with a change of 73,741 people representing 20.76%. In 2014 at the rate of 3.74%, the 
population was 299,991 people with an increase of 101,125 people representing 31.32% growth. 
Lastly, in 2024 at the growth rate of 3.75%, the population increased to 458,884people with 
increase of 158,893 people representing 47.91%. The study further established climate change, 
Biodiversity loss, altered hydrological cycles, soil degradation and pollution as the major 
environmental impact of LULC change as a result of urbanization processes. The study therefore 
recommended; introduction and further expansion of family planning policies to control birth rate, 
incorporate the use of remote sensing and GIS in its entire sectors to enhance data sharing and 
monitoring and planning for a better and sustainable development. In addition, incorporating the 
use of geo-tech analysis (remote sensing and GIS) in its entire sectors to enhance data sharing 
and monitoring of a better and sustainable development is recommended. There should also be a 
strict adherence to land use control measures in order to strike a balance between economic 
development and eco-system conservation, constantly monitor land developments activities; to 
check land resource degradation and improving management through involvement of local 
communities.

key: environmental and social impacts of deforestation from palm oil cultivation mining and log
title: Environmental and Social Impacts of Deforestation from Palm Oil Cultivation, Mining, and Logging in Indonesia (20102025): A Systematic Literature Review
abstract: Deforestation in Indonesia is a major environmental and social challenge that is rapidly increasing, driven by palm oil plantations, mining, and logging. However, the existing literature remains fragmented and focuses on single drivers or regions. There are limited systematic literature reviews that have integrated both environmental and social impacts across all three drivers for the 2010-2025 period. This study analyzes and synthesizes that literature, aligned with Indonesia's major forest governance reforms. The systematic literature review followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines. A search of the Scopus database identified 3,131 records, from which 191 studies met the eligibility and methodological quality criteria for analysis. The results indicate that Indonesia has lost an estimated 9.75 million ha of primary forest between 2010 and 2022. The other environmental impacts include carbon emissions from the forestry and agriculture sectors, which contribute about 73-75% of total national greenhouse gas emissions. Social impacts include land conflicts in nearly 20,000 villages, the displacement of up to 100,000 indigenous Papuans, and a 37-57% household income decline following land transfer. This study suggests the implementation of sustainable forest management and an inclusive decision-making process for indigenous people to address the root causes of deforestation and balance economic development and environmental conservation.

key: coastal sand mining potential and sustainable resource development in akwa ibom state nige
title: Coastal Sand Mining Potential and Sustainable Resource Development in Akwa Ibom State, Nigeria
abstract: Background: This study assessed the sand mining endowment of Akwa Ibom State in order to ascertain its potential for the development of the State within the context of the Blue Economy. However, in order to give more reliable results with greater precision and power, it was necessary to double the sample size of 384 to 768 for the purpose of this study. Objective: The questionnaire was administered to the respondents using the purposive sampling technique. Methods: A total sample size of 384 respondents was obtained using the Godden’s (2004) formula for selecting sample sizes. The relief features of the area were determined using the observation method. For the evaluation of the sand mining sector of the Blue Economy in the study area, the consumer willingness-to-pay (WTP) method in market price approach was employed. Results: The result showed the major sand mining sites as Esin Ufot, Ibaka, Ikot Unyeghe, and Inua Eyet Ikot communities respectively. It also showed that the major potential customers for these resources are builders, civil engineers, Government, schools, households, and companies. The study showed that the present economic valuation of the sand mining sector within the blue economic framework in the study area is economically viable; hence worthy of investment by both government and the private sector. Conclusion: A total of twenty-nine coastal communities with a direct connection to the Atlantic Ocean were selected from the five local government areas of the State.

key: ephemeral and territorialised oil palm trees
title: Ephemeral and Territorialised Oil Palm Trees
abstract: The oil palm agroindustry is advancing over many different territories worldwide, especially in Southeast Asia and South America, with impacts on forests and human and non-human communities. Production has expanded to supply refined palm oil and its derivatives, widely used in the manufacture of processed foods, cosmetics and cleaning products, as well as producing biodiesel. Because of this contemporary market demand, oil palm has become an agent of destruction, leading to critiques and denunciations from environmentalist agencies and civil movements. However, these discourses and actions seldom if ever mention the historical relationship of African and Afro-diasporic societies with the oil palm and remain silent on the colonial past responsible for transforming Central and West Africa into key territories for the production of palm oil for export markets. This is a topic already explored in historiography but so far not by anthropology to any significant degree. Based on ethnographic data, the present article analyses the historicity of the relational universe of oil palm in villages in the Mayombe forest region, showing temporalities and rhythms encompassed by a human-plant relationship. Inspired by this case study, I advance the concepts of ephemeral and territorialised plants, which could be extended to think about other ethnographic contexts.

key: social and environmental effects of land use changes in ijagun ogun state
title: SOCIAL AND ENVIRONMENTAL EFFECTS OF LAND USE CHANGES IN IJAGUN, OGUN STATE
abstract:
Land use changes come with their social and environmental consequences. Rapid land use changes in Ijagun,
a medium-sized settlement in Ogun State, Nigeria, is driven, largely, by the expansion of the Tai Solarin
Federal University of Education located in the town. This paper analyzes the growth of Ijagun between the
year 2000, when the University was established, and 2025. It further investigates the social and environmental
effects of the land use changes that have taken place in the town during the period. Data for the study was
collected through satellite imageries and questionnaire administration to a purposively selected sample of 200
Ijagun residents. Using the supervised maximum likelihood classification technique, the Landsat imageries
were analyzed to extract land use classes and for change detection. The social and environmental effects were
extracted from the questionnaire responses and analyzed quantitatively. Findings reveal that built-up areas
increased markedly by 417% from 0.70 km² in 2000 while vegetal cover decreased from 5.23km2
(76.4% of the land cover) to 3.11 km² in 2025. Major social effects of the land use changes identified were population
congestion and housing shortages, increased vehicular traffic and cost of living, increased rent, social vices
and crime, and increased opportunities for income diversification. The environmental effects were waste
management problem, water shortages, noise and air pollution, erosion and loss of farmlands. While land use
change reflects modernization and growth in Ijagun, the negative effects of the change underscore the urgent
need for effective planning, environmental management, and infrastructural development.

key: mining linked livelihoods institutional constraints and community resilience in selected m
title: Mining-Linked Livelihoods, Institutional Constraints and Community Resilience in Selected Mining-Affected Settlements of Jos South L.G.A., Plateau State, Nigeria
venue: International Journal of Transdisciplinary Research and Perspectives
abstract: Artisanal and Small-scale Mining (ASM) provides important livelihood opportunities in mining affected communities but may simultaneously weaken the environmental, institutional and adaptive foundations required for long term resilience. This study examined mining linked livelihoods and community resilience among 100 adults in selected mining affected settlements of Jos South L.G.A., Plateau State, Nigeria. Data collected using KoboCollect were analysed through descriptive statistics, a five-component formative Community Resilience Index (CRI), internal consistency diagnostics, exploratory factor analysis, group comparisons, spatial analysis and Heteroskedasticity Consistent (HC3) multivariable regression. 80% of respondents recognised an active or abandoned mining site near their communities, 71% reported living within 1Km of mining activity and 41% reported household involvement in mining. The overall CRI was 1.99 (SD = 0.34; 95% CI = 1.92 – 2.06), with 95% of respondents classified within the study defined low or very low resilience bands. Institutional Support recorded the lowest component mean (1.32), followed by Perceived Environmental Condition (1.96), Adaptive Capacity (1.97), Social Resources (2.16) and Economic Resources (2.55). Component Omega Coefficients ranged from 0.49 to 0.94, while Exploratory Factor Analysis retained four factors, supporting interpretation of the CRI as a multidimensional formative composite rather than a single latent construct. Household mining involvement was not significantly associated with overall CRI, although mining involved households reported significantly lower Institutional Support. Proximity within 1Km was also not significantly associated with overall CRI in the Bivariate Analysis. Although proximity became significant in the adjusted model, this association disappeared when perceived environmental condition were excluded from the composite. Rural residence were associated with lower resilience, whereas longer residence duration was positively associated with CRI. The findings reveal a livelihood resilience paradox in which mining related earning opportunities coexist with weak institutional support, limited financial resources, environmental stress and constrained adaptive capacity. Strengthening local governance, technical services, environmental rehabilitation, access to finance and realistic livelihood diversification is therefore essential for building durable resilience in mining affected communities.

key: analysis of fire trends and losses in vietnam during 20212025
title: Analysis of Fire Trends and Losses in Vietnam During 2021–2025
venue: Global Journal of Education, Finance and Management
abstract: Against the backdrop of rapid urbanization and economic development in Vietnam, fires continue to cause substantial human and property losses. This study analyzes trends and the magnitude of fire-related losses in Vietnam during 2021–2025 using annual secondary data on fire incidents, fatalities, injuries, and property damage. Descriptive statistics and a linear time-trend regression are employed. Over the five-year period, 14,689 fire incidents were recorded, resulting in 531 fatalities, 512 injuries, and estimated property damage of VND 3,330.727 billion. Fire incidence fluctuated markedly, rising from 1,741 incidents in 2022 to 4,112 in 2024 before declining to 3,151 in 2025. The estimated regression is Ŷ = 1,682.9 + 418.3t, with R² = 0.488, adjusted R² = 0.317, and p = 0.190 for the time coefficient. Although the estimated time coefficient is positive, the evidence is insufficient to establish a statistically significant linear trend over the study period. Given that the series contains only five annual observations, the regression is interpreted as exploratory rather than predictive. The findings support further standardization of fire statistics, stronger risk-prevention and infrastructure measures, and greater use of information technology in fire prevention, firefighting, and rescue management.

key: quantifying the environmental impact of artisanal and smallscale mining an integrated appr
title: Quantifying the Environmental Impact of Artisanal and Small‐Scale Mining: An Integrated Approach for Sustainable Development Insights
abstract:
Artisanal and small‐scale mining (ASM) provides livelihoods for over 44.5 million people globally, yet its largely unregulated nature causes severe environmental degradation in host communities. In Nigeria, where ASM accounts for over 90% of solid mineral production, the sector increasingly encroaches on agricultural land. Despite growing recognition of ASM's environmental impacts across West Africa, no study has yet applied the novel SDGSAT‐1 satellite purpose‐built for SDG monitoring at 10 m resolution to quantify ASM land degradation in Nigeria, and few studies simultaneously integrate multi‐sensor remote sensing, in‐situ soil contamination assessment, and hydrological transport modelling within a single integrated framework. This study addresses that gap. This study integrates SDGSAT‐1 Multispectral Imager and Landsat 9 imagery (both acquired 12 January 2024) with field‐based soil sampling (November 2023, dry season) and GIS hydrological modelling for Igbojaiye community, Oyo State, Nigeria. Eight vegetation, water and soil indices (NDVI, EVI, SAVI, TSAVI, TVI, NDWI, BSI) and Land Surface Temperature were derived from satellite imagery. Soil samples from eight mining‐affected points and four undisturbed control points were analyzed for physicochemical properties and heavy metals (Fe, Pb, Zn) using Atomic Absorption Spectrometry. Contamination Factor, Geoaccumulation Index, Pollution Load Index, and a Potential Ecological Risk Index were computed. A Digital Elevation Model was used to delineate contaminant transport pathways. ASM‐affected areas exhibited severe vegetation loss (68% of land within 500 m of mining pits classified as Degraded; mean NDVI −0.08 vs. +0.18 in control areas) and elevated Land Surface Temperature (mean 35.2°C ± 1.3°C vs. 28.9°C ± 0.8°C in controls). Mining soils showed markedly degraded physicochemical properties (organic carbon 4× lower, moisture 5× lower, pH more acidic). Lead exhibited very high contamination (mean Contamination Factor 10.0; Geoaccumulation Index Class 3: moderately to heavily contaminated) with a statistically significant distance‐decay gradient (
 r
 = −0.60,
 p
 = 0.04). No metal exceeded WHO/FAO soil limits in absolute terms. Hydrological modelling identified direct flow pathways from mining pits to downstream farmland and waterbodies. ASM in Igbojaiye initiates a cascade of compounding degradation, soil toxicity, microclimatic disruption, and hydrological pollutant dispersal that collectively undermine agricultural productivity and water security, directly impeding SDGs 2, 6, 13, and 15. This study represents one of the first applications of SDGSAT‐1 for ASM monitoring in Nigeria, establishing a replicable multi‐sensor framework for evidence‐based environmental governance of ASM in data‐scarce sub‐Saharan African contexts. Remediation priorities include sediment traps at mining pit outflows, phytoremediation with native metal‐tolerant species, and satellite‐based biannual monitoring protocols.

key: challenges of goronyo dam in the agricultural activities in sokoto state 1984 2025 from hi
title: Challenges of Goronyo Dam in the Agricultural Activities in Sokoto State 1984 -2025: From Historical Perspectives
venue: African Journal of History and Archaeology
abstract:
Although the challenges encountered due to the Goronyo Dam disaster have caused agricultural 
backwardness, socio-economic and environmental effects in the area of study are worthy of 
discussion, therefore, this paper seeks to examine the nature and magnitude of the soil erosion, 
flooding, among others which is the major factor in this content. Also, identify the real causes of 
these and a historical review of the challenges of Goronyo Dam in agricultural activities in 
Sokoto State and other Dams as well. The paper has also examined the damages and changes it 
has coursed on vegetation covers, agricultural production water bodies, residential areas, 
infrastructural facilities, and bare surfaces around the river basin in the study area of Sokoto 
State. Hence, most of these challenges concerns have historically been regarded as socio
economic issues associated primarily with direct damages to agricultural products. And 
environment also, the impact of Goronyo dam on the communities and individuals in the area of 
study (Sokoto State) that hinders agricultural development, via socio-economic activities, such 
as gully erosion (Soil erosion), frequent reallocation process, displacement, [farmers disposed of 
their productive farmland) inadequate compensation and destruction of economic trees, health 
hazards (water pollution), and destruction of physical infrastructure (roads and bridges) among 
others have also been analyzed. In other words, the focus of this paper has been the anticipated, 
emerging challenges, and future prospects of the Goronyo Dam, as well as the way forward for 
agricultural activities in Sokoto State from 1984 to 2025. 
This paper has also explored the challenges of the Goronyo Dam on agricultural activities in 
Sokoto State. It has examined the projected corporate social responsibility efforts of the 
managing agencies toward the host communities and the state at large. Various programs and 
projects that have been executed by federal and state governments to enhance agricultural 
development and improve the livelihoods of the local communities have also been analyzed. The 
paper has discussed socio-economic contributions such as employment opportunities, income 
generation, infrastructure development, and the potential boost in agricultural productivity. 
Furthermore, seasonal population growth driven by migration for marketing and commerce in 
the dam area has been highlighted as part of the dam’s broader economic influence.Despite its projected benefits, the paper has investigated anticipated challenges associated with 
the Goronyo Dam, particularly those arising from flooding disasters. These will include threats 
to agricultural productivity and adverse environmental impacts. The paper has sought to 
understand the causes and scale of these flooding events, tracing the historical and 
environmental roots of these problems. Attention has been paid to the damages on vegetation 
cover, crop fields, residential zones, water bodies, infrastructure, and surrounding ecosystems in 
the Sokoto River Basin. The study has assess how these challenges, such as soil erosion, forced 
relocation, destruction of farmlands, insufficient compensation, and damage to economic trees 
and infrastructure, and the weakening of transportation links like roads and bridges was 
strategies. Health risks due to water pollution That hinders sustainable agricultural 
development. Also form part of the analysis, helping to shape informed recommendations for 
future mitigation and management

key: assessing the effectiveness of ganga rejuvenation and water conservation schemes in prayag
title: Assessing the Effectiveness of Ganga Rejuvenation and Water Conservation Schemes in Prayagraj City
venue: Integrated Journal for Research in Arts and Humanities
abstract: Prayagraj, at the confluence of the Ganga and the Yamuna, has been the target of national river and water programmes since 1986, yet city-level appraisal of their effectiveness is scarce. This paper reviews 16 central and state schemes launched between 1986 and 2022 and appraises them with an input–output–outcome framework, rating the strength of evidence for each. Reported figures are cross-checked, where possible, against the 2024 compliance report of the U.P. Pollution Control Board (UPPCB) to the National Green Tribunal. Reported fund utilisation is high, averaging 86% across five schemes with Prayagraj-specific figures, and outputs are substantial: ten operational sewage treatment plants (STPs) with 340 MLD of installed capacity, including 72 MLD commissioned under Namami Gange in 2023. Outcomes lag outputs. Sewage generation is 468 MLD, leaving a treatment gap of 128 MLD (27%); 44 of 81 drains remain untapped; the flow reaching STPs is 116% of installed capacity; and ₹129 crore of environmental compensation was imposed on the municipal corporation in 2024. STP effluent met prescribed norms on the sampling day and river water met bathing criteria for BOD and dissolved oxygen, but faecal coliform exceeded the desirable limit at four of five river points. Conservation schemes report outputs such as 200 million litres of rainwater harvested a year, but the reported volumes together equal about 1 MLD, or 0.4% of daily tube-well abstraction, and claimed groundwater improvements of 5–15% lack baselines. Only three of 16 schemes (19%) have outcome evidence that can be independently checked. Reported spending on river-focused programmes is about thirteen times that on groundwater schemes, although groundwater supplies 77% of the city’s piped water. The schemes have been partially effective in building infrastructure but are not yet demonstrably effective in securing outcomes. Outcome-based monitoring, completion of the sewage gap and recharge targets tied to abstraction are recommended.

key: assessing the impacts of anthropogenic activities on land cover change in rwanda case of k
title: Assessing the Impacts of Anthropogenic Activities on Land Cover Change in Rwanda: Case of Kamonyi District
venue: East African Journal of Environment and Natural Resources
abstract: Land use and land cover (LULC) change has become a matter of great concern in Kamonyi District due to increasing population, agricultural activities, and rapid settlement expansion. The current study evaluated the effect of anthropogenic activities on LULC change using a mixed methodology research design comprising remote sensing and a socioeconomic survey. The study involved 100 households selected through appropriate sampling procedures, as well as purposively selected key informants comprising 5 local leaders, 8 land management officers, and 1 District Environmental Officer. The combination of geospatial analysis and socioeconomic information enabled the study to comprehensively assess the patterns, drivers, and effects of human activities on LULC change. Image processing revealed that the percentage of built-up cover increased from 4% to 18%, while forest and natural vegetation decreased between 2015 and 2025. Moreover, croplands remained the dominant land cover. Population pressure (4.36 ± 0.78) and settlement development (4.28 ± 0.83) were the leading anthropogenic activities that triggered LULC change in the study area. Pearson correlation and multiple regression analysis showed a positive relationship between human activities and land cover change. In particular, the study found that settlement development (r = 0.91) and population pressure (r = 0.88) had the greatest impact on LULC change. The study also found that 92% of the variations in built-up and 89% of the variation in vegetation changes were explained by the model. The study recommends sustainable land-use planning and regulation of settlements to promote environmental management in Kamonyi District.

key: land use and land cover dynamics and environmental impacts in garanduwa lagoon weligama sr
title: Land Use and Land Cover Dynamics and Environmental Impacts in Garanduwa Lagoon, Weligama, Sri Lanka (2013–2023)
abstract: Garanduwa Lagoon, located within the Weligama Divisional Secretariat in southern Sri Lanka, is one of the remaining ancient mangrove ecosystems and holds significant ecological and cultural value within the locality. However, increasing human activities and unplanned land use changes have threatened the sustainability of the lagoon ecosystem, yet limited research has been conducted to monitor these changes over time. This study examines land use and land cover changes within a 1 km buffer around the lagoon from 2013 to 2023. Landsat satellite imagery from both years were analyzed using GIS and supervised classification to map and quantify land cover changes. Furthermore, a community survey was conducted among 120 participants residing within the 1 km buffer area surrounding the lagoon. The survey aimed to identify the drivers of land use change and evaluate their associated impacts. The results show a noticeable expansion of commercial land (50% increase) due to tourism expansion. The community survey points to the perceived drivers of change as unregulated tourism development (37%), mangrove removal (29%), and rapid urbanization (21%). Respondents also highlighted key impacts, including overfishing, agricultural runoff, land reclamation, and widespread pollution. They particularly emphasized the dumping of solid waste and plastics into the lagoon. Weak law enforcement, the absence of clear conservation boundaries, and limited community engagement emerged as major governance gaps. These findings underscore an urgent need for integrated land use planning, stronger regulations, and locally led conservation. Without timely action, the lagoon’s ecological health and the livelihoods and cultural heritage it supports face serious and potentially irreversible degradation.

key: environmental toxins and public health crises of illegal mining in nigeria
title: Environmental Toxins and Public Health Crises of Illegal Mining in Nigeria
venue: International journal of research and scientific innovation
abstract: Illegal and artisanal mining has become one of the most consequential drivers of environmental contamination and public health deterioration in Nigeria, particularly across the gold and base metal belts of Zamfara, Niger, Osun, Ebonyi, and Plateau States. This research synthesises recent peer reviewed empirical evidence to examine how unregulated ore processing releases lead, mercury, cadmium, and arsenic into soil, water, and food systems, and how this contamination translates into measurable harm to human health. Drawing on soil and water assays, blood lead level studies, and health risk assessments from mining communities across the country, the chapter traces the pathway from geochemical contamination to clinical outcome, with particular attention to the disproportionate vulnerability of children. It situates this evidence within a rentier state framework, arguing that weak regulatory capacity and elite complicity in illegal mining networks have allowed environmental exposure to persist largely unabated since the 2010 Zamfara lead poisoning disaster. The research further considers the political economy of who benefits from illegal mining and who bears its health costs, before reviewing the record of remediation efforts and the policy reforms needed to break the cycle of contamination. It concludes that Nigeria's illegal mining crisis is fundamentally a public health emergency masquerading as an economic and security problem, and that any durable response must integrate environmental remediation, health surveillance, and formalisation of artisanal mining livelihoods.

key: araguaia river socioeconomic and environmental aspects of riverside municipalities
title: ARAGUAIA RIVER: SOCIOECONOMIC AND ENVIRONMENTAL ASPECTS OF RIVERSIDE MUNICIPALITIES
abstract: Municipalities along the banks of Araguaia River experience a surge in tourist traffic—especially in July—seeking to enjoy its waters, while also engaging in cattle ranching and, more recently, expanding soybean production. In these areas, economic, social, and environmental conditions are largely unfavorable to social well-being. This situation prompted an effort to gain a more detailed understanding of the reality in these municipalities, with the aim of identifying elements for a policy agenda focused on improving the population's living conditions. A literature review was conducted. The study covered municipalities in the states of Goiás and Tocantins. The main issues identified were: small populations—often with declining numbers of inhabitants; low income levels; few formal-sector workers; low Municipal Human Development Index (IDH-M) scores; a negligible contribution of tourism revenue to the local economy; and a heavy reliance on fund transfers from other levels of government. Forested areas have been severely impacted by agricultural expansion, particularly soybean farming. Nevertheless, it is a beautiful river that offers potential for sustainable development.

key: post flood livelihood switching and sand mining an ethnographic study of flood risk feedba
title: Post-Flood Livelihood Switching and sand Mining: An Ethnographic Study of flood-Risk Feedback in Mmiata-Anam, Anambra State Nigeria
venue: Journal of Policy and Development Studies
abstract: Communities living in the riverine areas of Anambra State suffer annual flooding caused by the Omambala and Anambra rivers. The floods of 2022, which were the most severe in Nigeria since 2012, forced more than 650,000 people to leave their homes in six riverine local government areas, one of which is Anambra West, the area in which Mmiata-Anam is situated. This study examined the links between recurring flooding, disrupted livelihoods and sand mining in Mmiata-Anam. The research is grounded in ethnographic observation and a focus group interview with seven farmer-sand miners between the ages of 18 and 40. The findings revealed that following the floods people change the way they earn a living. Sand mining ceases during the flood period and then restarts when the water levels fall, typically from September or October, with the main mining season lasting from December to either June or July. The participants stated that they switch between farming, fishing and mining according to the season. They also noted that the floods refill the areas where sand has been removed. Moreover, they recognised the advantages of flooding, such as improved soil fertility and an increase in fish, yet they did not see a connection between sand mining and riverbank erosion or greater flooding. Applying political ecology and livelihood diversification frameworks, the study concludes that post-flood sand mining is a form of maladaptation driven by the need to generate income. While it may provide a logical explanation for the loss of sand, it could also reduce the river's capacity to protect against future floods. It should be made clear that this research is not concerned with the extent to which sand mining contributes to flooding; instead it focuses on the seasonal nature of the relationship between the disaster and the resource.

key: assessing ecological degradation under multi decadal urban expansion in kolkata india
title: Assessing ecological degradation under multi-decadal urban expansion in Kolkata, India
abstract: Environmental disruption is an inevitable issue faced by top-tier cities worldwide. In the present study, ecological degradation induced by changes in land use and land cover (LULC) within the Kolkata municipal corporation (KMC) was analyzed over the last 30 years (1994–2024). The comprehensive ecological evaluation index (CEEI) and Carbon Storage and ecosystem service values (ESV) were used as indicators of ecological conditions in terms of quality, quantity, and economy. Based on a comparative analysis of Google Earth Engine classifiers, the Random Forest algorithm was found to be the most suitable classifier for a humid-tropical city such as KMC. The LULC transition analysis showed that the built-up area increased by almost 50% from 1994 to 2024, while vegetation, water bodies, and Bare land decreased by 38%, 27%, and 47%, respectively. As a result, indicators of ecological conditions have declined. The minimum CEEI decreased from 0.32 to 0.21 between 1994 and 2024, indicating massive qualitative degradation. The city lost 0.4 million Mg of stored carbon and 3.7 million $USD/year in ESV during the period, at a rate of −0.08 million $USD/year. The results of the cluster analysis show that the Low Cluster, which comprises 75%–90% of compact built-up areas, is steadily spreading from the north towards the south of the city. The Moderate Cluster represents the transitional zone that was vegetation-dominant in the earlier years but transformed into built-up areas in the later years. The Good Cluster, which is a vegetation- and waterbody-dominant cluster that spread across the vegetated lands of southern Kolkata in 1994, shrank towards the Eastern Kolkata Wetlands region in later years. The findings of the study reveal that the Moderate and Good clusters, although already in a declining trend, still have scope for improvement with proper planning to counter the push effects of the low cluster.

key: identifying the trends of international research on forest roads using text mining and co
title:
Identifying the Trends of International Research on Forest Roads
 using Text-Mining and Co-Word Analysis
abstract: Research trends on forest roads, despite their essential role in forest management, have not been systematically synthesized. This study examined spatio-temporal trends in international forest-road research through text mining and co-word analysis of 9,244 SCI(E)-indexed papers from Web of Science using VOSviewer. Publication output increased sharply after 2012, with China (1,588 papers) and the United States (1,534 papers) leading. Co-word analysis identified four major research areas: (i) wildlife habitat fragmentation and landscape connectivity; (ii) soil and hydrological impacts of road operations; (iii) road detection, classification, and safety analysis using machine learning and remote sensing; and (iv) landslide susceptibility assessment near forest roads. The second area dominated in 1991-1999 (about 37%), whereas the fourth became dominant in 2020-2025 (about 30%). The third area exhibited the largest growth, from about 11% to 24%. Although South Korea showed low shares across all areas, domestic research exhibited distinctive characteristics: predominantly site-specific in scale, limited in machine-learning applications, and closely tied to national forest-road expansion policy. These findings provide baseline information for future research on forest roads in South Korea, particularly toward broader-scale analyses and integration of advanced analytical techniques.

key: overview of landslide disaster mitigation knowledge levels among hikers on mount lawu
title: Overview of Landslide Disaster Mitigation Knowledge Levels Among Hikers on Mount Lawu
venue: OVUM : Journal of Midwifery and Health Sciences
abstract: Landslide incidents in Indonesia between 2020 and 2024 totaled 3,720 events nationwide, resulting in 541 fatalities and 1,235 injuries. Public knowledge regarding landslide disasters in Indonesia remains relatively low. This study was motivated by the landslide risk in the Mount Lawu area, which is characterized by steep slopes, high rainfall, and dense hiking activity, thereby increasing hikers' potential exposure to hazards. The aim of this study was to describe the level of landslide disaster mitigation knowledge among hikers on Mount Lawu. This study employed a quantitative descriptive design with an observational method. The sample consisted of 95 respondents selected using accidental sampling among hikers who met the inclusion criteria. The instrument used was a Guttman-scale questionnaire covering indicators of definition, purpose, warning signs, prevention, and landslide countermeasures. The majority of respondents were in the late adolescent category (17–25 years old), male, had a senior high school/vocational school/Islamic senior high school or equivalent educational background, and had prior hiking experience. The majority of respondents' knowledge of landslide disaster mitigation on Mount Lawu was categorized as good.

key: examining urban growth dynamics and sprawl patterns of ludhiana city punjab a geospatial s
title: Examining Urban Growth Dynamics and Sprawl Patterns of Ludhiana City, Punjab: A Geospatial Study
abstract: Accelerated urbanization has led to an increasing demand for land to build new areas of settlement and related infrastructure. This growing demand for land shows an encroachment onto related land uses and other natural areas. Therefore, it is important to critically examine the changing land-use/land-cover (LULC) patterns, particularly in highly urbanizing areas. This study is based on the Local Planning Area of Ludhiana, one of the most urbanized and industrialized cities in the state of Punjab, India. This study is aimed at evaluating changes in LULC over a period of forty-five years using remote sensing and GIS tools. A total of five LULC classes were used for the study: agriculture, built-up areas, forests, barren land and water bodies; and changes in area have been calculated for the years 1979, 1994, 2009 and 2024. The study utilizes the Landsat images, and classification was performed using the maximum likelihood technique with supervised classification using ArcGIS Pro. The study reveals that the area under agriculture was 72.22% in 1979, which dropped to 54.66% in 2024, whereas the area under built-up was 6.86%, which drastically increased to 30.76% by 2024. The other land use classes also witnessed a significant change, but the major transition was from agriculture to built-up, which is 39.08% of the total transition. To assess the urban sprawl, Shannon's entropy has been used. The results of Shannon's entropy revealed that the study area has a high level of urban sprawl, having relative entropy of 0.9773, 0.9729, 0.9691 and 0.9732 for years 1979, 1994, 2009 and 2024, respectively. The study offers insights into the nature of urban growth and sprawl in the Local planning Area of Ludhiana.

key: utilization and valorization of mining tailings through a comprehensive approach in centra
title: Utilization and Valorization of Mining Tailings Through a Comprehensive Approach in Central Peru
authors: Roi César De La Cruz Castillo
abstract: To determine the reprocessing potential of mining liabilities, a comprehensive evaluation of the tailings deposit at the former Halcón mining unit in central Peru was conducted. Direct and indirect methods were employed, including geophysical surveys, sampling through six drill holes reaching depths of up to 9.62 m, textural analysis, mineralogical characterization using optical microscopy, SEM, XRD, and reflectance spectroscopy, and ICP-MS chemical analysis, complemented by geostatistical modeling for resource estimation. Geochemical and mineralogical results reveal highly oxidizing and acidic conditions (pH 1.83–4.91) along with significant concentrations of Zn (5.46%), Pb (1.58%), Cu (1.29%), Ag (244 ppm), and Au (3.6 ppm). These economic minerals predominate in fine-grained fractions, which exhibit high degrees of liberation and therefore favor metallurgical recovery. Geostatistical modeling estimated a total tailings tonnage of 87,642 tons, highlighting zones with high localized economic potential, particularly for Zn and Ag. Considering specific recovery scenarios, penalties, operational costs, and metal prices, a preliminary economic benefit of approximately USD 11.36 million was estimated. This pioneering study demonstrates the feasibility of converting environmental liabilities into economic assets through strategic reprocessing initiatives, providing a robust model for the valorization of mine tailings within the framework of the South American circular economy.

key: implication of mining activities to socio economic transformation among communities adjace
title: Implication of Mining Activities to Socio-economic Transformation Among Communities Adjacent to Mining Centers in Tanzania
venue: Journal of Environmental and Development Studies
abstract: The Socio-economic transformation of communities adjacent to mines is indeterminate, necessitating this study amid the rapid expansion of mining activities in mineral-endowed areas. This paper identified the contribution of mining activities to the socio-economic transformation of people living adjacent to mining sites in Tanzania, specifically in Patamela, Saza, Maleza, and Mbangala villages of Songwe District in Songwe Region. A cross-sectional design and mixed-methods approach were adopted, while random and purposive sampling were used. Household questionnaires, key informant interviews, and observation were used to obtain data, while SPSS and content analysis were used for qualitative and quantitative data analysis, respectively. Communities adjacent to mining centers have generated income, replaced low-quality housing, and met livelihood needs. Through mining activities, households have also acquired natural, financial, and human capital. Nevertheless, environmental pollution, disease outbreaks, damage to houses and infrastructure, and soil and land degradation are more prevalent in these areas. To improve livelihood transformation in these mining-adjacent communities, it is essential to provide financial education, establish environmental restoration programs, facilitate diversified income sources, create local employment and self-employment opportunities, and strengthen local supply chains.

key: multi temporal lulc change and future urban expansion in faridpur municipality bangladesh
title: Multi-Temporal LULC Change and Future Urban Expansion in Faridpur Municipality, Bangladesh: A CA-ANN Based Simulation
abstract: The study examines land use and land cover (LULC) conversions and forecasts future urban growth in Faridpur Municipality, Bangladesh. Despite substantial urbanization in recent years, smaller cities such as Faridpur have been largely absent from LULC studies. Using Landsat data from 2004, 2014, and 2024, the research employed Maximum Likelihood Supervised Classification (MLSC) to identify land cover changes. It used an Artificial Neural Network (ANN) with Cellular Automata (CA) to anticipate LULC trends for 2034, 2044, and 2054. Findings indicate that urbanized areas grew from 2.18% in 2004 to 7.31% in 2024, initially replacing vegetation and cropland, and are projected to expand further to 15.04% by 2054. An R2 of 0.9164 represents a strong statistical fit of the plotted built-up-area trend; however, for greenspace, farmland, and water, such expansion into the projected future is not promising. Geospatial analysis suggests the most developed areas are in the northeast and southwest regions, which offer greater connectivity and are the two growth magnets. Validation of the model consistently showed an accuracy of 92.56%, Kappa of 0.878, Kappa (histogram) of 0.9829, and Kappa (location) of 0.8940, which indicates that the model reproduces the observed spatial pattern reasonably well. Thus, the findings suggest that urban planners need to pay attention to trends in sustainable expansion and in the creation of agricultural space. By conveying practical understandings into growth patterns, it supports policymakers, local authorities, and urban planners in monitoring and predicting future urbanization in Faridpur Municipality.

key: new frontier of expansion and protected areas in the state of amazonas
title: NEW FRONTIER OF EXPANSION AND PROTECTED AREAS IN THE STATE OF AMAZONAS

key: deforestation in nigeria the causes impact and management strategies
title: Deforestation in Nigeria: The Causes, Impact and Management Strategies
venue: Global Journal of Science Frontier Research
abstract: Deforestation is a pressing issue in Nigeria, with significant impacts on both the environment and the people who rely on it. Deforestation in Nigeria is undeniable, and urgent action is needed to address this issue. According to the United Nations, Nigeria has the highest deforestation rate in the world, with an estimated 3.7% of its forest lost every year. Many of our forests are gradually turning into grasslands due to the incessant felling of trees without the planting of new ones. The law in the advanced world, is that you replace every tree you fell with three seedlings of that very specie. However, in Nigeria, those who are into timber business pay for tree seedlings, but are never given to plant as replacement for the trees they fell. Twenty years from now, some wood species may go into extinction in Nigeria. The aim of this study therefore, is to examine some causes of deforestation in Nigeria, its impact on the environment and our economy and to suggest some management strategies. The methods adopted for this study are analytical and phenomenological. The findings of this study are as follows: deforestation is a recognized indicators of environmental degradation and its effects span the macro and micro levels, moving from adverse impacts on the economy to posing danger to human health. Given the inherent benefits of forest resources, which include income and economic growth, they are liable to continuous exploitation. This, without adequate policy restriction can lead to environmental problems that were once prevented by the existence of forests. It is therefore recommended that the government should put in place, poverty reduction programs, which are pivotal in reducing deforestation and degradation of the forest.

key: representasi isu lingkungan dalam cerpen koran indonesia tahun 2023 2025 kajian ekokritik
title: REPRESENTASI ISU LINGKUNGAN DALAM CERPEN KORAN INDONESIA TAHUN 2023-2025: KAJIAN EKOKRITIK GREG GARRARD
venue: LANGUAGE Jurnal Inovasi Pendidikan Bahasa dan Sastra
abstract:
ABSTRACT
This study unravels the articulation of environmental crises in 13 Indonesian newspaper short stories published between 2023 and 2025 through Greg Garrard’s ecocriticism framework. The study aims to describe and analyze the representation of ecological issues based on the tropes of pollution, wilderness, apocalypse, and animals, in order to deconstruct anthropocentric perspectives in literature. The corpus was selected using purposive sampling based on inclusion criteria regarding the sufficiency of contemporary environmental crisis discourses in national and regional print media. Utilizing a descriptive qualitative approach with note-taking techniques and descriptive-interpretive analysis, 28 textual data units were identified, demonstrating the dominance of the apocalypse category with 10 data units (35.7%) manifesting in floods, landslides, abrasion, and extreme droughts. The pollution category comprises 7 data units (25.0%) representing haze exposure and industrial residues, wilderness accounts for 5 data units (17.9%) related to deforestation and forest exploitation, while animals includes 4 data units (14.3%) regarding habitat fragmentation and threats of species extinction. In addition, 2 data units (7.1%) emerged as additional findings depicting mangrove restoration efforts and indigenous area protection. These findings reinforce the position of newspaper short stories as reflective spaces that potentially foster public ecological awareness, while simultaneously enriching the integration of fiction into Indonesian language pedagogy.
ABSTRAK
Kajian ini membongkar artikulasi krisis lingkungan hidup dalam 13 cerpen koran Indonesia terbitan 2023–2025 melalui pisau analisis ecocriticism Greg Garrard. Penelitian bertujuan mendeskripsikan dan membedah representasi isu-isu ekologis berbasis kerangka pollution, wilderness, apocalypse, dan animals, guna meruntuhkan cara pandang antroposentrisme dalam sastra. Korpus dipilih secara purposive sampling berdasarkan kriteria inklusi kecukupan wacana krisis alam kontemporer pada media cetak nasional dan regional. Melalui pendekatan deskriptif kualitatif berbasis teknik simak-catat serta analisis deskriptif-interpretatif, teridentifikasi 28 unit data tekstual yang memperlihatkan dominasi kategori apocalypse sebanyak 10 data (35,7%) berupa manifestasi banjir, longsor, abrasi, dan kekeringan ekstrem. Kategori pollution hadir melalui 7 data (25,0%) berupa paparan kabut asap dan residu industri, wilderness mencakup 5 data (17,9%) terkait deforestasi serta eksploitasi hutan, sedangkan animals memuat 4 data (14,3%) mengenai fragmentasi habitat dan ancaman kepunahan satwa. Di samping itu, terungkap 2 data (7,1%) temuan tambahan berupa gerakan restorasi bakau dan proteksi kawasan adat. Temuan ini mempertegas posisi cerpen koran sebagai ruang reflektif yang berpotensi menumbuhkan kesadaran ekologis publik, sekaligus memperkaya pemanfaatan fiksi dalam pembelajaran Bahasa Indonesia.

key: beyond 2025 surface mine tamnava west field mining basin kolubara western serbia developme
title: Beyond 2025: Surface mine tamnava West field, mining basin Kolubara, Western Serbia: Development of works on mixed levels
abstract: The Kolubara coal basin with its approximately 2.8 billion tons of remaining geological resources and lignite reserves represents an exceptional potential for coal production in Serbia. The aforementioned coal resources represent an important potential for mining production within the EPS. Currently, there are three surface mines in operation - Radljevo, Polje E and Tamnava-Zapadno polje. At the Tamnava-Zapadno polje surface mine, coal mining has been going on for 30 years, starting in 1994. Surface mining is the backbone of the mining production in the Kolubara mining basin, with quantities of mined coal of about 12M t/year.In recent years, open pit mining has left the zone of simple and favorable geological structure and entered an area characterized by significant layering of coal seams and difficult exploitation conditions. For this reason, mining works are designed and carried out on combined levels, where the same excavator digs alternately coal or tailings. Such conditions will last until the end of the century of exploitation at this surface mine.In this work, we deal with the projected parameters and realized indicators of mining production at this mine. We will deal with this issue in the following chapters.

key: by heavy metals in the zone of influence of the nikolaevskaya enrichment plant
title: BY HEAVY METALS IN THE ZONE OF INFLUENCE OF THE NIKOLAEVSKAYA ENRICHMENT PLANT

key: evaluation of land use as drivers of gully erosion in uyo capital city
title: Evaluation of Land Use as Drivers of Gully Erosion in Uyo Capital City
abstract:
Gully erosion poses a critical environmental challenge in urbanizing areas like Uyo Capital City, Nigeria. This study extensively investigated its drivers, focusing on evolving land use types and the perceived effectiveness of government policies using both geospatial and survey data. It surveyed 382 respondents across five gully-prone areas. Demographic data revealed respondents were primarily 25–34 years old (41.10%) and female (46.07%), often educated to secondary or tertiary levels, and either self-employed or unemployed. Geospatial analysis showed significant urban expansion from 2005 to 2024, with built-up areas increasing from 23.34% (7,755.43 ha) to 63.52% (21,849.99 ha), while farmlands, forests, and water bodies decreased. Respondents identified vegetation removal for road construction (Mean = 4.21) and disregard for proper drainage during construction (Mean = 4.15) as major erosion drivers. Multiple linear regression analysis confirmed a significant relationship between land use changes and gully erosion severity (R² = 0.551, F (3, 378) = 154.82, p < 0.001). However, an ANOVA indicated that current government policies and mitigation measures did not significantly mitigate land use drivers triggering gully erosion (F (4, 377) = 0.518, p = 0.722), highlighting an enforcement and implementation gap. This emphasizes the urgent need for robust policy implementation, sustainable land management, improved enforcement of zoning regulations, and community engagement to address the escalating erosion crisis effectively.

Keywords: Geospatial Analysis, Urbanization, Policy Implementation Gap, Environmental Risk Modeling, Sustainable Land Management.

key: urban land use dynamics and changing landscapes in kano nigeria 19502020
title: Urban land-use dynamics and changing landscapes in Kano, Nigeria (1950–2020)
abstract:
Kano is one of the rapidly urbanizing cities of sub-Saharan Africa, characterized by a growing population, sprawling development, and weak planning controls. Understanding the city’s land-use dynamics is vital for its sustainability. This study examines the decadal land-use dynamics of the Municipality, between 1950 and 2020. Using unsupervised classification, topographic sheets, and multi-date satellite imagery, the city’s growth patterns were quantified geospatially. The results show that Kano expanded from 27.50 km
 2
 in 1950 to 355.25 km
 2
 in 2020, an increase of 1,192.73% over 7 decades, and the average annual growth rate of 3.71%. The highest growth was recorded between 1975 and 1990 (72.75 km
 2
 to 162.00 km
 2
 ), with an annual growth rate of 5.53%, while the slowest growth was recorded between 1990 and 2000 (1.66% per year). Corridor-based analysis reveals pronounced variability, with the Kano–Panshekara (5.47%), Kano–Gwarzo (4.95%), and Kano–Dawanau (3.13%) corridors emerging as the fastest-growing axes, while Kano–Hadejia–Nguru (1.52%) and Fanisau (1.08%) corridors record lower growth. The study concludes that transportation development has played a significant role in shaping Kano Municipality’s spatial expansion. It also highlights the need to integrate transport investment with land-use planning, infrastructure provision, and environmental management to promote a more connected, resilient, and sustainable urban system.

key: the potential use of post coal mining land of pt bukit asam ombilin mining unit sawahlunto
title: The potential use of post-coal mining land of PT Bukit Asam Ombilin Mining Unit, Sawahlunto City, West Sumatra, Indonesia, for animal feed production
venue: Journal of Degraded and Mining Lands Management
abstract: Post-mining land in the Ombilin Mining Unit is a state-owned asset managed by PT Bukit Asam (PTBA) and cannot be transferred to private ownership. However, several parties have utilized the land for productive activities without a clear legal basis. Recognizing the economic and ecological benefits, PTBA subsequently granted limited-use rights to livestock farming groups to cultivate forage to support local economic empowerment and environmental restoration. This study was conducted in Sawahlunto City, West Sumatra Province, on the post-coal mining land managed by PTBA's Ombilin Mining Unit. The research objective was to describe the regulatory framework for post-mining land use and to analyze its economic prospects through forage farming. A mixed-methods approach was employed, combining qualitative and quantitative descriptive analyses. Qualitative data were obtained through observation, in-depth interviews, and documentation studies covering aspects of policy, licensing, governance, implementation, monitoring, and evaluation. Quantitative data were collected through a census questionnaire administered to PTBA-assisted farmer groups to assess the feasibility of the forage business using cost, income, and revenue-to-cost (R/C) ratio analysis. The results showed that the regulatory framework for land utilization still lacks legal certainty. Nevertheless, governance mechanisms are well-structured, and the forage business demonstrates economic feasibility, as reflected by a positive R/C ratio. Therefore, the productive utilization of post-mining land represents a sustainable strategy for strengthening the local economy while maintaining the land's ecological functions.

key: biodiversity reporting in the coal mining industry an institutional theory perspective
title: Biodiversity reporting in the coal mining industry: an institutional theory perspective
abstract:
This study is motivated by the progressive loss of biodiversity, the impact of coal mining on it, and the need for companies to report transparently on biodiversity. The study aims to investigate how the largest coal mining companies across major coal-producing regions (Australia, China, India, Indonesia, the EU, and the USA) account for biodiversity in their corporate reports and examines the institutional pressures associated with these reporting practices.
 
 
 
 We adopt an exploratory qualitative design and perform a cross-regional analysis of 28 major coal mining companies from six regions. We apply content analysis to examine biodiversity reporting and employ institutional theory to evaluate the coercive, mimetic, and normative pressures associated with these practices.
 
 
 
 Our findings indicate weak and fragmented biodiversity reporting, with a notable trend towards more comprehensive reporting in Indonesia and India. We identify a pattern of fragmented isomorphism, in which common reporting responses coexist with substantial regional variations associated with differences in institutional pressures across regional contexts.
 
 
 
 We recommend mandatory reporting obligations aligned with recognised voluntary standards, including species- and context-specific indicators to support more substantive biodiversity impact disclosure. We further emphasise the importance of biodiversity expertise in reporting processes and strengthening biodiversity-related competencies in business education. For companies, industry-specific frameworks can support them in identifying context-specific biodiversity impacts and developing science-based, time-bound biodiversity targets.
 
 
 
 The study contributes to biodiversity reporting and institutional theory by identifying fragmented isomorphism within a single high-impact industry, where differences in institutional pressures across regional contexts are associated with non-uniform reporting patterns.

key: evaluation of the spatio temporal dynamics of the fetore sub basin between 1990 and 2020
title: EVALUATION OF THE SPATIO-TEMPORAL DYNAMICS OF THE FÉTORÉ SUB-BASIN BETWEEN 1990 AND 2020
venue: World Journal of Advanced Research and Reviews
abstract:
The Fétoré sub-basin, a tributary of the Konkouré River, is located in the Fouta-Djalon massif, an area known as the "water tower of West Africa." For several decades, this territory has faced increasing pressure from human activities specifically agricultural expansion, land clearing, and urbanization compounded by climate variability. These factors contribute to gradual headwater degradation and disrupt the basin's hydrological functioning.
This study analyzes the spatiotemporal dynamics of land use in the Fétoré sub-basin between 1990 and 2020/2022 to identify key changes and their underlying drivers. The methodology combines basin delineation using a digital elevation model, supervised classification of Landsat satellite imagery, result validation via a confusion matrix and Kappa coefficient, and change analysis using a transition matrix and field surveys.
The results reveal a continuous decline in natural vegetation cover, whereas open forests have expanded significantly, rising from 20.12 % in 1990 to 41.15 % in 2022. Cropland and fallow land, bare rock, and water bodies have also changed. These transformations, driven primarily by population pressure, agricultural expansion, and rainfall variability, exacerbate the hydrological vulnerability of the sub-basin and the Fouta-Djalon headwaters. They highlight the need to implement appropriate integrated management and restoration strategies.

key: assessment of forest cover change in luang prabang province lao p d r
title: Assessment of Forest Cover Change in Luang Prabang Province, Lao P.D.R.
venue: International Journal of Advanced Multidisciplinary Research and Studies
abstract:
Through the development policies of the Lao government, particular attention has been given to the forest sector in order to achieve the objectives of the Forestry Strategy 2020, which was implemented from 2005 to 2020. One of the main goals of this strategy was to increase forest cover to 70 percent by 2020, with the longer-term objective of maintaining or increasing forest cover toward 2035. This research concerns changes in forest cover in Luang Prabang Province, Lao P.D.R. The study aims to assess changes in forest cover over different periods. A quantitative research method was used to describe the characteristics and trends of forest cover changes. The results indicate that forest cover in Luang Prabang Province changed significantly during the period from 2002 to 2010. During this period, forest cover increased by approximately 3.11% per year, indicating significant forest recovery. Approximately 31.10% of the area had strong potential for natural forest regeneration, while the remaining areas required forest restoration and development activities, such as tree planting. During the period from 2010 to 2015, the proportion of primary forest cover increased by approximately 22.34%, representing an average annual increase of 4.47%. In contrast, the proportion of secondary forest cover decreased by approximately 18.95%, equivalent to an average annual decrease of 3.79%.
During the period from 2015 to 2019, forest cover showed an overall negative trend, with tree-cover loss occurring each year in Luang Prabang Province. The years 2016, 2017, and 2019 experienced particularly high levels of forest loss, with losses exceeding 50,000 hectares in each of these years.

key: descriptor participatory mapping of trade in pangolin scales and other wildlife in cameroo
title: Descriptor: Participatory Mapping of Trade in Pangolin Scales and Other Wildlife in Cameroon Dataset (PMTPSOWC)
abstract:
Illegal trade in pangolin scales and other wildlife is a crime affecting the environment imposing diverse harms to people and ecosystems. Cameroon features prominently on lists for illegal trade in pangolins and their parts (e.g., scales), but data remains sparse. Participatory mapping is widely used in data deficient contexts, including illegal wildlife trade. We created a novel spatial dataset containing information about trade in pangolin scales and other wildlife in Cameroon. Data about 16 activities associated with illegal trade was collected using participatory mapping with local community members (n = 190) and subject matter experts (n = 90). The attributes of this dataset can support exploration of inferences or trends associated with illegal scale trade and highlight supply chain characteristics. A total of 44 participatory maps were produced between July 2024 and July 2025, which were scanned, digitized, cleaned, and audited to create the dataset. The processed dataset includes 7138 points, each about one of the 16 pangolin-associated activities. This dataset can be used to explore economic market characteristics of the trade, which have bearing on market resilience, opportunities for disruption, supply chain network structure, risk exposure, and actor specialization.

key: solar parks threat to biodiversity and ecosystem in the thar desert of western rajasthan i
title: Solar Parks: Threat to Biodiversity and Ecosystem in the Thar Desert of Western Rajasthan, India
abstract:
Abstract
India's push to install 500 GW of renewable energy by 2030 has made the Thar Desert of western Rajasthan a major hub for utility-scale solar development. The 2,245 MW Bhadla Solar Park, which covers more than 5,700 hectares, is the most prominent example. Much of this land has been allocated cheaply because state revenue records describe it as unproductive wasteland (banjar), a label that masks its ecological and cultural value. This paper presents findings from field surveys conducted between 2021 and 2024 across Jodhpur, Phalodi, and Jaisalmer districts, combining botanical assessments, key-informant interviews, and focus group discussions with a review of published ecological, wildlife, and legal literature.
The findings show that solar park construction is causing serious and lasting damage to this fragile ecosystem. Mechanical clearing strips away biological soil crusts, releasing windblown dust that reduces panel efficiency by 20 to 35 percent and forces bi-weekly washing using groundwater drawn from non-renewable fossil aquifers. Thousands of mature Khejri trees (Prosopis cineraria), the ecological backbone of the Thar, have been felled at construction sites, with developers paying a legally permitted fine of just Rs. 100 per tree. High-voltage transmission lines running through bird habitats near Pokhran and Ramgarh kill an estimated 84,000 birds each year, including the critically endangered Great Indian Bustard (Ardeotis nigriceps), whose total wild population is now below 150. Sacred community forests known as Orans are being enclosed and cleared without the knowledge or consent of the pastoral communities who have protected them for centuries.
The paper also provides with policy recommendations based on the current situation which include mandatory Environmental Impact Assessments for all solar projects above 1 MW, formal legal protection for Orans, underground transmission cabling within bustard habitats, and a shift toward agrivoltaics and waterless panel-cleaning technology.

key: study of the spatio temporal dynamics of forest cover in eastern cameroon the case of bert
title: Study of the Spatio-temporal Dynamics of Forest Cover in Eastern Cameroon: The Case of Bertoua2
venue: International Social Sciences and Education Journal
abstract:
The forests of Eastern Cameroon, particularly those of Bertoua 2, are increasingly subject to deforestation. This deforestation is leading to a strong trend of rainforest loss, hence the concern of public authorities to address this problem. Faced with such a situation, examining the spatio-temporal evolution of forest cover becomes crucial in order to accelerate the protection and sustainable management of forest resources. This is the purpose of the present study, which focuses on analyzing the evolution of forest cover in Bertoua 2 district and the drivers responsible for this dynamic. The analysis is based on the use of Landsat satellite images acquired from the United States Geological Survey for the years 2000, 2010 and 2025, as well as on fieldwork. The results obtained indicate massive forest losses in Bertoua 2, perceptible by a decrease of- 8.07% in rainforest accompanied by an increase of +2.56 % in agroforestry mosaics between 2000 and 2025; thus showing a significant dynamic in forest cover. This observed dynamic results from several drivers: agriculture, illegal logging, urbanization…Therefore, in order to protect our forest, we propose that an impact assessment for the species and areas most affected by deforestation be carried out by the public authorities each year; in order to measure the impacts of deforestation, anticipate forest losses, and implement measures to avoid or compensate for forest losses. In particular, the restoration of areas that have experienced forest losses, practicing agroforestry, and above all involving the local population in the process of sustainable forest conservation and management. 
Les forêts de l’Est-Cameroun plus particulièrement celles de Bertoua 2 font de plus en plus l’objet de déforestation. Cette déforestation entraine une forte tendance de perte de forêts humides, d’où l’inquiétude des pouvoirs publics de prendre en compte ce problème. Face une telle situation, l’examen sur l’évolution spatio-temporelle du couvert forestier devient judicieux afin d’accélérer la protection et la gestion durable des ressources forestières. C’est l’objet de la présente étude axée sur l’analyse de l’évolution du couvert forestier de l’arrondissement de Bertoua 2 et des moteurs Responsables de cette évolution. Cette analyse repose sur l’exploitation des images satellites Landsat acquises auprès de United States Geological Survey pour les années 2000, 2010 et 2025 ; et sur les travaux de terrain. Les résultats obtenus indiquent des pertes massives de forêts dans Bertoua 2, perceptible par une diminution de -8,07% des forêts humides accompagné par une progression de +2,56% des mosaïques agroforêts entre 2000 et 2025 ; montrant ainsi une dynamique notable au niveau de la couverture forestière. Cette dynamique observée résulte de plusieurs moteurs : l’agriculture, l’exploitation forestier illégal, l’urbanisation... Ainsi afin de protéger nos forêts, nous proposons qu’une étude d’évaluation d’impact pour des espèces et les zones les plus touchées par la déforestation soit faite par les pouvoirs publics chaque année afin de mesurer les impacts de la déforestation ; anticiper les pertes forestières et mettre en place les mesures pour éviter ou compenser les pertes forestières. Notamment la restauration des zones qui ont connu des pertes de forêts, pratiquer l’agroforesterie ; et surtout impliquer les populations locales dans le processus de conservation et gestion durables des forêts.
